text:
Every candidate promises to fix homelessness. One candidate on today's ballot put a date on it.

Steve Hilton's plan (@SteveHiltonx), announced October 17 in San Diego — stated plainly, as a campaign promise, not a result:

· Audit every dollar of homelessness spending. His name for it: Operation Zero Waste.
· Build Homeless Recovery Centers — beds, meals, showers, medical care, drug treatment, job training — with one named person responsible for each resident's path back to stable housing.
· Declare a homelessness emergency to cut the permitting delays.
· Deadlines with teeth: local leaders get until Labor Day 2027. Every encampment in California cleared by December 31, 2027 — and if local government doesn't act, the state steps in.

Why does the audit come first? Because of what the State Auditor already found: California allocated nearly $24 billion over five years, the council in charge stopped tracking the money after 2020–21, and for three of the five big programs reviewed, the state could not say what the money bought.

Hilton's own words: "Leaving people to deteriorate in tents is a disgrace."

Agree with his plan or not, notice the difference: it can be checked. A date either happens or it doesn't. An audit either publishes or it doesn't. That is more than the last decade offered.

Polls close at 8:00 PM.

Should the next governor be the one who finally audits the $24 billion?

text:
Gibraltar / Brownstown Township (Carlson High School), Michigan: Bomb threat ~3:30 p.m. forced evacuation; voting continued outdoors. Threat unfounded, adult suspect identified, felony charges expected. Resolved (cleared, voters returned inside).

Toledo (Beverly Elementary), Ohio: Bomb threat ~10:30–10:50 a.m. evacuated the site for ~1.5–2 hours; voting continued outside with extra machines. Cleared by noon; hours extended to 9:15 p.m. for provisional ballots. (Other nearby schools threatened but not polling sites.) Resolved.

Westchester County (countywide), New York: Ballot scanners rejected paper ballots due to a programming update mismatch. Voters used emergency paper ballots (to be scanned later). Affected a competitive House race. Partially resolved / ongoing (ballots secure, counting later).

Linwood (Leavenworth County), Kansas: Ballot shortage (clerical error: ~100 delivered instead of 1,000). Some voters left. Extra ballots and express machines delivered by ~9–10 a.m. Resolved.

Duncanville (Dallas County Public Library), Texas: Power outage ~8:20–9:10 a.m. prevented new ballot printing (machines ran on battery). Fewer than 50 voters redirected to nearby centers. Resolved.

Chicago (multiple precincts), Illinois: Paper ballot shortages. Officials delivered extras and directed voters to alternatives; no turnaways reported. Resolved.

Prince George’s County (Brandywine Elementary, Laurel/DiPietro Center, others), Maryland: Ballot shortages or incorrect/blank pages caused long lines; some voters left. Replenished by truck. Resolved.

Broward County, Florida: ~20-minute morning delay from a new safety-feature malfunction. Resolved.

Multiple South Florida counties, Florida: Polling locations relocated due to flooding/heavy rain. Voters directed to check county sites for updates. Ongoing (logistical, not equipment failure).

Duval County (Jacksonville sites including Atlantic Beach, Regency Square, Arlington), Florida: Power outages and machine issues; generators/replacements used, ballots held in emergency boxes. Resolved quickly.

Maricopa County (Laveen Elementary District Office, Copper Hills Church/Peoria), Arizona: Power outages delayed openings or printers (one site temporarily closed). Reopened early; any county vote center accepted voters. Resolved.

Milwaukee (Hampton School, Silver Spring Neighborhood Center, Saveland Park, Central Count), Wisconsin: Power outages at two sites, one machine malfunction (~100 ballots secured), and tabulator issues. All repaired. Resolved.

New Bedford (4 precincts), Massachusetts: Internal wire interference prevented ballot feeding. Adjusted; machines restored. Resolved.

Multiple counties (Columbus/Tabor City, Hertford, Lenoir/Kinston, Wilson), North Carolina: Computer crashes, printer problems, and other technical glitches delayed openings. Hours extended 15–45 minutes at five sites; results delayed statewide until ~8:15 p.m. Issues fixed. Resolved (with extensions).

Chester County (3 precincts: Easttown Library, St. John’s Presbyterian, Goshen Baptist), Pennsylvania: Machine setup delays postponed openings. Hours extended 30 minutes (to 8:30 p.m., provisional after 8). Resolved.

Jackpot (Elko County), Nevada: Voting machines temporarily unavailable; paper ballots offered. Restored by ~8:30 a.m. Resolved.

Wallingford, Connecticut: Multiple sites ran out of ballots ~4–5 p.m. (coding differences from early/absentee). Reprinted; hand count planned after close. Resolved with contingency.

Westchester County, New York: Scanners still rejecting paper ballots (programming update mismatch). Voters are still casting ballots into emergency bags until polls close at 9 p.m. ET. Those bags get transported under escort for central scanning after close—it’ll take hours and delay results in the competitive House race. Some machines are being reprogrammed on the fly, but the bag method is the main workaround. Voting ongoing..

text:
For Home Instead® co-owners Creighton and Tracey Gibson, receiving the annual Best of Iredell Award never gets old. This year’s honor is Home Instead’s fourth straight since 2023. “These awards belong to our incredible Care Professionals, dedicated team, wonderful clients and families, and the community that continues to place its trust in us. Thank you, Iredell County, for your continued support,” said the couple, who also will be celebrating their Home Instead franchise’s 24th anniversary of ownership Nov. 18.

The Best of Iredell Awards are sponsored by the Statesville Record & Landmark and the Mooresville Tribune. The Gibsons’ Home Instead franchise, which serves Mooresville, Statesville and Taylorsville and the surrounding areas, has been a mainstay in its Best of Iredell Awards category of Best Home Health/Home Care Services. The Best of Iredell Award and the franchise’s 24thanniversary not only were a cause for celebration, but also provided a time for reflection for the Gibsons.

They recalled the unique reasons for starting their franchise. Creighton and Tracey didn’t want others to go through the same ordeal Creighton’s parents and family experienced when his mom and dad needed help to remain in their home. Before embarking on a career of service to seniors and their families, the successful manufacturing executive and his wife prayed long and intensely. Having received spiritual inspiration, Creighton left a lucrative career position to start the Home Instead franchise in 2002.

Remembering their family caregiving challenges, Creighton explained: “I looked for in-home care for my parents, and I could not find anyone in our area at that time who offered the type of care they needed, nor the level of compassion and understanding they deserved.” Creighton lost his 58-year-old mother, an amputee, to diabetes in 1992. “I’ll never forget the evening when I went to Dad’s home and couldn’t find him until I searched outside the house. He had fallen in the garden and had been there all day. Two months later, he fell inside his home, didn’t want to bother anyone and waited for hours for us to come check on him,” Creighton said.

“Dad moved in with us, and a year and a half later, he suffered a major stroke. He ended up in a nursing home, and it was not a great experience. I fed him every day for two years. Two months after he died, Tracey and I were talking about creating a service for seniors and their families,” recalled Creighton, who researched in-home senior-care companies and narrowed the field from 15 franchise possibilities to three finalists.

“The faith-based aspect of Home Instead appealed to us. Nobody compared to Home Instead with formal training and dementia training. Their vision was my vision for serving others such as my father. Making the decision to quit a good, stable, 16-year career with J.C. Steele and Sons was the scariest day of my life and a real leap of faith. Having made such a major move, I wanted to be a trusted source of service in the community,” said Creighton, who is active in his community just as Tracey is. Creighton has been a deacon at the Bristol Baptist Church. Tracey has served as the board chairwoman at the Greater Statesville Chamber of Commerce as well as the secretary and treasurer at Bristol Baptist Church.

The Gibsons have never stood still with the ways they provide award-winning senior care. The Gibsons pushed ahead with a new initiative in 2025 to help vulnerable seniors even more. Home Instead added a specialized medical-care component by unveiling its Nurse Directed Services, a program that’s been licensed by the State of North Carolina. With the program, Home Instead aims to keep its clients at home even as some of their needs become increasingly challenging and require medical care that previously hadn’t been a necessity.

Nurse Directed Services provides specialized care, addressing complex needs and managing medical care. Its services are tailored to individual needs and can include medical support, medication management, wound care management, vitals observation and other selected forms of support, including assistance with daily activities.

While adding the Nurse Directed Services, the Gibsons’ franchise always has stayed on course with the basics of senior care. Creighton pointed out: “The first of the four core values that Home Instead co-founders Lori and Paul Hogan wrote in 1994 is, ‘We honor God in all we do.’ Home Instead principles of ‘Build Trust, Take the Lead and Share Your Heart’ also are meaningful to us and our Care Pros. Our Care Pros build trustby being responsible and professional in dealing with clients, their families and our office.”

Creighton added. “Our Care Pros take the lead by engaging clients in meaningful activities and encouraging them in many different ways. Our Care Pros share their hearts as compassionate, smiling and thoughtful senior-care specialists. We’re invested in our community on a very personal level.”

Learn more about Tracey, Creighton and their Home Instead team: https://t.co/kaO8yP1GJ7

text: Josh Shapiro: "i could not be more humbled and grateful for the opportunity to keep serving our commonwealth. thank you from the bottom of my heart for the trust and the confidence. i just got off the phone with stacey garrity, who wished me well, and said she wants to work together to serve the people of pennsylvania. look, we have plenty of disagreements. that's part of a healthy democracy, and i appreciate her service to our commonwealth and our country. look, the results are still rolling in, but the picture is starting to come into focus. this is a good night for our commonwealth. and it's looking like it could be a pretty good night for our country, too. two hundred and fifty years since we declared our independence from a king. our nation has been through ups and downs and everything in between. look, these past two years in particular have tested our will in previously unimaginable ways. and you, you had every reason to throw up your hands, to tune out, to walk away, but that's not what you did. you kept the faith. you used your power. you not only entrusted me with the opportunity to continue to serve as your governor, you did your part to help change the very trajectory of this country. you declared within the borders of this commonwealth and all across this nation that we still determine our future and no one gets away with compromising our shared values. tonight, pennsylvania, you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty and this rampant corruption that raises our costs and rattles our conscience. you declared loud and clear that you will wait no longer for a new chapter that restores the voice of the people, that returns accountability, and that revitalizes the american spirit that has defined us since our founding. yes, this is a night for relief and for resolve because what you did tonight fits squarely in the great legacy of this commonwealth and this nation. you know, when they finished drafting the constitution, the framers left independence hall and ben franklin was approached by elizabeth willing powell as he stepped out onto the cobblestone streets of philadelphia. she looked him in the eye and asked him, dr. franklin, what do we have here, a monarchy or a republic? and franklin replied with what i think may be the most prescient words ever spoken in america. a republic if you can keep it. not the powerful, not the people used to calling the shots. you, you get the power. and that's what you did tonight, pennsylvania. you kept this republic. you kept the flame alive. i know it wasn't easy, and i'm clear eyed that there's going to be a whole lot more work ahead, but tonight, the people of pennsylvania are speaking with resounding force. you left no doubt. you are done with leadership that fails to make life better. done with waiting around for results. done with hearing politicians talk about how bad the other guys are when you're spending on groceries what you used to spend on a car payment. done with being sold big lives from one side and a 15 point plan that never delivers from the other. that's why you elected not just me, but a whole bunch of folks who actually want to get stuff done. i know that here in pennsylvania, you want leaders who deliver results, not just rhetoric. you want leaders who unite, not drive wedges between us. you want people who know how to build bridges and fix them too. and i know you want a government that reflects the basic desires that we all share, good schools for our kids, safe neighborhoods, a job that pays you for your hard work, a faith, a faith that if we play it straight and treat each other right, that things should get better. pennsylvania, if we keep working and keep fighting for what we believe in, i promise you, our best days are still out there in front of us. that's the spirit that over the past four years, that's helped us take on the big fights and win. it's how we saw graduation rates rise and crime rates fall. it's how we created more jobs and lower taxes. it's how we made sure that big tech doesn't get to write the rules that shape our future, but instead the folks in our local communities get the final say. it's how here, in the swingiest swing state in the whole country, with a divided legislature split almost exactly 50-50, we brought a majority of democrats and republicans together to make real progress and to deliver real results. and it's how we're going to do even more in the years ahead to make life even better for pennsylvanians. tonight the people have spoken. they want us to raise the minimum wage to 15 an hour. they want us to build more housing and strengthen our infrastructure. they want us to invest in our kids, our cops and our communities. they want us to enshrine abortion rights for women in the constitution of this commonwealth. tomorrow morning i'll be back at my desk continuing to work for the good people of pennsylvania. the way things are starting to look tonight, i think i'm going to have plenty of gsd democrats by my side who are ready to make more progress. that starts with my history-making governing partner, the best lieutenant governor in the country, who also happens to be the youngest, he reminds me, austin davis. i'm proud, i'm truly proud to be on this journey with austin. you know, you heard him speak before, we were both called to a life of service in different ways. but our combined force is making a difference for people from all different walks of life. and listen, we're still waiting on the final tallies. but because you made your voices heard, it looks like we will continue to have a strong democratic majority in the pennsylvania house of representatives, led by our history-making speaker joanna mcclinton and majority leader, my friend, matt bradford. and once all the votes are counted, my hope is that jake costa and vince hughes are going to be leading a democratic majority in the pennsylvania senate. and it's looking good tonight, i am hopeful that we will be sending some new leaders to washington too, to take on the corruption, to be a check on donald trump and deliver real results for pennsylvania. our victories tonight up and down the ballot are because we organized together, we mobilized together, and we believed in one another. i was proud to lead the way along with the team at the pennsylvania democratic party, led by chairman eugene depasquale and executive director larry halesham. they've done a hell of a job. i want to say a special thanks to our campaign team, our coordinated staff who worked tirelessly to elect me and democrats up and down the ballot at a moment where our country needed people to get off the sidelines and get in the game and do their part. that is exactly what you did. thank you, thank you, thank you. and to the finest, the finest staff that has ever been assembled in the nation, led by our chief of staff dana fritz, i want to say thank you, thank you. thank you, not just for helping me, but most importantly, putting your heart and soul every day into serving the people of pennsylvania. our commonwealth is better off because of your service. now listen, i can tell you i wouldn't be here tonight without the people who are at the center of my world. the love of my life, the love of my life since the ninth grade, and pennsylvania's first lady, lori shapiro. you know, laura and i have dedicated our lives to serving others, and along the way we've been blessed to be reminded of why we do what we do by our four children who are everything to us, sophia, jonah, max, and ruben. you know, the biggest sacrifice that comes with a career in public service isn't made, and austin knows this, it isn't made by those who get elected. it's made by blair and lori and harper and soph and jonah and max and ruben. you know, you have all been through so much. it's been hard, and frankly sometimes it's been terrifying. you have filled this work and this life with love and laughter and joy. i love you all so much, i love you. and finally, i want to say thank you to all of you. together, our army of nearly 16,000 volunteers knocked on 1.4 million doors, made a half a million phone calls throughout the course of this campaign. we spent real time listening to our black and latino communities in the pennsylvania democratic register. more voters on college campuses this election than ever before, ever before. and every single one of those conversations, every one of those conversations contributed to that feeling we all have here tonight. you know, these past few weeks reminded me of when i got started on this whole journey. knocking on 18,000 doors back home in abington and upper dublin to hear from folks about what mattered most to them. i've also been reminded of some of those lessons i learned from my parents. my dad, who's here tonight, has been a pediatrician for decades. i can still remember as a kid the phone ringing in our house, beck and adam remember this, at all hours of the night with a worried parent on the line, living through those terrifying moments where parents, you know this, you would trade anything just to know that your child was going to be okay. i learned what mattered more than what my dad said by what he didn't say. see, my dad listened, he offered more than a prescription, he offered a conversation. so i learned from an early age that when people are hurting, when people are counting on you for real answers, when people are tossing and turning, thinking about what the next day might bring, what matters isn't how well you talk, it's how well you listen. over the last four years as governor, i've had the privilege of listening to you, hearing your stories, witnessing your strength. and i want to be very honest here, that's what kept me going through all these hard times. you. look, i know how adrift everything feels right now. over the past few months, more of you than ever have come up to me with tears in your eyes, rightly worried about the nation that we love so much, feeling like it's slipping away. and like so many of you, i've been shocked and saddened by what we have seen out of our country's current leadership, the shamelessness, the self-dealing, the brutality, the cruelty. it struck a nerve with so many of us because it just feels bigger than politics, bigger than policy. every bit of it designed to compel us to turn away from one another, to see our neighbors as a little less human, to forget about who we are. but i've noticed something, pennsylvania. every time i set my phone down, i turn off the tv. every time laura and i get the privilege of traveling across this state to meet with all of you, we see a totally different picture. i see the farmers who don't have much, but still take some of their milk and potato, their fruits and vegetables to the local food bank, making sure people in their community have enough to eat. i see the school counselor who spends extra time with a child, even though they know full well there won't be any extra pay. i see the folks right here in camp hill, down the road at a coffee shop run by people with disabilities, folks making a living for themselves and making everybody's day a little brighter. i see the worshippers. i see the worshippers at the pike county islamic center, who just days after bullets full of lead and hate were fired through their windows, opened up their doors with love, welcoming neighbors of every faith to remind us all that we have so much in common. we're living together in this moment when a small handful of powerful and influential men claim to have all the answers. they puff themselves up behind a podium and they scheme in gilded ballrooms before bedding down for the night in their bunkers. every day, from the policies they push to the posts that they boost in our feeds, these men demonstrate that they are capable of thinking of only one thing, themselves. well tonight, pennsylvania, with your vision and your votes, you showed that your belief in our future is so much bigger than those small and selfish men. tonight, you showed that you believe what our founders did, that america is not a bounty to be plundered, but a treasure to be shared by one and all, a place that is far more valuable than the sum of its parts. and tonight, tonight you have shown me that we don't have to look far for the answers we hope for, because the answer is right here, in you. as scripture says, the path forward won't be found in the big and noisy chaos around us, not in a windstorm or an earthquake or fire, no. just like the story of the prophet elijah, the answer comes to us in a still, small voice. not in a shout, but in a whisper. the answer comes, the answer comes in our kindness, in our decency, in that warm cup of coffee handed across the counter, in a warm meal from a neighbor or the warmth of a hug when it feels like all is lost. that is the message you have all sent to me every day as your governor, in your stories, in your handshakes, and in your prayers. and tonight, well tonight you showed the whole country the undeniable strength of that kindness. you showed that together our small voices can make a big statement about the changes we all want to see and about the results we all deserve, about the kind of place we want to live in and the kind of people that we want to be. so most of all, i want to thank all of you, the good people of pennsylvania, because even as so many forces are trying to convince you otherwise, you continue to believe that your voice matters. i can't promise you that the road ahead will be smooth and easy or that i won't make some mistakes along the way, but i can promise you this. if we keep that american spirit, that anything is possible, if we keep the hopefulness that brought you to the polls today, if we keep faith in one another, if we stop looking for answers in the rearview mirror and keep our eyes trained on the horizon, then yes, pennsylvania, the answer to that question from all those years ago is we are going to keep this republic that we love. we are pennsylvania. we are going to keep our optimism. we are going to keep our empathy that sees the dignity in every last one of our neighbors. we are going to keep our conviction that fairness and freedom will win out in the end. we are going to keep showing the world that tomorrow will be better than today. thank you all so much for the trust you have placed in me and austin and everyone we elected tonight. i love this commonwealth. i love you. god bless pennsylvania. thank you. thank you."

text:
WHAT EXACTLY IS KEYTRUDA?

Keytruda, whose scientific name is pembrolizumab, is a cancer medication developed by pharmaceutical company Merck. It is used to treat several cancers, including certain types of lung cancer, melanoma, bladder cancer and head and neck cancer.

But unlike traditional chemotherapy, Keytruda doesn't primarily work by directly attacking cancer cells. It helps the body's own immune system recognise and fight them.

Here's how.

Our immune system has specialised cells called T-cells that identify and destroy abnormal cells, including cancer cells.

However, some cancers exploit a biological mechanism called the PD-1 pathway to switch off these attacking cells. Think of it as cancer finding a way to tell the body's soldiers to stand down.

Keytruda blocks the PD-1 receptor, effectively helping to release that brake and allowing the immune system to continue attacking cancer cells.

It doesn't work for every cancer or every patient, but it has become one of the most important immunotherapy treatments in modern oncology.

SO, WHAT DOES SPACE HAVE TO DO WITH IT?

This is where things get interesting.

Merck wanted to develop a version of Keytruda that could be administered through an injection under the skin rather than the traditional intravenous drip.

The challenge was that the drug contains complex proteins that are difficult to formulate into a highly concentrated injection.

Scientists began experimenting with growing its protein crystals in microgravity aboard the International Space Station.

Why space?

On Earth, gravity influences how particles settle and interact as crystals form. In microgravity, those effects are reduced, allowing scientists to study different crystal structures and formation processes.

The experiments provided useful information that helped researchers improve the manufacturing process back on Earth.

The result was significant.

In September 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Keytruda Qlex, a new formulation that can be administered under the skin in approximately one minute.

It also contains an enzyme that helps the medication spread through the tissue.

So, instead of spending considerably longer receiving an intravenous infusion, eligible patients can receive the new formulation much more quickly.

NOW, ENTER ELON MUSK AND SPACEX.

SpaceX is exploring another dimension of this possibility through Starfall, a spacecraft designed to carry materials into orbit, expose them to the conditions of space and return them to Earth.

Its first demonstration mission launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket in June 2026.

The ambition is to make space-based manufacturing commercially useful, including for pharmaceuticals and advanced materials.

The idea is simple but extraordinary: some products may be manufactured more effectively in the unique environment of space than they can on Earth.

WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR THE FUTURE OF MEDICINE?

It means space exploration may eventually contribute to developing medicines, improving existing treatments and producing materials that are difficult to manufacture under normal conditions.

It does not mean every drug needs to go to space, or that zero gravity automatically produces better medicine. The science is still developing, and every proposed benefit must be demonstrated through proper research and clinical testing.

But Keytruda offers a compelling example of how research conducted in orbit can translate into practical improvements for patients on Earth.

For decades, we have looked at space exploration largely through the lens of astronauts, rockets, planets and the possibility of finding life beyond Earth.

Perhaps we should also begin looking at it as an extension of our laboratories.

Because the next major medical breakthrough may not begin in a hospital or a research facility on Earth.

It might begin hundreds of kilometres above us.

text:
# Voter Confidence in Governance Slips

A fresh batch of polling data shows public satisfaction with how democratic systems function is falling sharply across the United States and its European allies.

A recent Pew Research Center survey captures the trend: 69% of Americans are dissatisfied with the way democracy works in their country. The figure stands at 69% in France, 68% in Spain, 62% in Italy and 47% in Poland. Tracking data from leading pollsters including Ipsos and Gallup reinforces the finding: disillusionment among voters with existing governance frameworks has grown from scattered grievances into a widespread cross-country sentiment.

This frustration is not confined to survey responses. It has spilled onto the streets. The U.S. and European nations grapple with distinct, stubborn challenges: frequent cabinet reshuffles in some European capitals undermine policy continuity; immigration integration keeps societies divided; the shift to clean energy inflicts pain on workers in legacy industries; identity and class tensions keep intensifying. Across party lines and social strata, voters share similar priorities: tougher anti-corruption measures, greater accountability for officials, policies that address ordinary people’s concerns, and a seat at the table for grassroots voices.

For years, many voters took it for granted that regular elections lay at the heart of democracy. Proper electoral procedures, they assumed, would translate public will into policy. But a growing number now see voting as little more than a periodic ritual. A ballot cast on election day offers no guarantee that citizens can shape day-to-day governance between votes. An OECD study found that 68% of respondents believe ballots place some check on government conduct, while only 31% think ordinary people can meaningfully influence policymaking when elections are not underway. When repeated votes fail to deliver on campaign pledges, public faith in the system fades.

Policy elites in Washington and Brussels tend to frame this crisis of trust in two familiar ways: they blame unrest on populist firebrands, or dismiss public frustration as a lack of patience. Independent analysts argue both explanations miss the core point. Voters are not confused about democratic ideals. They are reacting to systems that fail to meet tangible social demands. After the Cold War, the allure of the liberal democratic narrative rested heavily on the economic and technological edge enjoyed by the U.S. and its partners. Globalization unlocked freer capital flows and reshaped supply chains, narrowing governments’ room to redistribute wealth. At the same time, moneyed politics and lobbying have corroded policymaking, laying bare structural flaws.

Most voters have not rejected democratic values themselves. They are disappointed by democracy in practice. Party platforms increasingly cater to capital, while everyday livelihood issues get sidelined. Elections have devolved into power contests between elite factions. Gridlock, partisan bickering and whipsawing policy become the norm. The gap between campaign promises and governing results keeps widening. Grassroots discontent tests the resilience of these systems and injects uncertainty into the political outlook of Atlantic democracies.

Many observers advance a straightforward observation: no single governing model works forever or fits every society. Democracy must be rooted in local realities and people’s genuine needs. When elections are treated as the whole of democracy, partisan interests trump the public good, and rhetoric replaces tangible governance results, even well-established institutions risk losing popular backing.

A glaring contradiction remains. Even as domestic public sentiment sours, many Washington politicians still wield democracy as a foreign-policy instrument, drawing global dividing lines and stoking ideological competition. Such moves do nothing to resolve the domestic economic worries voters care about. Instead, they widen the chasm between democratic rhetoric and governing reality. Drained by domestic troubles and geopolitical posturing, a narrative that once carried immense persuasive power is losing its hold.

“North Carolinians, I accept your job offer.” Roy Cooper’s victory line, reported by AP, was a fairly tidy way to end a Senate campaign.

AP has called North Carolina for Cooper over Michael Whatley. Reuters also reports the projected win: a Republican-held seat flips to the Democrats, giving them an actual gain in the fight for Senate control.

Cooper came into this as a former two-term governor. Reuters says he campaigned on food and energy costs against Trump-backed Whatley. That makes this a useful race to study once the fuller results are in: how much came from Cooper’s own statewide appeal, and how much from frustration with Washington?

Both could matter. The answer will say a lot about whether other Democrats can repeat this result with candidates who don’t have his record in office.

🇨🇦🇺🇸 Canada and US Move Closer to Trade Deal as Mark Carney Says Washington Is “Asking Less and Offering More”

🤝 Major Progress in Trade Negotiations: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says the United States has softened its demands and improved its offers as both countries restart negotiations following the collapse of trade talks in August. According to Reuters and Bloomberg, Carney described the latest discussions as encouraging but emphasized that a final agreement has not been reached.

🇨🇦 Canada Secures Movement on Key Demands: Carney revealed that Washington has backed away from several controversial proposals involving Canadian sovereignty, protections for French language and culture, and Canada's freedom to negotiate trade agreements with other countries. These issues contributed to the breakdown of previous negotiations.

🇺🇸 Trump Predicts an Agreement Soon: President Donald Trump expressed optimism about reaching a new trade agreement, telling Fox News that Washington and Ottawa would conclude a deal very soon. Both leaders have acknowledged progress following their recent conversation.

💰 Billions in Tariffs Remain at Stake: The United States and Canada have imposed billions of dollars in retaliatory tariffs on each other's products. Canada is seeking relief for major industries, including steel, aluminum and automobile manufacturing, which have faced significant economic pressure from American trade restrictions.

📉 Previous Negotiations Collapsed in August: Earlier discussions broke down after Canada rejected American demands that Ottawa considered unacceptable. The collapse triggered additional tariffs and heightened tensions between two of the world's largest trading partners.

🏭 Economic Implications for Both Countries: A successful agreement could reduce costs for manufacturers, stabilize supply chains and ease pressure on businesses operating across the border. The automotive, agricultural, energy and metals industries have substantial exposure to the trade dispute.

🗣️ Carney Says More Work Is Needed: Speaking during a Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, Carney acknowledged that negotiations have become more intensive. He emphasized that Washington is now making fewer demands and presenting more attractive proposals, but important differences remain unresolved.

text:
Sephiroth is unquestionably one of the most iconic villains. No argument there. His appearance, dialogue, music, overwhelming power, and psychological manipulation of Cloud make him very unforgettable.

Being memorable and being exceptionally well-written are two different things.

If we're discussing the greatest villain ever written, we need standards beyond popularity, intimidation, and presentation.

My criteria are as follows.

Character Development. Does the story establish the character's personality, flaws, relationships, and motivations?

Transformation. Does their descent into villainy happen through a convincing sequence of events rather than an abrupt personality change?

Psychological Believability. Are their actions consistent with their established personality and experiences?

Motivational Justification. Does the narrative sufficiently explain why they make their decisions, even when those decisions are morally indefensible?

Character Progression. Do they continue developing as the story unfolds, or become a largely static obstacle for the protagonist?

By these standards, I would argue that Walter White, Griffith, and Michael Corleone are all better-written villains than Sephiroth.

1. Walter White, Breaking Bad

Walter White is an extraordinary example of how to write a believable descent into villainy.

He begins as an intelligent but deeply dissatisfied chemistry teacher who learns that he has terminal cancer. Facing his mortality and worrying about his family's financial security, he turns to manufacturing methamphetamine.

His initial motivation is understandable, even if his methods are morally reprehensible.

But the story gradually reveals something more complicated.

Walter is prideful, resentful, insecure, and desperate to feel important. These characteristics exist from the beginning. His criminal activities simply provide opportunities for those flaws to grow.

When his former business associates offer to pay for his medical treatment, Walter refuses. His pride matters more to him than accepting a legitimate solution to his financial problems.

That decision is significant because it exposes the weakness of his justification for entering the drug trade.

Over five seasons, Walter becomes increasingly manipulative, ruthless, and obsessed with power.

But his transformation is never disconnected from the man we originally met.

Each major decision builds upon an established character flaw, previous experience, or consequence of an earlier decision.

And unlike Sephiroth, Walter eventually confronts the truth about his own motivations.

He admits that his criminal empire was never entirely about protecting his family. He pursued it because it made him feel powerful, accomplished, and alive.

This admission completes his psychological journey.

Why is he better written than Sephiroth?

Because Walter's transformation is demonstrated rather than merely explained.

We witness the progression from desperation to rationalization, from rationalization to ambition, and from ambition to moral corruption.

His eventual villainy is the culmination of five seasons of character development.

Sephiroth, by comparison, undergoes his defining transformation during a relatively brief episode of psychological collapse.

Both characters have understandable reasons to experience profound personal crises.

The difference is that Breaking Bad thoroughly develops the connection between Walter's experiences and his eventual behavior.

Final Fantasy VII leaves much more of Sephiroth's psychological transformation unexplored.

 Griffith from Berserk

Of the three examples, Griffith is arguably Sephiroth's most direct comparison.

Both begin as celebrated military leaders. Both possess extraordinary abilities, tremendous charisma, and the admiration of those around them.

Both eventually become monstrous figures pursuing ambitions that threaten countless lives.

But Griffith's transformation is far more extensively developed.

From the beginning, Griffith dreams of ruling his own kingdom. His ambition isn't something he suddenly discovers. It defines his personality, relationships, and decisions.

He inspires loyalty and genuine affection among his followers, but he also possesses a dangerous tendency to place his ambitions above the people who help him achieve them.

His relationship with Guts exposes this contradiction.

Griffith genuinely values Guts, yet struggles to accept his independence. When Guts leaves the Band of the Hawk, Griffith experiences a devastating emotional crisis.

He subsequently makes an impulsive decision involving Princess Charlotte, resulting in his imprisonment and prolonged torture.

By the time he's rescued, his body has been destroyed, his military accomplishments have effectively been erased, and his dream appears permanently beyond his reach.

Then comes the Eclipse.

Griffith is presented with an opportunity to reclaim his ambitions by sacrificing the people who trusted and followed him.

He accepts.

His transformation into Femto is horrifying, but it is fundamentally consistent with the flaws established throughout his character arc. The supernatural forces involved manipulate and pressure him, but the choice exploits an ambition the audience already understands.

Why is he better written than Sephiroth?

Because Griffith's betrayal is not simply the result of discovering something devastating about himself.

It emerges from an established conflict between his ambition, his attachments, and his inability to accept losing control.

The audience witnesses the relationships that define him, the decisions that destroy him, and the psychological deterioration that precedes his ultimate betrayal.

His transformation doesn't require us to accept that an otherwise comparatively well-adjusted individual suddenly abandoned his previous moral boundaries.

The seeds of Griffith's villainy were planted long before the Eclipse.

His later characterization is more static in certain respects, but his continued pursuit of a kingdom remains consistent with the ambition established before his transformation.

Sephiroth has a comparable opportunity for tragic characterization, particularly given his portrayal in Crisis Core.

We see his friendships, loyalty, moral restraint, and growing disillusionment with Shinra.

Yet his transformation into a mass murderer receives relatively little psychological development.

Griffith's downfall is a tragedy we experience. Sephiroth's is largely a tragedy we're told has occurred.

 Michael Corleone  The Godfather

Michael Corleone provides perhaps the most psychologically grounded example of the three.

When we're introduced to Michael, he's a decorated military veteran who has deliberately distanced himself from his family's criminal activities.

He doesn't initially aspire to become a Mafia boss.

He wants a different life.

But when his father becomes the target of an assassination attempt, Michael begins involving himself in the family's affairs.

His initial decisions are motivated largely by loyalty and a desire to protect those he loves.

However, each successive decision draws him deeper into organized crime.

Michael eventually becomes the ruthless leader of the very organization he once sought to avoid.

As his power grows, so do his paranoia, need for control, willingness to employ violence, and emotional isolation.

By The Godfather Part II, Michael has become willing to authorize the murder of his own brother. What makes this transformation exceptional is the consistency of its development.

Michael doesn't simply wake up one day and decide to become a monster. His moral deterioration occurs through decisions that progressively compromise the principles he originally possessed.

Even his most reprehensible actions follow a recognizable psychological pattern. He increasingly convinces himself that protecting his family requires controlling everything around him.

Ironically, his obsession with protecting his family ultimately contributes to its destruction. His later attempts at redemption further develop the consequences of the man he became.

Why is he better written than Sephiroth?

Because Michael's transformation is built upon a continuous progression of choices and consequences.

His circumstances explain why he initially becomes involved in criminal activities. His established personality explains why he gradually embraces increasingly ruthless methods.

And the consequences of his decisions explain why he becomes more isolated, controlling, and destructive.

The audience doesn't have to imagine the missing psychological development between Michael the war hero and Michael the Mafia boss.

The story shows us that transformation.

 This is where Sephiroth Falls Short.

Sephiroth's greatest weakness isn't that his backstory lacks potential. It's that his transformation fails to capitalize fully on that potential.

Crisis Core establishes that Sephiroth was capable of friendship, loyalty, independent judgment, and moral restraint.

He wasn't simply a monster waiting for an excuse.

He was an accomplished soldier who maintained meaningful relationships despite the extraordinary circumstances surrounding his existence.

Then comes Nibelheim. Sephiroth discovers Shinra's experiments, investigates his origins, and develops a profoundly mistaken understanding of his relationship to Jenova and the Cetra.

He spends several days researching these revelations approximately a week in Crisis Core before his murderous rampage begins.

The circumstances provide a credible foundation for an identity crisis. But an identity crisis and a sudden willingness to exterminate innocent people are not the same thing.

The existence of a traumatic revelation does not eliminate the writer's responsibility to develop a convincing psychological response.

Why does Sephiroth's disillusionment with Shinra become hatred toward humanity?

Why does someone previously capable of questioning authority so readily embrace a distorted understanding of his ancestry?

How does his shattered identity develop into a conviction that he deserves dominion over the Planet?

The narrative supplies explanations for his beliefs and ambitions, but devotes comparatively little attention to the psychological process that transforms him into the villain we encounter.

And once that transformation is complete, Sephiroth's characterization becomes comparatively static.

His objectives and methods develop. His relationship with Cloud remains compelling. Later entries introduce additional dimensions to his plans and presence.

But his fundamental personality and superiority complex undergo relatively little meaningful change. That isn't automatically a flaw. Static villains can be exceptionally effective.

However, when the defining transformation of a character is already underdeveloped, the absence of substantial subsequent psychological progression becomes a more significant limitation.

Walter White, Griffith, and Michael Corleone demonstrate three different approaches to exceptional villain writing.

Walter demonstrates how existing personal flaws can gradually evolve into moral corruption.

Griffith demonstrates how overwhelming ambition can ultimately destroy the relationships and loyalties that once sustained it.

Michael demonstrates how understandable decisions, repeated moral compromises, and escalating consequences can transform someone into the very thing they initially rejected.

None of these characters requires the audience to morally approve of their actions.

They simply provide sufficient characterization and narrative development for us to understand how those actions became possible.

And that's the distinction.

Sephiroth is an exceptional antagonist in terms of presentation, atmosphere, intimidation, and his psychological influence over Cloud.

Those accomplishments deserve recognition.

But when evaluating character development, transformation, believability, motivational justification, and progression, I would argue that all three of these characters surpass him.

And yes, Walter White and Michael Corleone are protagonists of their respective stories. That doesn't prevent them from becoming villains. Being the central character of a story does not make someone its moral hero.

If the comparison must involve a traditional antagonist, Griffith alone provides an exceptionally strong alternative.

Ultimately, my criticism isn't that Sephiroth is a bad villain.

It's that Sephiroth's reputation is built more upon how effectively he's presented as a villain than how thoroughly he's developed as a character.

There's a difference between writing a villain who commands the audience's attention and writing one whose motivations, transformation, and decisions withstand serious psychological scrutiny.

Sephiroth unquestionably accomplishes the former.

Walter White, Griffith, and Michael Corleone provide stronger examples of the latter.

text:
Good Evening, Canada, and friends who follow this Annealed Mind and his trusty workmate, Asop.

I am struggling a touch to keep this civil this evening...

I've had my usual day of keeping up with events. Some David from Moose on the Loose, a few clips from Parliament, and finally, The Really Big Show with Jim and Iain.

That, my friends, was the last straw.

I listened to David examining potential conflicts of interest. Then I learned that our Prime Minister was off in the Caribbean attending another international summit, announcing over $70 MILLION in new commitments across the Commonwealth.

Meanwhile, back in Parliament, I watched Dominic LeBlanc trading insults with Pierre Poilievre over the trade negotiations, while Canadian workers and their families continue facing uncertainty about their jobs and futures.

And finally...the latest statistics on the struggles of ordinary Canadians.

31% of Canadians surveyed have skipped meals or reduced their portions because they couldn't afford groceries.

2,355,075 food bank visits in a SINGLE MONTH. AN ALL-TIME RECORD!

Jobs lost. Financial security disappearing. Families struggling to keep a roof overhead and food on the table.

And still, we hear the speeches, the promises, the declarations of tremendous leadership and how wonderfully this government is defending Canadians.

I think something inside me finally snapped.

I am so SICK AND TIRED of being SICK AND TIRED of this garbage!

Any fool willing to look beyond the political announcements can see the hardship and despair.

Where I am staying this winter, I see young families with preschool children living in trailers. I don't know their personal circumstances, but I find myself wondering how many Canadian families are struggling just to establish a secure future.

The other day, while visiting a mall, I watched a young woman digging through a dumpster behind a store.

Today, a young man who appeared to be having a difficult time knocked on my truck window and asked if I could spare him a cigarette.

At all hours of the night, sirens wail through the surrounding community.

These are the things I am seeing and hearing. They stay with me.

And I cannot help thinking about the country I have loved all my life, the working class I spent 42 years proudly belonging to, and the opportunities we once believed our children would inherit.

WHAT HAS HAPPENED TO THAT CANADA?

I see a government that seems endlessly capable of finding money for new initiatives, announcing grand ambitions, and congratulating itself on its leadership.

But where is the urgency when it comes to Canadians who cannot afford to feed their own families?

Where is the humility?

Where is the accountability?

WHERE IS THE STEWARDSHIP?

Our Prime Minister stood in Parliament and declared that affordability was the best it had been in over a decade. He later clarified that he was referring to rental affordability.

Well, Mr. Carney, perhaps you should spend a little more time listening to Canadians who are struggling to pay for BOTH their rent and their groceries!

ENOUGH!!!!!!!

This country has GOT TO WAKE UP!

We cannot continue measuring the success of our government by its announcements, its ambitions, its slogans, or the international company our Prime Minister keeps.

We must measure it by the lives Canadians are actually able to live.

By the jobs they can depend upon.

By the homes they can afford.

By the food they can put on their tables.

And by the futures they can realistically offer their children and grandchildren.

That is STEWARDSHIP.

There are six federal by-elections coming on December 7. An opportunity for Canadians to demand answers and accountability.

And before Ottawa rushes further into grand new arrangements with Europe, perhaps someone could explain how all of this is supposed to improve the lives of Canadians who are struggling RIGHT NOW!

Because I see a country that was promised prosperity, strength, and affordability...

And far too many Canadians who have instead been left struggling with uncertainty, hardship, and despair.

A country's success is NOT measured by the ambitions of its Prime Minister.

It is measured by the well-being of its PEOPLE!

Nuff Said....

The Annealed Mind

We research, write & draw — You think!

text:
This is a slogan, not a fact. "Most corrupt president in history" is a ranking with no evidence attached, and it comes from a senator in the middle of a political fight.

Americans have every right to scrutinise any president's business dealings. Questions about Trump family ventures deserve answers through courts, inspectors general and a free press. That's how a free country works. But history sets a high bar. Warren Harding's administration gave us Teapot Dome, where the Interior Secretary went to prison for taking bribes over federal oil leases. Ulysses Grant's term had the Whiskey Ring, which cost taxpayers millions in stolen revenue. Richard Nixon ran Watergate from the Oval Office and resigned before Congress could remove him. Superlatives take evidence and comparison, and the post offers neither.

It's also selective. Senator Warren was quiet when President Biden pardoned his own son in December 2024 after promising he wouldn't. She's the same senator who claimed Native American heritage for years, then apologised in 2019 after a DNA test went badly. If she wants to talk about honesty in public life, specific evidence would persuade more people than one more all-caps style headline. Liberty depends on holding every powerful person to the same standard, whichever party they belong to.

In the matter of illegal arrest/ abduction of Abshir Ahmedsadak Abdi, Advocate 

Under the Constitution:

​Article 49(1)(f): An arrested person must be brought before a court as soon as reasonably possible, but no later than 24 hours after being arrested, or the end of the next court day.

​Article 29: The right to freedom and security of the person forbids arbitrary detention without trial or deprivation of freedom without just cause.

​Article 23(3)(f): The High Court possesses unyielding authority to issue an order of habeas corpus to compel the Inspector General of Police, the DCI, or any detaining authority to produce the subject alive and justify any deprivation of liberty.

​Where the police disclaim custody, the threshold remains strict: law enforcement agencies cannot simply offer passive denials. They hold a statutory and constitutional duty to investigate, locate, and secure the release of any missing officer of the court.

​An attack on or unlawful disappearance of an advocate is a direct assault on the independence of the legal profession, the administration of justice, and the rule of law. The demand for his immediate, unconditional production before a court of competent jurisdiction is both legally sound and non-negotiable.

text:
Mike Tyson, Jimmy Jacobs, and Jose Torres at Cus D'Amato's funeral on November 4, 1985.

D'Amato trained three world champions: heavyweights Floyd Patterson and Mike Tyson, and light heavyweight Jose Torres.

Jimmy Jacobs dominated the sport of Four-Wall Handball from 1955 to 1969, winning every match he played during that 15-year span. He won six United States Handball Association National Singles Championships, four YMCA National Championships, three AAU National Championships, countless regional championships, as well as the World Singles Championship.

In a 1966 Sports Illustrated article titled "Really The Greatest," Robert H. Boyle wrote: "Jacobs is generally hailed as the finest player of all time. Indeed, there are those who say Jacobs is the best athlete, regardless of sport, in the country."

Beginning in the 1940s and accelerating in the late 50s and early 60s, during his international handball travels, Jacobs began to indulge his passion for boxing and collecting rare fight films. 

"I adored boxing, and that led me to become a serious film collector," he said. "By 17, 18 years old, I was trading fight films and learning who the collectors were. If a person is a real collector, of anything, there is a compulsion which is irresistible toward acquisition. . . . But films were difficult to come by. Remember, Congress had passed a law prohibiting interstate commerce of fight films after Johnson beat Jeffries in 1910. That fight film had been shown all over the United States and there were race riots. So Congress banned transportation of fight films from one state to another from 1910 to 1940. For example, when Dempsey fought Willard, it was a violation to show the film in New York. So fight films were sent all over the world because they couldn’t be exploited in this country. Joe Louis fought Jim Braddock in Chicago; the film couldn’t be shown outside Illinois. Most people can’t believe this. The law was repealed in 1940. In my travels, I visited all the museums to make deals, to get these fight films back to the U.S."

Jacobs was also an avid collector of comic books. He started collecting them when he worked as a volunteer on paper-collection drives during World War II. He would take home discarded comics he found as he sorted through the old newspapers and magazines donated to aid the war effort. Mike Tyson biographer Peter Heller wrote of Jacobs collection: "At the time of his death in 1988, it was probably the largest and most valuable collection of its kind anywhere, containing some 800,000 comic books with a value of perhaps $2 million."

In 1959, Jacobs contacted Bill Cayton, another collector of fight films and founder of Big Fights Inc., to find out if he was interested in trading fight films. The two men hit it off when they met, and Cayton offered to do more than swap films: He offered Jacobs a job with his company. In time, the two merged their collections and became business partners.

Jacobs and Cayton produced two films that were nominated for Best Documentary Feature at the Academy Awards: Legendary Champions in 1968 and Jack Johnson in 1970. Among the other films they produced were A.K.A. Cassius Clay and Sugar Ray Robinson: Pound for Pound.

In 1998, ten years after Jacobs died, Cayton sold the company's 16,000-film boxing library to ESPN for a reported $100 million.

On March 23, 1988, Jacobs died from lymphocytic leukemia at the age of 58. He had suffered from the disease for nine years. He was survived by his wife, Loraine, and a sister, Dorothy.

Jacobs received many tributes after his death that showed how highly regarded he was in the world of boxing.

Muhammad Ali said, "Jimmy Jacobs has always been a good friend of mine. I will truly miss him. I not only respect him, I had admiration, compassion, and love for this man."

Howard Cosell wrote in the New York Daily News, "In the dirty world of boxing, Jacobs was a clean man. He was proof that boxing and character need not be mutually exclusive. . . . And boxing is that much less a sport without his presence."

Sportswriter Doug Krikorian stated, "The beleaguered sport suffered another damaging blow the other day when it lost its most eloquent spokesman, Jimmy Jacobs. . . . He was respected and trusted by bitterly divisive factions and his sound reputation was never tainted by rumors of dishonesty-rumors that inevitably curse everyone in the sport who reaches Jacobs' lofty status."

Promoter Don Fraser claimed, "I never heard a bad word about him."

Gene Kilroy, Muhammad Ali's former business manger, insisted, "If there's anyone in boxing who didn't like Jimmy Jacobs, then he didn't like him because Jimmy wouldn't sell out."

Shortly after Jacobs died, sportswriter Jack McKinney said Jacobs was secretly trained by D'Amato to challenge Archie Moore for the World Light Heavyweight Championship in 1961. At that time, Moore had held the title for almost nine years and was in his mid-40s.

In an article that appeared in the Philadelphia Daily News on March 30, 1988, McKinney wrote:

D'Amato used to engage me in deep discussions about the state of the art in boxing. It was during one such session that he first hooked me on his secret vision. "I'm going to take a mature, world-class athlete who's never boxed before and make him a champion," Cus confided. "He'll have no amateur bouts, no pro preliminaries, so no bad habits. I'll put him through a program of intensive instruction in gym, utilizing his already developed physical attributes. Then, when he's ready for his ring debut, it will be for the world championship. And he'll make history by winning it!" Cus said his prospect had already achieved "dominance in another sport." Among those "already developed physical attributes," he mentioned "strength, quickness, stamina, exceptional hand-eye coordination," and other impressive factors, along with "great intelligence and an enormous will to excel." At various times, I guessed Tom Gola, Jim Brown, John Havlicek and a virtual who's-who of other likely suspects. But Cus always smiled mysteriously and said he'd tell me when he was ready. Only after he died, with his project unfulfilled, did it dawn on me that Cus D'Amato had been thinking all along of the man Sports Illustrated once described as the most dominant athlete in the world — Jimmy Jacobs himself.
Writer Pete Dexter was asked by Playboy to do a piece on Tyson in 1987. McKinney wrote in the Daily News article, "Pete asked me for a door-opener, and I suggested Jacobs, who'd assumed the role of Tyson's adviser after the death of father-figure Cus D'Amato." McKinney said Jacobs admitted to Dexter that "he had been D'Amato's secret prospect, honed to readiness over six months of intense tutelage for a covertly arranged shot at Archie Moore's long-rusting light-heavyweight title."
The fight never took place because, so the story goes, Moore detected no potential upside. He is said to have told Jacobs "there are two possibilities: either you win or I kill you. Both are intolerable to me". "Or perhaps it never happened because it was a benign myth spun from irresistible strands of truth," wrote Mark Singer, a staff writer at The New Yorker. Singer said two close friends of Jacobs insisted that, his reverence for D'Amato notwithstanding, there's no way he would have seriously considered the proposition.
