text:
AI's Wild October

October's AI news was wild: 83% diagnostic accuracy on difficult medical cases, agents accessing bank accounts, models solving research-level physics problems and checking mathematical papers for serious errors.

Across those stories, AI is starting to act inside systems built around human decisions.

Start with cybersecurity. Late October brought two serious PHP vulnerabilities and security incidents at Railway, Zeabur and LiteLLM, part of the wave being called “Black October.”

Microsoft described Storm-0940 using an AI penetration-testing framework in a campaign that attempted sign-ins across more than 2,250 tenants. Its separate password-spraying activity peaked at more than 2,900 attempts per minute.

At Stanford, Sam Altman argued for a new kind of AI-powered defensive shield as patching individual vulnerabilities becomes increasingly inadequate.

When attacks run at machine speed, how do defenders keep up if patching still depends on people working through a queue?

Now look at banks. Axios reported on October 22 that major US banks were finding third-party agents inside customer accounts, with some activity appearing to go beyond user instructions. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and JPMorgan were among the institutions restricting access.

The central problem is authorization: who is acting, what did the customer approve, and can the bank tell?

Walmart is taking another route. Its planned Agent Gateway gives shopping agents their own identities and lets customers approve each purchase or set a spending limit, such as $50, $100 or $200. Amazon has restricted outside shopping agents.

The internet now has to decide who can authorize an agent to spend money.

AI developers are still working out how to monitor their own agents. On October 22, METR and Redwood Research published findings from a three-week assessment of OpenAI's internal monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21. Their 61-page report was shared internally.

They estimated that roughly 75–94% of qualifying internal agentic Responses API traffic was eligible for monitoring, with substantial uncertainty, and identified gaps affecting some coding-agent activity. In an October 29 update, they relayed OpenAI's statement that most vulnerabilities had been patched, with one fix still in progress; the remaining issue did not affect its misuse safeguards stack.

As agents gain access to more services, technology companies are racing to build the interfaces people use to direct them. OpenAI brought GPT-6 with Intelligent UI to ChatGPT: answers can include charts, forms and calculators people can use inside the conversation.

Google's Gemini 4 Argon added a task mode that can work across Google services and more than 40 connected apps. Its enterprise coworker agents can have their own email addresses, calendars and storage, research information, write documents and run code.

It starts to feel like hiring a digital employee who never sleeps.

That raises a harder question for people trying to get their first job.

Anthropic's internal study offers a concrete view. By August, employee-directed agents accumulated about six hours of runtime for each estimated human work hour, with the human baseline calculated using a 40-hour week. Code commits per engineer reached five times the rate six months earlier.

The share of junior employees in technical departments fell from 21% to 14%; juniors' share of technical hires fell from 27% to 9%. Hiring priorities shifted toward judgment, autonomy and the ability to direct AI.

Everyone wants experienced people who can supervise agents. But the first job that gives newcomers that experience may be getting harder to find.

Meanwhile, the technical results keep coming.

Anthropic used Claude to generate about 180 million lines of formal proofs across 123 open-source libraries, discovering hundreds of bugs along the way. Under specified execution assumptions, those proofs establish particular security properties of compiled code.

Formal verification uses mathematics to show that defined classes of failure cannot occur within the modeled conditions. The same technology accelerating attacks is also making stronger defenses practical.

In medicine, Microsoft's MAI-DxO reached 83% diagnostic accuracy in a study using complex New England Journal of Medicine cases. Physicians working with reference materials reached 36%. The comparison came from a structured diagnostic research evaluation.

In TheoPhysEval, GPT-6 Astra running in Codex, with literature search and computational tools, produced correct final answers for 49 of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical-physics problems.

Another study used GPT-6.1 Sol to examine 793 mathematical preprints. Among 656 papers published before August 2026, it flagged major errors in about 6% that could require reworking central claims.

We used to ask AI to sit exams. Now it is helping check the work humans submit.

In robotics, progress in software runs up against physical constraints.

On Tesla's third-quarter earnings call, Musk put expected Optimus deliveries to outside companies around the end of 2027. He pointed to the hand's electromechanical design, AI, reliability and useful life as work still to be solved.

A factory needs a robot that grips reliably and survives repeated use. Software can improve overnight. Mechanical durability takes engineering and time.

Then there is the money. Meta forecast 2026 capital expenditure of $135–145 billion, including principal payments on finance leases. Capital is flowing into compute while the shape of work is changing.

Anthropic announced a plan, subject to stockholder approval, to commit 5% of its equity to a public benefit fund. Musk then said he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America in 2027.

At a rough 72 million children and $146 per share, that would amount to about $10.5 billion. The distribution mechanism had not been set out in the announcement.

There is something surreal about watching an AI company's share of junior hires shrink while technology leaders discuss distributing wealth to the public.

Across these October stories, AI is moving into banking, companies, medical research and scientific work—and starting to act.

Much of our login infrastructure and corporate approval machinery still assumes a person is acting. Once a model can carry out work, who authorizes it? Who can see what it did? Who is responsible when something goes wrong?

My view: the next decisive advantage will come from putting AI safely to work in real organizations. Intelligence without dependable authorization, oversight and accountability can make the consequences of a mistake much larger.

That is what made October so wild.

text:
For organizations in finance, aerospace, healthcare, defense, and high-tech R&D, adopting AI in the cloud presents a dangerous paradox:

While multi-agent velocity delivers undeniable productivity gains, compliance standards and non-disclosure mandates are uncompromising: proprietary source code, customer identities, financial ledgers, and trade secrets can never leave internal perimeters.

Consequently, many forward-thinking enterprises deploy self-hosted foundation models (such as private Llama, Qwen, or DeepSeek clusters) on local GPU racks. However, lacking purpose-built collaboration software, these on-premises models remain trapped as isolated single-turn chat windows—unable to coordinate across departments, collaborate in group chats, or drive end-to-end engineering lifecycles.

The open-source multi-agent platform Grix breaks this deadlock: completely open source and engineered for 100% offline, air-gapped, on-premises private deployment! Organizations can bind directly to internal LLM endpoints, local Codex instances, and custom agents, assembling autonomous digital workforces with guaranteed zero data leakage!

The Air-Gapped Blueprint: Why Grix Ensures Total Data Sovereignty

As an open-source platform, Grix offers a lean, decoupled architecture built specifically for enterprise security:

100% Open Source & Auditable: The Go backend, multi-platform Flutter clients, and admin console are fully open source, enabling comprehensive white-box audits by internal security teams with zero cloud telemetry;
Universal Private LLM Compatibility: Whether running open models via vLLM, Ollama, TGI, or private enterprise endpoints, Grix connects effortlessly via the standard ACP bridge protocol or native agent interfaces;
True Physical Isolation:
Contact books, historical threads, and execution contexts remain exclusively in internal databases;
All code workspaces and file attachments live directly on internal network storage (NAS) or local developer machines;
External Internet access can be severed completely without degrading real-time collaboration.

The On-Premises Workforce: Cross-Functional Velocity Behind Corporate Firewalls

Behind your firewall, open-source Grix transforms raw private computing into specialized, cross-functional sub-agent teams:

1. The Core Engineering Lifeline: Air-Gapped Code Delivery

Deploy primary Codex coordinators and private code models on internal development clusters:

Ingest local GitLab / Gitea commit hooks and CI error logs;
Automatically initiate private project groups, routing tasks across Architect and Developer agents;
Compilations, unit test runs, and static audits execute entirely on local hardware, ensuring intellectual property never leaks.

2. Financial & Legal Governance: Private Audit & Document Review

Hatch compliance and legal audit agents tailored to internal governance standards:

Review confidential investment contracts, payroll sheets, and audit filings securely;
Agents verify clauses and flag regulatory risks without sending text to public foundation model APIs.

3. In-House Knowledge Retention: Immune to Staff Turnover

By encapsulating roles within Grix, every department preserves operational intelligence:

Proprietary SOPs (SKILL.md), troubleshooting playbooks, and internal tool signatures remain in-house permanently;
New hires join Grix project channels, query private agents, and onboard in hours rather than weeks.

4 Steps to Deploy Your Sovereign Enterprise AI Infrastructure

Enterprise IT can roll out private multi-agent collaboration in four clean steps:

Step 1: Spin Up Grix on Internal Infrastructure

Launch the open-source Grix backend on internal Linux servers, Docker containers, or Kubernetes clusters, binding to internal private IPs or a corporate Tailscale network with zero open public ports.

Step 2: Bridge Private Models & Local Agents

Configure local endpoint URLs in the Grix admin panel, adding internal LLMs, Codex instances, or proprietary agents directly into the company contact book.

Step 3: Mount Internal Workspaces & Hatch Specialized Roles

Mount internal project repositories and documentation libraries to dedicated roles. Define specialized agents for architecture, development, QA, and operations via standard Grix skill schemas.

Step 4: Full Multi-Platform Access Across the Local Network

Employees connect over corporate Wi-Fi or VPN across Mac, Windows, Linux, and mobile devices. Coordinate in groups, dispatch tasks, and approve releases behind the enterprise firewall with total confidence!

Retain Your Code; Retain Your Edge

For enterprises demanding absolute sovereignty:

Zero Security Compromise: 100% compliant with internal audits; sensitive data stays physically on-premises;
Zero Functional Compromise: Enjoy multi-agent group chats, event routing, and cross-platform continuity;
Permanent Organizational Assets: Every skill, context stream, and procedural improvement belongs exclusively to your company.

text:
YOU ARE USING CLAUDE AT 20% OF ITS POWER. THE OTHER 80% IS A SKILL YOU CAN LEARN NOW

Two people open Claude on the same morning with the same plan.

One types "write me a sales email" and gets something bland. He sighs, edits half of it, and decides AI is overrated.

The other spends ninety extra seconds setting things up. She gets a draft she can send almost as is, plus three subject lines and a note on which one to test first.

Same model. Same price. Different operator.

That gap is the real Claude skill. It has nothing to do with secret prompts. It is a handful of habits that pros repeat until they become automatic. My feed this week is full of people sharing prompting cheat sheets and long tip threads, and most of them circle the same idea: Claude rewards people who brief it like a sharp new colleague, not like a search bar.

Here are 12 habits that move you from casual user to pro. Each has a before, an after, and a prompt you can paste today.

BRIEF IT LIKE A NEW HIRE ON DAY ONE

Before: "Write a LinkedIn post about our product launch."
After: you explain who reads it, what they already know, and what you want them to do next.

A new hire with no context guesses. So does Claude. Three lines of background usually beat thirty lines of rules.
Copy this:
Context: I sell accounting software to dental clinics in India.
Readers: clinic owners who hate paperwork and distrust tech.

Goal: get them to book a 15 minute demo.
Task: write a LinkedIn post announcing our new GST report feature.

Ask me anything you need before you start.

LET IT INTERVIEW YOU FIRST

Before: you write a long prompt, guess at what matters, and still miss something.

After: you flip the roles. Claude asks the questions, you answer, and the final draft is built on real details instead of filler.
This one habit fixes most generic output.

Copy this:
I need a one page proposal for redesigning a gym's website.
Before writing anything, ask me up to 7 questions, one at a time,
that would most change the quality of this proposal.
Wait for each answer before asking the next.

SHOW ONE GOOD EXAMPLE

Before: "Make it sound professional but friendly." Nobody, human or machine, agrees on what that means.
After: you paste a sample you like and name what to copy from it.
Copy this:
Here is an email I wrote that got a great response:
[paste email]
Match its sentence length, warmth, and structure.
Do not reuse any of its phrases.
Now write a follow up to a client who has gone quiet for two weeks.

ASK FOR A PLAN BEFORE THE WORK

Before: you ask for a 2,000 word guide and get a wall of text pointed in the wrong direction.
After: you approve an outline first. Fixing a bad outline takes ten seconds. Fixing a bad draft takes an hour.
Copy this:
I want a beginner guide to filing freelance taxes in India.
Step 1: give me only an outline with section titles and one line each.
Stop there. I will approve or edit it before you write.

SET HARD LIMITS, NOT SOFT WISHES

Before: "Keep it short."
After: a number, a format, and a list of things you never want to see.
Claude follows clear constraints well. Vague ones get interpreted, and interpretation is where drift creeps in.
Copy this:
Rewrite this product description.
Max 90 words. Two short paragraphs. No exclamation marks.
Avoid these words: innovative, cutting edge, world class.
End with a single plain sentence that tells the buyer what to do.

MAKE IT ARGUE WITH ITSELF

Before: you accept the first answer because it sounds confident.
After: you ask Claude to attack its own work as a tough reviewer would, then fix what it found.
Pros do this on anything that matters: pricing pages, pitch decks, contracts in plain English, hiring plans.
Copy this:
Read the plan you just wrote as if you were a skeptical investor
who has seen 500 pitches. List the 5 weakest points, ranked.
For each, suggest a specific fix. Then give me the revised plan.

GIVE IT THE REAL FILES

Before: you summarize a 30 page report from memory and ask for advice on your summary.
After: you upload the actual report, the spreadsheet, or the screenshot, and point Claude at the exact part you care about.
Your summary already filtered out the detail that might matter. Let Claude see the source.
Copy this:
I have attached last quarter's sales sheet.
Find the three products with falling repeat purchases.
Show the numbers you used, quote the rows,
and tell me what you would check next before believing the trend.

BUILD A PROJECT FOR WORK YOU REPEAT

Before: every Monday you paste the same background about your business into a fresh chat.
After: you set up a Project. Anthropic describes Projects as separate workspaces with their own chat history and knowledge, where you can add documents and custom instructions that carry into each chat inside it.
Put your style notes, price list, and past best work in once. Every new chat in that Project starts informed.
Instructions to paste into a Project:
You help me run a small interior design studio in Pune.
Always write in Indian English, warm but brief.
Quote prices from the attached rate card only.
If a client asks for something we do not offer, say so plainly
and suggest the closest service we do offer.

ASK FOR A FINISHED THING, NOT A CHAT REPLY

Before: Claude explains how a budget tracker could work, and you are left to build it.
After: you ask for the actual deliverable. Anthropic's help center now describes artifacts as the things Claude makes that you would show someone, from a polished document or slide deck to a working mini app.
Name the format and who will look at it.
Copy this:
Build me a simple interactive tool where I enter monthly income
and fixed costs, and it shows how much I can save each month
and how long it takes to reach 3 lakh rupees.
Keep the layout clean enough to show my partner.

SPLIT BIG JOBS INTO A CHAIN

Before: one giant prompt asking for research, strategy, copy, and a calendar at once. Each part comes out thin.
After: you run it as a chain. Each step gets its own message, and you check the output before moving on.
Example chain for a festive sale campaign:
Step 1: List what our past three campaigns did well and badly
(paste notes). Stop.
Step 2: Based on that list, suggest two campaign angles. Stop.
Step 3: For the angle I pick, write five ad lines. Stop.
Step 4: Turn the approved lines into a 10 day posting plan.
Slower on paper. Much faster in practice, because you never redo the whole thing.

MAKE IT SHOW ITS UNCERTAINTY

Before: you take a confident sounding fact and put it in a client deck. Later you find it was wrong.
After: you ask Claude to separate what it knows from what it is guessing, and to tell you what to verify.
This is the habit that keeps pros out of trouble.
Copy this:
Answer my question below. Then add a section called CHECK THESE
listing every claim a careful editor should verify,
with a note on how sure you are about each one.
If you do not know something, say so instead of filling the gap.

END EVERY GOOD SESSION WITH A REUSABLE BRIEF

Before: you get a great result, close the tab, and start from zero next time.
After: you ask Claude to turn what worked into a template you can reuse. Over a month, you build a personal library of briefs that already work.
Copy this:
That last draft was exactly right.
Write me a reusable prompt template that would produce
work of this quality again, with blanks in square brackets
for the parts that change each time. Keep it under 150 words.

THE MISTAKES THAT KEEP PEOPLE AT 20%

Treating the first answer as final. The first draft is a starting point. The second and third rounds are where quality shows up.
Being polite but vague. "Could you maybe improve this a bit?" gives Claude nothing to act on. Say what is wrong and what good looks like.

Dumping everything into one endless chat. Long threads drift. When the topic changes, start a new conversation, or keep related work inside a Project.

Never reading the output closely. Claude can be wrong with total confidence. Anything with names, numbers, dates, or legal meaning needs your eyes before it goes out.

Copying prompts from strangers without changing them. A prompt built for someone else's business carries their assumptions. Swap in your own context every time.

START THIS WEEK

You do not need to adopt all twelve at once. Try this instead.
Monday: use habit 1 and habit 2 on one real task you were going to do anyway.

Wednesday: pick the work you repeat most and set up a Project for it.

Friday: run habit 6 on something you plan to send next week, then save the prompt with habit 12.

By next Monday you will notice the difference without trying. Your drafts will need fewer edits, and you will stop blaming the tool for answers that were really a briefing problem.
One honest warning: none of this replaces your judgment. It just gives your judgment better material to work with.

The people getting pro results are not smarter. They are just more deliberate about what they hand over.

Save this post now. You will want these twelve prompts within reach the next time a draft comes back flat. And follow @amitmuflis, where I share what actually works with AI tools, tested on real jobs.

Note: Claude features and limits vary by plan and keep evolving, so confirm what your account offers today.

text:
Jayanti of Vasudev Balwant Phadke, often called as the father of the Indian armed revolt, one of the great revolutionary heroes of freedom struggle.

A Chitpavan Brahmin from Konkan, who rallied the lower peasant castes like Dhangars, Kolis, Bhils as well as warrior communities like Ramoshis against British rule. He often attacked rich English businessmen or zamindars, to raise funds for his liberation struggle.

He was born in the coastal Konkan village of Shirdhon, in Raigad district, on November 4, 1845. He showed no interest in regular school education, and preferred to learn wrestling, horse riding.  He dropped out from school, and after some time managed to secure a job as a clerk in the military accounts department in Pune.

His mentor was Krantiguru Lahuji Salve, an expert wrestler, and Dalit belonging to the Mang community, who taught him sword fighting, dandapatta.

But more than anything, Salve, emphasized the importance of getting the backward communities in the freedom struggle to Phadke.

It was during this time too that Phadke, began to attend lectures by M.G.Ranade where he came to know of the Economy drain.

He founded the Aikya Vardhini Sabha, a voluntary organization in Pune to educate the youth, and inculcate nationalist feelings.

He along with Laxman Indarpukar, and Waman Bhave also formed the Poona Native Institution which became MES, one of the leading institutes now.

He   later started the Bhave School in Pune, and currently the MES runs around 77 institutes in Maharashtra.

When the Gaekwad ruler of Baroda was deposed by the British in 1875, Phadke launched the protest against the Govt, and toured the Deccan, then reeling under a severe famine.

However with most of the upper castes not supporting him, he felt only a mass based armed revolt, involving the smaller peasant communities, could strike against the British rule.

These men were taught shooting, horse riding and fencing, and soon Phadke created an armed insurgent group of 300, that aimed to liberate India.

In need of funds, he made his first raid on a small village near Shirur on a local businessman Balchand Sankla.

Phadke attacked Sankla’s home, took the money for the benefit of the villagers, but was branded as a dacoit.

Now on the run, he traveled from village to village, sheltered often by his followers most of whom were the poor peasants.

His followers were mainly peasants, from the backward communities, who were worst hit by the British rule.

Soon he began to conduct many more such raids, primarily around Pune and Shirur, his followers began to swell. His raids were to raise funds for feeding the famine affected peasants, and would often involve cutting off all communications and raiding the treasury.

However Phadke suffered a major blow when his close associate, the Ramoshi leader,Daulat Rao Naik, was killed at Ghat Matha in Konkan on May 10,1879 by Major Daniel, while returning from a raid.

He moved further south, to Srisailam, to escape from the British, where he spent some time incognito at the Mallikarjuna Temple.

Phadke tried to get the Rohillas in the Nizam’s army to fight along side him. However Abdul Haq then Police Comissioner of Hyderabad State, along with Major Henry Daniel, got wind of the plans, and he once again was on the run.

The bounty offer by British was a succces, as one of his associates betrayed Phadke, and on July 20, 1879 he  was captured in a temple at Kaladgi( now in Bagalkot dt), en route Pandharpur, after a bitter fight.

Phadke was taken to Pune for trial, where he was was defended by Ganesh Vasudev Joshi, a prominent lawyer, also called as Sarvajanik Kaka, after the organization he founded.

He was housed in Pune for some time  district sessions court jail, located near Sangam Bridge that currently houses the state CID Dept.

Phadke was later transported to Aden, from where he tried to escape in 1883, breaking the prison door. He however was recaptured and went on  a hunger strike unto death in prison. 

Finally on Feb 17, 1883, he breathed his last in prison, giving up his life for freedom. Coincidentally it was the same year that a certain Vinayak Damodar Savarkar would be born.

Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's epic novel Ananda Math based on the Sanyasi revolt, incorporated episodes from his life too, as part of the story.

There is a pretty good movie in Marathi on Vasudev Balwant Phadke, with Ajinkiya Deo in the lead role, and co starring Sonali Kulkarni, Vikram Gokhale.  Worth a watch.

Star Trek Generations is a 1994 American science fiction film and the seventh installment in the @StarTrek  film series. Malcolm McDowell joins cast members from the 1966 television show Star Trek and the 1987 sequel series The Next Generation, including William Shatner and Patrick Stewart. In the film, Captain Jean-Luc Picard of the USS Enterprise-D joins forces with Captain James T. Kirk to stop the villain Dr Tolian Soran from destroying a planetary system in his attempt to return to an extra-dimensional realm known as the Nexus.

Generations was conceived as a transition from the original cast of the Star Trek films to the cast of The Next Generation. After developing several film ideas concurrently, the producers chose a script written by Ronald D. Moore and Brannon Braga. Production began while the final season of the television series was being made. The director was David Carson, who previously directed episodes of the television series; photography was by franchise newcomer John A. Alonzo. Filming took place on the Paramount Studios lots, and on location in Valley of Fire State Park, Nevada, and Lone Pine, California. The film's climax was revised and reshot following poor reception from test audiences. The film uses a mix of traditional optical effects alongside computer-generated imagery and was scored by regular Star Trek composer Dennis McCarthy.

Star Trek Generations was released in the United States on November 18, 1994. Paramount promoted the film with merchandising tie-ins, including toys, books, games, and a website—a first for a major motion picture. The film opened at the top of the United States box office its first week of release and grossed a total of $118 million worldwide. Critical reception was mixed, with critics divided on the film's characters and comprehensibility to a casual viewer. It was followed by Star Trek: First Contact in 1996.

Plot
In 2293, retired Starfleet officers James T. Kirk, Montgomery Scott, and Pavel Chekov attend the maiden voyage of the USS Enterprise-B. During the shakedown cruise, the starship is pressed into a rescue mission to save two El-Aurian refugee ships that a massive energy ribbon has snared. Enterprise saves some of the refugees before their ships are destroyed, but becomes trapped by the ribbon, and Kirk goes to a control room to help the ship escape. While Enterprise is freed, Kirk is presumed lost in space and dead after the trailing end of the ribbon tears open the ship's hull.

In 2371, the crew of the USS Enterprise-D is in a holodeck computer simulation, celebrating the promotion of shipmate Worf to lieutenant commander. Captain Jean-Luc Picard learns his brother and nephew have been killed in a fire, and is distraught that the Picard family line will end with him. Enterprise receives a distress call from a stellar observatory, where an El-Aurian, Dr. Tolian Soran, launches a probe at the nearby star. The probe causes the star to implode, creating a shockwave that destroys its planetary system. Soran kidnaps Enterprise engineer Geordi La Forge and is transported off the station by a Klingon Bird of Prey belonging to the Duras sisters.

Enterprise crewmember Guinan tells Picard that she and Soran were among the El-Aurians rescued in 2293. Soran—who lost his family when their homeworld was destroyed by the Borg—is obsessed with returning to the energy ribbon to reach the "Nexus", an extra-dimensional realm of wish fulfillment outside normal space-time. Picard and Data determine that Soran, unable to safely fly a ship directly into the ribbon, is altering its path by removing the gravitational effects of nearby stars. Soran plans to destroy another star to bring the ribbon to the planet Veridian III, consequently killing millions on a nearby inhabited planet.

Upon entering the Veridian system, Picard offers himself to the Duras sisters in exchange for La Forge but insists on being transported to Soran directly. La Forge is returned to Enterprise, but unwittingly exposes the ship's defense details through the transmitter installed in his VISOR device. The Duras sisters attack, and Enterprise sustains critical damage before destroying the Bird of Prey by triggering its cloaking device, and firing photon torpedoes when its shields drop. When La Forge reports that the starship is about to suffer a warp-core breach as a result of the attack, Commander William Riker evacuates everyone to the forward saucer section of the starship, which separates from the engineering section just before the breach occurs. The resulting shockwave sends the saucer-section crashing onto the surface of Veridian III.

Picard fails to stop Soran from launching another probe. The Veridian star's resulting destruction alters the ribbon's course, and Picard and Soran enter the Nexus before the shockwave destroys Veridian III. Picard is surrounded by an idealized family, but realizes it is an illusion. He is met by an "echo" of Guinan left behind in the Nexus. Guinan sends him to meet James T. Kirk, who is safe in the Nexus. Though Kirk is initially entranced by the opportunity the Nexus offers to atone for past regrets, he realizes it lacks danger and excitement. Having learned that they can travel whenever and wherever desired through the Nexus, Picard convinces Kirk to return with him to Veridian III, shortly before Soran launches the probe.

Working together, Kirk and Picard distract Soran long enough for Picard to lock the probe in place; it explodes on the launchpad and kills Soran. Kirk is fatally injured in the effort, and Picard buries him at the site. Three Federation starships arrive to retrieve the Enterprise survivors from Veridian III. Picard muses that, given the ship's legacy, the Enterprise-D will not be the last vessel to carry the name.

Star Trek’s Only Christmas Movie Is Sad & Bleak
By Mark Donaldson
Published Dec 24, 2023, 12:00 PM EST
Released in November 1994, Star Trek Generations is the franchise's only Christmas movie, and it's an incredibly sad and bleak story that is all about grief and loss. Generations paired up Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) and Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) for a movie that served as a cinematic passing of the torch between the casts of Star Trek: The Original Series and Star Trek: The Next Generation. As well as being the movie that killed off the legendary Jim Kirk, Star Trek Generations holds the distinction of being the only time that the franchise has explicitly acknowledged Christmas.

As Gene Roddenberry was a passionate atheist, it was very rare that Star Trek celebrated Christmas, barring a handful of references to Charles Dickens and a staff party aboard Kirk's Enterprise. Star Trek Generations changes all this when Captain Picard finds himself inside the heavenly realm of the Nexus, where he gets a glimpse of the life he could have had. However, far from a joyous celebration of the holidays, the illusion of a Picard family Christmas, and the overall story of Star Trek Generations make the festive season a deeply sad time for Jean-Luc.

Star Trek Generations Makes Christmas Sad & Bleak
From the grieving Dr. Tolian Soran (Malcolm McDowell) to the death of Captain Kirk and the destruction of the USS Enterprise-D, Star Trek Generations is a movie about loss. That's not necessarily a bad thing for a Christmas movie, as many of the best holiday movies have a tinge of melancholy to them. It's a Wonderful Life is about a struggling father who contemplates suicide, while every adaptation of A Christmas Carol has to depict the tragic death of Tiny Tim. However, Christmas movies have a happy ending, as Ebenezer Scrooge and James Stewart's George Bailey have a renewed lust for life by the end of their respective stories.

Tragically, Star Trek Generations doesn't provide a happy ending for Captains Picard or Kirk. When Generations starts, Jean-Luc learns about the tragic deaths of his brother Robert and nephew René in a horrific fire. Picard laments now being the end of the family line, and his idyllic Christmas in the Nexus gives him a chance to finally embrace fatherhood. He rejects that idyllic family Christmas to save the universe from Soran. While it's the right thing to do, no Christmas miracle saves Robert and René, nor does Picard learn a valuable lesson from William Shatner's Kirk, who is effectively Jean-Luc's ghost of Christmas past.

Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").

Sako

In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).

text:
Sunset Dunes forever! Thank you San Francisco for voting to save our magnificent coastal park. 

The sacrifice to make Sunset Dunes possible was worth it. Every day is a reward when you get to see thousands of people improving their physical and mental health with an ocean view. Along with all the kids and seniors discovering maximum joy in life.

Sunset Dunes is a success story. The feared traffic “carmageddon” never happened. Yet the positive impact on the environment, local businesses, and every park visitor is very real. And everyone is able to get where they need to go.  

I’m proud that Sunset Dunes is good for the environment and makes life better for people. Let’s celebrate the largest pedestrianization project in California history. We must stop centering public policy decisions around cars if we want to take climate change seriously and help future generations. 

Now that we’ve voted on this issue three times in four years, it’s time to accept that Sunset Dunes is here to stay. There’s no reason to keep fighting over one of San Francisco’s most popular parks.

We are fortunate in life to be able to argue as much as we have about a road and a slightly different driving route. Let’s focus our energy now on addressing the true hardships in the world. 

The process that ultimately created Sunset Dunes was democracy. A vote by the people is the most open and transparent process possible. Each voter had an equal say about what to do with their coast because the coast belongs to everyone.

Support for Sunset Dunes is only growing in areas that voted against it. Before long, a majority in every neighborhood won’t be able to imagine San Francisco without a coastal park and all the benefits it offers. 

We don’t have to fear change. Doing bold and positive things like creating Sunset Dunes is how we create our best San Francisco. 

Our kids, grandkids, and great-grandkids will thank us for choosing the right side of history. 

Read more about why Sunset Dunes is on the right side of history: https://t.co/FjO38YY1Ma

text:
Engineering Wednesday 

100% True story - 

More meaningful for semi folks.

When I graduated with my first engineering degree I had been working nights at an HP fab and going to Chem E classes during the day. The market was red hot. I had offers from :

- Intel Colorado Springs and Arizona (went on tours too) and I recall being told by one hiring manager that he didn't know which fab he was even at, and another manager wanted me in Ireland in two weeks but it was 3 mos to graduation- I was fairly freaked out.

- The HP plant I was at but the engineers urged me to go somewhere else because it was basically sustaining 6 inch technology. 

- LSI Logic (forgettable)

- Philips in New Mexico (closed soon after)

- An optics company still in business

Many of my college classmates though were going to ramp the first 12 inch/300 mm  plant in the USA on the east coast.  So I wanted an interview there - but my on campus interviews with this company were not stellar and the recruiter didn't like me for whatever reason- I later found out he had a good reason. He was on his way out and disliked the company so was suspected of picking questionable candidates.

Anyways, I had the business card of the recruiter, it had phone/Fax. Every day I would get to the student lounge after work and prior to taking an hour nap before classes started I would fax my resume to that number. Every single day for weeks and I had the student lounge phone number as one of my contact numbers since I was never home and I was not carrying a cell phone- too expensive. 

One day someone ran and got me out of the student center and said there was a call for me in the lounge. It was a hiring manager. Ends up this manager went over to the print station to get a blank sheet of paper to write some stuff out on and flipped it over and saw my resume. Then saw my resume was scattered all over the place. He had been screaming at HR to find him some candidates and hadn't liked them.

I started in June of that year When I showed up for work a massive hit to the market took place and they decided against ramping the fab- I ended up going to a sustaining night shift position- engineering would wait a few months longer. More than a couple of my classmates were told there was no longer a job for them, some had even put offers down on homes. It was tough. 

I worked for 8 yrs at that location and extended overseas for various assignments - winning Technical awards, including the most prestigious Technical Award, and various team awards.   I found myself moving into operations management after doing tech development and transfer. Super amazing times with great colleagues I still keep in touch with, we sometimes worked 48 hour shifts in the fabs with cots- 7 days a week on startups but having a great time and appreciating my amazing team and being appreciated. That manager who hired me? Friend for life like many others there.

All because I persistently faxed my resume every day- after no less than 5 rejections, otherwise, I would be telling stories about Intel... but I do have stories about Intel, but that was a later chapter in my life. 

Don't give up and keep applying.

text:
This assessment gained significant support in strategic analyses conducted during the second half of 2026. While the stated objective of the war launched by the United States against Iran in February 2026 was to dismantle Iran’s status as a regional power, various independent assessments—including those from *Asia Times*, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Spanish defense ministry think tank, and an Israel-linked research center—concluded that Iran’s regional influence actually increased, rather than diminished, following the military strikes. This was particularly evident in its control over the Strait of Hormuz and its leverage over energy security in the Persian Gulf. The outcome was not merely a case of the U.S. "failing to win"; rather, the war itself reshaped Iran’s strategic position, transforming it from a state that relied on a network of proxies for "forward defense" into one that employs the blockade of the Strait and economic coercion as its core instruments of "homeland deterrence."

The Divergence Between War Objectives and Actual Outcomes

In an analysis from June 2026, *Asia Times* highlighted this irony: "The United States set out in February 2026 to destroy Iran’s status as a regional power, only to end up consolidating its dominant position." The analysis argued that Iran’s "victory" did not lie in a military defeat of the United States, but rather in the fact that it preserved its regime, demonstrated military and industrial resilience, eroded its adversary’s political will to continue the conflict, and emerged from the war with greater domestic legitimacy and regional prestige. Although the U.S. declared "total victory" in early March, the situation had shifted completely by June—Iran had effectively gained control over the Strait of Hormuz, granting it leverage over the global economy that "no amount of U.S. naval presence could easily offset."

A September analysis by CSIS provided further detail on the mechanisms at play: Iran achieved its two primary strategic objectives—the destruction of U.S. military bases in the Persian Gulf and the exertion of pressure on the global economy through strikes on civilian infrastructure and the closure of the Strait. By the fifth month of the war, Iran had effectively "de-based" the U.S. military from the Persian Gulf, forcing the United States to relocate its assets and operations to bases in Israel, Jordan, and Syria. The CSIS explicitly points out that, for Tehran, this represents not only a strategic victory in wartime but also a crucial step toward achieving its long-term objective: compelling U.S. forces to withdraw from the Gulf region.

The Collapse of Gulf States’ Trust in U.S. Security Commitments

In an analysis from March 2026, CESEDEN—an institution under the Spanish Ministry of Defence—noted that while the "Axis of Resistance" had been severely damaged in less than two years, it had not been destroyed; consequently, Iran would be forced to seek international negotiations to ensure the survival of its regime. However, as the war progressed, this assessment shifted. Citing a report from an Israeli center for security research, Iran’s ILNA news agency acknowledged that the war had not improved the strategic position of the Gulf states; rather, it had rendered their situation more complex and precarious. Deeply skeptical of U.S. security guarantees, the Gulf states began shifting toward a policy of "balancing"—maintaining their reliance on Washington while simultaneously bolstering their own military capabilities, expanding ties with other major powers like China, and working to de-escalate tensions with Iran.

The crux of this assessment is that Iran’s attacks on Gulf territory—while infuriating its neighbors—did not rally them around the United States. Instead, the Gulf states came to view U.S. bases as a "liability rather than a protection," as these facilities brought war, economic devastation, and the destruction of infrastructure to their own soil. Iran reinforced this narrative, signaling to its neighbors that future peace would only be possible if U.S. bases did not return to the Gulf.

A Shift in Iran’s Strategic Focus: From Proxies and Forward Defense to the Straits and Economic Coercion

An analysis from *El País* in October 2026 clearly outlines this transformation: prior to October 7, Iran’s deterrence strategy centered on Hezbollah in Lebanon, based on the logic of "confronting enemies abroad to make any attack on Iran prohibitively costly." Yet, following 2023, Israel demonstrated both the willingness and the capacity to absorb such costs; Hezbollah was severely weakened, Hamas was marginalized, and the Assad regime collapsed. Iran’s strategy of "forward defense" had failed. The new strategy is predicated on a harsher premise: if Iran can no longer keep war from its own borders, it can ensure that the costs of such a conflict extend far beyond them. Its allies are no longer merely a defensive perimeter, but rather instruments for regional and global coercion—driving up costs for the United States, disrupting trade and energy flows, and exposing Washington’s Arab partners to risk, thereby compelling the U.S. to limit its own military operations and restrain Israel. The strategic center of gravity has shifted from the Levant to the Arabian Gulf and the Red Sea.

Defining the Boundaries

This assessment is supported by several independent sources, though they do not entirely align. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) notes that while the future of the U.S. military presence in the Gulf remains uncertain, Iran has already secured a significant strategic victory by "reducing its scale and casting doubt on its value" in the eyes of the Arab Gulf states. *Asia Times* offers a more blunt conclusion: "The hegemon the U.S. sought to destroy is one of its own making." Yet, these analyses converge on a point that does not imply Iran is "invincible." Instead, they suggest that the way the U.S. has waged war—most notably its failure to shield Gulf partners from Iranian retaliatory strikes—has produced a paradoxical outcome: even as Iran’s coercive military capabilities have been diminished, its strategic leverage has been politically enhanced.

"We must come to terms with a civilisation -- the Persian civilisation -- which is millennia-old and combines doctrine and religious faith, the concept of jihad as an armed struggle to the point of ultimate sacrifice, as well as death for one's country and religion," states Cardinal Sako. "The way of thinking and reasoning," he warns, "is different, and this is where the question arises as to how it is possible to establish a dialogue. And the answer is neither easy nor immediate." When discussing Iran, it is essential to understand that "we are not merely dealing with a political phenomenon; we must also take the religious dimension into account. And this element is absent in the West." "In our Eastern world," he adds, "priority is often tied to religion, unlike in the West, where politics and economic interests usually prevail." As has been observed on several occasions in the past, in this sense Christians (and the Church) can play a fundamental role as a bridge between the two cultures, between the two hemispheres of the globe which often struggle to communicate and understand one another: "Peace is not achieved through weapons!"

Patriarch for the whole of Iraq

During his 13 years at the helm of the Chaldean Patriarchate -- one of the oldest rites of the Eastern Church but deeply linked to Rome and the Pope -- there has been no shortage of challenges and dramatic moments, starting with the tragedy of ISIS, which "affected me deeply: their rise has undoubtedly been the most significant event in the recent history of Iraq and its Christians", with the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people in Mosul and the Nineveh Plain. In recent years, a slow process of reconstruction has begun, which is struggling to ensure security and stability despite the efforts of the Church and the Iraqi government, rendering calls for the return of the diaspora communities futile so far. A veritable exodus which, since 2003 following the US invasion and the fall of Saddam Hussein, has led to a collapse in the Christian population, which has fallen from 1.3 million to fewer than 400,000 today. And it is to them that the cardinal's thoughts turn. "Before talking about a return [as promised by the Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to Patriarch Mar Paul III Nona, the cardinal's successor, at a meeting on 11 July]," observes Sako, "we must examine the conditions that drove Christians to leave."

Lasting stability, an environment in which people can live in peace even if they have lost faith in the possibility of achieving it; the prevalence of sectarian affiliations and divisions over the concepts of citizenship and justice; the lack of compensation for damage caused by Daesh [the Arabic acronym for ISIS] and Christian property confiscated by militias, which has not been returned; the spread of corruption; and the deterioration of essential services are just some of the many unresolved issues. "There is a lack of job prospects," he continues, "as well as infrastructure, schools, services and hospitals. Christians will not return unless the culture and laws change, with the establishment of a state founded on citizenship rather than on confessional divisions, and with a reform of the laws. In particular," explains the Patriarch Emeritus, "those relating to the Islamisation of minors and the appropriation of their rights and property. Furthermore, there is still a continuous exodus due to emigration. These are central, and unresolved, issues!"

Security, employment, services and the fight against "endemic corruption" are areas that affect the entire population and Iraq as a whole, a nation -- the cardinal reiterates once again -- that should "base its reconstruction on the value of citizenship". "In many of my speeches," recalls Cardinal Sako, "I have spoken not only on behalf of and to Christians, but also to Muslims, calling for the separation of religion from the state, and for the creation of common ground where all citizens enjoy equal dignity and their rights are respected." He then recalls the significant work carried out in favour of Islamic-Christian dialogue, which "has made great strides in recent years" and is evidenced by meetings with Sunni, Shia and Kurdish authorities, starting with Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, the most important Shia Muslim leader in the Arab country, "whom I have visited twice in Najaf". "Thanks to these efforts," he observes, "and to the relationships built up over time, we have been able to put an end to hate speech. Christians are no longer spoken ill of in the mosques!" "The only thing that struck me and caused me pain," he adds with a note of bitterness, "is the withdrawal of the patriarchal decree issued by the then-president Abdul Latif Rashid, behind which lay the manoeuvring and interests of a so-called Christian militia. However, I have always refused to have Christian militias or sectarian militias." "Before appealing to Christians to return," he emphasises, "the Church must help those Christians who have remained, and give them hope."

The Challenges Facing the Church

Having recently returned to Iraq after attending the last consistory convened by Pope Leo XIV at the end of June, the cardinal then turns his attention to the universal Church and the future of the mission. "The recent synodal experience," he says, "has been a source of satisfaction, because we in the East have been living it for some time. The Synod is a place and an opportunity for working together, for studying problems and challenges, desires and plans, and for making decisions together. This is the Church born of the pontificate of Pope Francis, who emphasised the theme of synodality, of walking together. This aspect is very positive." And regarding his successor, Pope Leo XIV, he says he appreciates his speeches, which are "brief and to the point, using language that speaks to the people. Pope Leo is no longer the head of a dicastery of the Roman Curia, but is the father and shepherd of the entire Catholic Church.

"I hope," he adds, "that his message is for everyone, not just for the West, because we need to speak to the whole world. And his apostolate is not just for Christians, but for everyone when he calls for peace, coexistence and dignity, and for how to engage with other religions, especially Islam."

In an age characterised by speed, the internet and artificial intelligence, in which the Church risks appearing 'slow' and 'wasting' time, he urges us to find new ways forward and 'immediate responses' capable of speaking to today's society. 'It is necessary,' he reflects, 'to seek an approach based on dialogue. People do not accept being guided as mere subjects. We bishops are fathers and shepherds; we must know how to understand them and adopt a style of paternal and fraternal dialogue." As for the Chaldean community, which is getting to know his successor, Patriarch Nona, the cardinal reiterates once more that he "will not comment on the direction or decisions taken, but will remain discreet. My time," he emphasises, "has come to an end, and now a new phase begins." "Every day," the cardinal confides, "I pray for the Patriarch, for the bishops, but above all for the Chaldean Church, which is and remains a MARTYRED Church that has much to offer the universal Church in terms of liturgy, spirituality and biblical pastoral care -- not merely scholastic or philosophical." And as for Iraq and its Christians, the cardinal concludes, "I am sure that the situation will change for the better; there will be full religious freedom and the Chaldean community will continue to grow. I pray for this."

Cardinal Sako was born in Zākhō (northern Iraq) on 4 July 1949. He completed his primary education in Mosul, before attending the local St Jean seminary, run by the French Dominican Fathers. Ordained a priest on 1 May 1974, he carried out pastoral work at Mosul Cathedral until 1979. Sent to Rome, he studied at the Pontifical Oriental Institute, obtaining a doctorate in Oriental Patrology, followed by a doctorate in History at the Sorbonne in Paris and a licentiate in Islamic Studies.

From 1997 to 2002, he served as rector of the Patriarchal Seminary in Baghdad. Upon his return to Mosul, he took charge of the Parish of Perpetual Help until his election as Archbishop of Kirkuk on 27 September 2003, with his episcopal ordination taking place on 14 November. On 31 January 2013, at the synod convened in Rome by Pope Benedict XVI following the resignation of Patriarch Cardinal Emmanuel Delly, he was elected Primate and received the Ecclesiastica Communio from the Pope on 1 February. On 28 June 2018, Pope Francis created him a cardinal. He is a member of the Dicastery for the Oriental Churches, for Culture and Education, for Interreligious Dialogue, and of the Council for the Economy.

text:
I don’t particularly object to a degree of socialism. However, after living in Finland, I’m experiencing increasing socialism and communism fatigue, particularly regarding the extent of state involvement in everyday life.

I miss when my government would let me die in the streets, hungry and cold. In Finland, the government resembles an obsessively controlling older sister who torments me softly, insists on participating in my daily affairs, and maintains an administrative presence in virtually everything I do.

I’m considering returning to the United States with my wife for approximately three months. The objective would be to work, spend time with my family, and accumulate capital while evaluating longer-term opportunities. Employment prospects in Central Finland remain limited, and after two and a half years abroad, I’m increasingly interested in reconnecting with home.

My wife, however, has considerable reservations about America. Apart from one trip to Spain, she has never traveled beyond the Nordic countries.

She also has a complex psychiatric history involving dissociation, bipolar disorder, and psychosis. Her condition has been relatively stable recently, to the extent that I sometimes overlook the difficulties she has experienced.

She endured a traumatic upbringing and was raised by the state. My own childhood, by contrast, was comparatively conventional, with an exceptionally supportive family environment.

These differences are important when considering our respective expectations, behavioral standards, and responses to unfamiliar circumstances. I recognize that my own experiences do not constitute a universal reference point.

A primary consideration is continuity of psychiatric care. Any extended stay in America would require appropriate arrangements for medication, treatment, and coordination with her Finnish healthcare providers.

I believe experiencing American society could be beneficial for her, although the possibility of a psychiatric crisis abroad requires serious consideration, particularly given the structural differences between American and Finnish healthcare.

My intention would be to establish an active itinerary incorporating new environments, experiences, and activities, providing structure and reducing the likelihood of returning to previous destructive behavioral patterns.

I have a generative PCB project in Finland over the next six weeks, so any extended visit would follow its completion.

After approximately two and a half consecutive years abroad, I’m also increasingly conscious of the psychological effects of living outside my native cultural environment.

Most people here treat me well, and I value the relationships I’ve established. Nevertheless, I occasionally encounter moments of cultural dissonance and, much more rarely, explicit xenophobia.

My friends generally do not exhibit these attitudes. Occasionally, someone will approach me and spend twenty minutes discussing stereotypes about California, Las Vegas, or Americans. In rarer instances, someone becomes disproportionately interested in my mixed ancestry.

These encounters are uncommon, but they illustrate how cultural assumptions can occasionally supersede individual identity.

From a professional standpoint, the current labor market presents more substantial concerns. Given the limited availability of suitable positions, particularly for professionals without Finnish-language fluency, maintaining a transatlantic working arrangement may be economically advantageous.

Spending three to six months annually in the United States could provide access to a broader commercial environment while preserving my professional and personal commitments in Finland.

Finnish startups and investment networks also tend to operate within a predominantly Nordic commercial framework. While regional cooperation has its advantages, I believe there is considerably greater potential in developing stronger relationships with American enterprise, capital markets, and industrial institutions.

My interest is in establishing a transatlantic framework for the circulation of investment, technical expertise, industrial capabilities, and professional talent.

The United States offers a scale of enterprise capital, industrial infrastructure, and commercial opportunity that is difficult to replicate within smaller European economies.

Finland, comparatively, is a geographically remote market with a national population smaller than that of a major American metropolitan area. Its advantages lie elsewhere, particularly in its educated workforce, technical competencies, institutional infrastructure, and potential for specialized industrial development.

The principal constraint is not necessarily a shortage of talent or viable ideas, but the availability and allocation of capital required to translate those resources into productive enterprises.

Entire blocks of buildings are becoming vacant in Central Finland, including properties with considerable architectural and commercial potential.

Meanwhile, the region retains an educated, generally well-mannered younger population whose capabilities are not being fully utilized by the local economy.

I see an opportunity to address these conditions through international enterprise development rather than relying exclusively on domestic investment and employment markets.

The objective would be to establish a commercial and industrial pipeline connecting technological innovation, capital formation, infrastructure development, and employment between the American West Coast and Central Finland.

My family’s contracting business in the United States provides a background in industrial operations and systems integration, including experience with major American enterprise environments. I intend to reassess its current activities and determine where those relationships and capabilities might support a broader international strategy.

Developing this network would require institutional partnerships, commercial agreements, and access to substantial investment capital. Organizations and investors operating at the scale of Peter Thiel’s or Elon Musk’s ventures illustrate the level of financial and industrial coordination relevant to such an undertaking.

The objective, however, is not dependence on any particular investor or corporation. It is to develop a commercially viable structure capable of attracting capital through its industrial applications, economic rationale, and long-term growth potential.

With appropriate capitalization and strategic partnerships, I believe an international technology and industrial network connecting the American West Coast with Central Finland could become a substantial enterprise.

There is also considerable potential for reciprocal workforce development. Finnish professionals could undertake temporary assignments in the United States, gaining exposure to larger industrial operations, developing international relationships, and transferring that experience back into the Finnish economy.

American companies, in turn, could establish a greater operational presence in Central Finland through joint ventures, industrial partnerships, research initiatives, and local employment.

Such arrangements should be structured to preserve Finnish cultural identity, economic autonomy, and local institutional interests rather than allowing external investment to displace them.

Under present economic conditions, I believe appropriately structured agreements could generate meaningful interest from regional stakeholders.

I have developed an established network in Central Finland and see opportunities to coordinate local capabilities with American enterprise resources.

The strategic priority is to identify commercially viable projects, align institutional and industrial partners, establish appropriate financing structures, and develop a sustainable mechanism for transatlantic economic cooperation.

I believe the underlying opportunity is substantial. The next step is converting that potential into an executable enterprise strategy.

text:
I was serious when I said I wasn't following it carefully. For example, I didn't know that Mike Rogers was the Republican candidate in Michigan and was also the person who said all those things about AES being connected to the Muslim Brotherhood. (I'm serious. Like, I always could tell who Rogers was from context, but if you had asked me out of the blue who the Republican candidate was in Michigan, I would have drawn a blank.) Anyway, I don't think that's right at all. I hope Rogers loses. 

But I HAVE been thinking about party loyalty and polarization lately. We have been asking activists to take it down a notch for the sake of the Democratic Party. In this context, polarization is usually cited as a bad thing that the most ideological voices foster. Focusing away from group-specific causes might truly be the best move for the Democratic Party, but I'm not sure it's automatically best for those causes. 

There's another way. After attempts at a national suffrage law failed, suffragists took their cause state by state to any candidates they could persuade. Then, when Congress passed the 19th amendment, they again had to go state by state to win ratification. Mostly Republican states ratified, but 7 Democratic leaning ones did too. Then the ratification of suffrage in the 36th state, Tennessee, added the amendment to the Constitution.  

There are lots of causes today that benefit women--like paid family leave--that could probably get support from either party. Rather than quieting down for a few election cycles in hopes that Democrats will be favorable enough to champion women again one day, activists could offer their support to whichever candidate offers to support the issues most important to them--provided the candidates aren't otherwise too abhorrent. This would also calm polarization by blurring the gender lines between the parties. And it might also help elect women, since they may be more likely to support these issues.

text:
No Room for Hate: American Voters Delivered a Clear Message Tonight

The 2026 midterm elections are sending a powerful message to politicians who underestimate the intelligence of American voters: fear, religious prejudice, personal cruelty, and divisive politics are no substitute for leadership.

As election results continue to emerge, Americans are demonstrating that they can see beyond political manipulation and campaigns built around personal attacks, religious identity, and manufactured fear.

Consider Ohio, where Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the governor’s race. The campaign featured an extraordinarily personal attack involving Acton’s estranged mother, dragging painful family history into the political arena. Have political campaigns become so desperate that even childhood trauma is considered a legitimate political weapon?

Michigan offered another disturbing example. Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and groups supporting him ran attacks against Democratic candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed that repeatedly invoked Islam, terrorism, extremism, and September 11.

Rather than focusing on El-Sayed’s policies and qualifications, these attacks attempted to turn his Muslim identity into a political liability.

Disagreeing with a candidate’s policies is democracy. Exploiting his religion to create fear is prejudice.

A Muslim American should never have to prove that he is more American than anyone else simply because of his name or faith.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s political messaging reflected a similar troubling pattern. His repeated warnings about Sharia law, actions targeting a proposed Muslim-led development, and designation of the Council on American-Islamic Relations as a terrorist organization raised serious concerns about the political targeting of Muslim Americans.

Abbott argues that his actions concern public safety and constitutional protections. But America’s Constitution already guarantees both the supremacy of American law and freedom of religion. Protecting one should never require undermining the other.

Muslim Americans are physicians, entrepreneurs, engineers, veterans, teachers, taxpayers, and public servants. They contribute to this nation, raise their families here, and proudly call America home.

Their faith does not make them any less American.

Meanwhile, millions of Americans are struggling with housing costs, healthcare expenses, inflation, wages, and economic uncertainty. Instead of offering meaningful solutions, some campaigns have spent enormous resources encouraging voters to fear their neighbors.

This is not about Democrats being right and Republicans being wrong. Neither party has a monopoly on morality. Both must reject prejudice, personal destruction, and political dishonesty.

Nor should we assume that every voter supporting a candidate endorses every campaign tactic. Americans make political choices for many legitimate reasons.

But politicians must understand that voters are capable of distinguishing between genuine policy disagreements and attempts to manipulate them through hatred and fear.

The greatest mistake any politician can make is to underestimate the intelligence of American voters.

America’s strength has never been that everyone looks alike, worships alike, or thinks alike. Its strength lies in the constitutional promise that people of different backgrounds can enjoy equal rights and opportunities.

As the final results are counted, political leaders should reflect not only on who won or lost, but also on the kind of political culture they are creating.

America does not belong to one religion, one race or one political party. It belongs equally to all Americans.

Those who continue building campaigns around religious suspicion and manufactured divisions should remember one fundamental truth:

American voters are not fools. Their intelligence should never be insulted and their differences should never be weaponized for political power.

THE GREAT TEXAS FLIP: THE NIGHT THE REPUBLICAN FORTRESS FELL!

Texas Turns Political History Upside Down as Democrats Deliver Stunning Election-Night Blows

By TrojanBeast Staff | November 3, 2026

They said Texas was untouchable.

They said the Republican machine was too powerful, too deeply rooted and too well-funded to be defeated.

For over three decades, Democrats tried to break through the red wall of Texas politics. Election after election, their ambitions collided with Republican dominance.

But on November 3, 2026, the political script changed.

Democrat James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in the race for the United States Senate, according to the Associated Press, becoming the first Democrat elected statewide in Texas in more than 30 years.

And the earthquake did not stop there.

In another stunning development, Republican Governor Greg Abbott conceded his reelection race to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, congratulating her and pledging to assist with the transition, even as the Associated Press had not yet formally called that contest.

The Lone Star State had delivered a warning nobody in the Republican establishment could afford to ignore.

THE COLLAPSE OF POLITICAL CERTAINTY

For years, Texas Republicans operated with a significant electoral advantage. Winning statewide was almost an automatic expectation.

The party controlled the governor's mansion, dominated statewide offices and helped shape the national conservative agenda.

But political dominance can create a dangerous illusion: that yesterday's victories guarantee tomorrow's survival.

The 2026 election exposed the weakness of that assumption.

Talarico's campaign focused heavily on affordability, political influence and the concerns of ordinary voters. Meanwhile, Paxton entered the contest carrying years of controversy, although allegations and investigations against him had not resulted in a federal corruption conviction.

The Republican candidate also struggled to reunite his party following a bruising primary.

The result was historic.

EVEN ABBOTT COULD NOT ESCAPE THE WAVE

Governor Greg Abbott had become one of the most recognizable Republican governors in America.

He had money, political infrastructure, incumbency and years of statewide electoral success.

Yet Hinojosa mounted a challenge built around public education, household costs, school vouchers and the influence of wealthy donors.

What once appeared to be an extremely difficult Democratic challenge became a serious threat to Republican control of the governor's mansion.

Abbott's concession was an extraordinary acknowledgment of how dramatically the state's electoral landscape had changed.

THE LESSON FOR REPUBLICANS — AND DEMOCRATS

The Texas results raise uncomfortable questions about political loyalty, candidate selection and the dangers of assuming that traditional supporters will remain permanently attached to one party.

A strong party structure cannot always overcome an unpopular candidate. Huge campaign spending cannot automatically purchase public confidence. And a state's electoral history is not a guarantee of its political future.

For Democrats, the breakthrough offers a potentially powerful model for competing in territory long considered safely Republican.

For Republicans, the message is equally important: Texas can no longer be treated as an unquestioned electoral certainty.

But one extraordinary election does not mean every Texas voter has abandoned conservatism or that the state has permanently become Democratic.

Whether this represents a lasting realignment will depend on what happens next.

THE VERDICT: TEXAS HAS SPOKEN

The greatest political shocks often happen where people have stopped expecting change.

For decades, Texas was the Republican Party's great electoral fortress.

On November 3, 2026, that fortress suffered a historic breach.

The Great Texas Flip is more than a campaign headline. It is a reminder that no political party owns the electorate, no political dynasty possesses a permanent mandate, and no electoral fortress is beyond the reach of determined voters.

Texas did not simply deliver election results. It delivered a political warning heard far beyond its borders.

🇺🇸 IOWA SENATE: AP CALLS IT FOR JOSH TUREK. A DEMOCRATIC FLIP IN A RACE THE PREDICTION MARKETS PRICED AT 50-50.

@turek4iowa (D) defeats @hinsonashley (R), flipping the seat held by retiring Republican Joni Ernst and helping Democrats secure control of the Senate.

AP called the race at 11:35pm ET.

With 93% counted:

🔵 Turek: 50.7%
🔴 Hinson: 46.2%

Some remarkable context.

Donald Trump won Iowa by 13.2 percentage points in 2024. Democrats hadn’t won a Senate election here since 2008.

Turek, a two-time Paralympic basketball gold medallist, has become the first Democrat since Barack Obama in 2012 to win a federal election in Iowa.

📉 HOW THE PREDICTION MARKETS MOVED

The reversal over the final days was extraordinary.

• December 2024: Kalshi’s Republican contract opened above 80%, before Hinson became the candidate.

• October 27: Hinson was still at 60% on Kalshi.

• November 1: Polymarket had Hinson at approximately 56%.

• November 2: Turek surged to 52% on Kalshi, taking his first lead.

• Election Day: Kalshi and Polymarket were both around 50-50.

After the result, Turek’s price shot towards 100%.

📊 WHAT DID THE POLLS SAY?

The final New York Times/Siena poll had:

🔵 Turek: 48%
🔴 Hinson: 47%

RealClearPolling’s final average was even closer:

• Turek: 47.1%
• Hinson: 47.1%

The polling average was tied. The prediction markets were effectively tied.

💰 OVER $22.6 MILLION IN REPORTED TRADING VOLUME

• Kalshi: $19,176,943
• Polymarket: $3,444,620

Combined: $22,621,563.

🎯 WHO BACKED TUREK BEFORE THE SURGE?

@PolyInsider_ recorded several interesting trades.

BreakTheBank

• Bought 136,352 Turek YES shares at 43.2¢.

• Total cost: approximately $58,900.

• Potential profit if held: $77,452.

But there’s more.

The same wallet also bought 155,819 Hinson NO shares at an average 43.3¢, costing approximately $67,522.

That position offered another $88,297 in potential profit.

Across those recorded trades, BreakTheBank could have made approximately $165,749 in combined profit if every position was held through a successful resolution.

zerosmart

• Bought 27,766 Turek YES shares at 42.8¢.

• Total cost: $11,884.

• Potential profit if held: $15,882.

📉 AND WHO WAS ON THE OTHER SIDE?

Another wallet, ndb1, took sizeable positions pointing towards a Hinson victory.

• $94,781 buying Hinson YES at 56.6¢.

• $104,717 buying Turek NO at 56.8¢.

That’s nearly $200,000 in recorded purchases backing the opposite outcome.

Before the election, former NBC political director @chucktodd identified an Iowa win as a potential indicator of a much larger Democratic Senate night.

That’s precisely the wider electoral significance the race eventually acquired.

📈 THE SEVEN-DAY REVERSAL

The chart from @betint_ai captures the story particularly well.

A Republican advantage narrowed. Turek moved into contention. The prices converged around 50-50.

Then the election result arrived and the market moved towards certainty.

What interests me is how much money was committed while the outcome was still so finely balanced, and how differently individual traders positioned themselves.

The polls said it was close.

The prediction markets gave both candidates a serious chance.

Iowa delivered a Democratic Senate flip that helped decide control of the chamber.

text:
🇺🇸 As Democrats, we have every reason to celebrate this electoral breakthrough. We have changed the balance of power in Washington and secured an opportunity to chart a different course. But victory is not an end in itself. It comes with responsibility, expectations and, above all, an obligation to deliver.

We will have the opportunity to shape the legislative agenda, restore congressional oversight and offer a credible alternative to the Trump administration. But winning elections is one thing; turning that victory into effective governance is quite another.

Our immediate task must be to establish clear priorities, rebuild public confidence in Congress and demonstrate that Democratic leadership can make a tangible difference in people’s lives.

We will have to address the cost of living, protect healthcare and voting rights, defend democratic institutions and hold the administration accountable. These objectives must be pursued through a coherent legislative programme rather than a succession of political confrontations.

But what kind of governing majority do we want to be? A Congress focused exclusively on investigating the administration risks missing an opportunity to articulate an alternative vision. Conversely, a legislative strategy that neglects accountability would leave an important part of our mandate unfulfilled.

We will need to find the right balance between oversight, legislation and political positioning. That balance will define the next two years.

The next phase will also test our internal cohesion. Our coalition brings together moderates, progressives, establishment figures and a younger generation seeking a different political direction. Electoral unity does not automatically translate into legislative unity. We will have to manage our differences without losing sight of the common purpose that brought us here.

And then there is 2028.

These midterms will inevitably reshape the presidential succession debate. Potential candidates will begin positioning themselves, alliances will emerge and disagreements over our party’s identity, economic priorities and foreign policy will become more visible. We must begin preparing for that debate without allowing the 2028 race to undermine the work we have to do now.

For Donald Trump, losing congressional control fundamentally changes the political environment of his final two years. Investigations, hearings, subpoenas and budget negotiations could become recurring confrontations. We will have oversight powers, but we will not have the votes to automatically override presidential vetoes or enact our entire programme. We must understand both the opportunities and the limits of our new position.

The immediate political message is clear: voters have entrusted us with a greater share of responsibility. We must rise to that responsibility.

Winning the midterms is the opportunity. Governing through Congress, exercising meaningful oversight and presenting a credible alternative for 2028 is our responsibility.

The blue wave has changed the political landscape. What we do with this mandate will determine whether this victory becomes a lasting political turning point or simply another electoral moment.
