8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

WWE Unreal Season 3 will be released on July 21.

How many episodes are in WWE Unreal Season 3?

WWE Unreal Season 3 will have five 50-minute episodes.

Here's the latest Netflix news as of mid-January 2026!

The streaming giant is kicking off the year strong with a packed slate of new releases, ongoing buzz around major deals, and continued subscriber growth.

Major Highlights

Netflix is reportedly in the midst of a blockbuster acquisition: the company has agreed to buy Warner Bros. in a massive deal valued at around $82.7 billion (with some reports citing $72 billion in equity value).

This move aims to supercharge its content library with iconic franchises like Harry Potter and classic films.

However, there's drama — Paramount Skydance has launched a competing hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, adding some high-stakes industry intrigue!

Netflix ended 2025 with over 301.6 million global subscribers, solidifying its position as the top streaming platform.

What's New & Coming in January 2026

January is loaded with fresh originals, from thrilling mysteries to romantic adaptations and long-awaited returns.

Here are some of the standout releases that are lighting up the charts and generating buzz right now:

People We Meet on Vacation — A charming rom-com adaptation of the Emily Henry novel, starring Emily Bader — it's been topping the charts as one of the biggest new movies of the year so far!

The Rip — This high-octane action-thriller directed by Joe Carnahan reunites Ben Affleck and Matt Damon — it's one of the most anticipated films dropping mid-month, perfect for fans of intense heist vibes!

His & Hers — A gripping mystery series starring Tessa Thompson and Jon Bernthal, following estranged spouses racing to solve a murder. It's been climbing the Top 10 with strong buzz around its twists.

Bridgerton Season 4 — The Regency-era drama returns later in the month (Part 1 premiering around Jan 29), with plenty of masquerade glamour and romance — the premiere events are already making waves!

Other notables include:

Kidnapped: Elizabeth Smart (true-crime docuseries)

New seasons of hits like Unlocked: A Jail Experiment, Love Is Blind: Germany, and WWE Unreal

Stand-up specials and reality shows keeping the variety flowing.

Plus, don't miss the Stranger Things 5 making-of documentary One Last Adventure, which premiered earlier this month for fans wanting a deep dive into the finale. Netflix is clearly doubling down on big stars, book adaptations, and high-energy originals to keep viewers hooked in 2026. (Grok)

Netflix: News

Netflix is a global streaming service providing a vast library of films, TV shows, documentaries, and mobile games. As of 2026, it has approximately 325 million paid members across more than 190 countries.

Pricing & Plans: Subscription plans typically range from $7.99 to $24.99 per month.

Content Offerings: Includes "Netflix Originals" (like Stranger Things and Squid Game), licensed content, and a growing selection of live programming and video podcasts.

Device Compatibility: Streamable on smart TVs, game consoles, smartphones, tablets, and via https://t.co/YlumK0CxOt.

Features: Supports offline downloads, personalized recommendations, and a dedicated "Netflix Kids" experience with parental controls.

Recent 2026 Developments

Warner Bros. Merger News: As of January 21, 2026, Netflix has moved toward an all-cash $27.75-per-share offer to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, aiming to outbid Paramount.

Market Reaction: Despite a Q4 earnings beat, Netflix shares saw a 7% decline in some markets (e.g., Frankfurt) on January 21, 2026, due to investor concerns regarding the financial weight of the Warner Bros. acquisition.

New Initiatives: The company is expanding into vertical video features for mobile and has recently launched video podcasts.

Live Events: Upcoming live events include the world-record climber Alex Honnold's "Skyscraper Live" ascent of Taipei 101 on January 23, 2026.

(In Case You Missed It)

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

Related promotional items and apparel are available, including:

Action Figures: Mattel has released sets like the "Hall of Champions" 4-pack featuring legendary superstars seen in the series.

Here's the latest Netflix news as of mid-January 2026!

The streaming giant is kicking off the year strong with a packed slate of new releases, ongoing buzz around major deals, and continued subscriber growth.

Major Highlights

Netflix is reportedly in the midst of a blockbuster acquisition: the company has agreed to buy Warner Bros. in a massive deal valued at around $82.7 billion (with some reports citing $72 billion in equity value).

This move aims to supercharge its content library with iconic franchises like Harry Potter and classic films.

However, there's drama — Paramount Skydance has launched a competing hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, adding some high-stakes industry intrigue!

Netflix ended 2025 with over 301.6 million global subscribers, solidifying its position as the top streaming platform.

What's New & Coming in January 2026

January is loaded with fresh originals, from thrilling mysteries to romantic adaptations and long-awaited returns.

Here are some of the standout releases that are lighting up the charts and generating buzz right now:

People We Meet on Vacation — A charming rom-com adaptation of the Emily Henry novel, starring Emily Bader — it's been topping the charts as one of the biggest new movies of the year so far!

The Rip — This high-octane action-thriller directed by Joe Carnahan reunites Ben Affleck and Matt Damon — it's one of the most anticipated films dropping mid-month, perfect for fans of intense heist vibes!

His & Hers — A gripping mystery series starring Tessa Thompson and Jon Bernthal, following estranged spouses racing to solve a murder. It's been climbing the Top 10 with strong buzz around its twists.

Bridgerton Season 4 — The Regency-era drama returns later in the month (Part 1 premiering around Jan 29), with plenty of masquerade glamour and romance — the premiere events are already making waves!

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

Related promotional items and apparel are available, including:

Action Figures: Mattel has released sets like the "Hall of Champions" 4-pack featuring legendary superstars seen in the series.

November 4, 1926 — The Flying Boat That Carried 60 People

On November 4, 1926, an extraordinary sight appeared over Lake Constance.

A Dornier Superwal flying boat took off carrying 60 people aboard — an impressive demonstration at a time when passenger aviation was still in its early years.

With the heavily loaded aircraft moving across the water, the Superwal gathered speed and lifted into the air. It remained airborne for about 45 minutes, covering more than 90 miles before returning safely to Lake Constance.

For people watching in 1926, aircraft capable of carrying large numbers of passengers were still something remarkable. Flying boats like the Superwal represented one possible future of long-distance air travel, using lakes, rivers, and coastal waters as natural runways.

One hundred years later, the flight offers a glimpse of an era when engineers were still discovering just how large — and how capable — passenger aircraft could become.

Beyond the Beaches: Kalymnos, Where the Mountains Meet the Climbers

Kalymnos may be known as a traditional island of sponge divers, but over the years it has developed another identity that attracts visitors from all over the world. Its spectacular limestone landscape has turned it into one of the Mediterranean's leading destinations for sport climbing.

The island's cliffs, caves and rock formations provide an extraordinary variety of routes, from beginner-friendly climbs to demanding challenges for experienced climbers. The scenery is equally impressive, with many climbing areas offering views across the Aegean and towards neighbouring islands.

Climbing has become an important part of Kalymnos' tourism scene, bringing an international community of visitors to an island that still retains a strong local character. The combination of outdoor adventure, traditional hospitality and beautiful coastal scenery makes it a destination with a very different feel from the typical beach holiday.

For anyone interested in discovering the climbing scene, there is plenty to explore:
•  Visit Grande Grotta: One of the island's best-known climbing areas, famous for its dramatic cave and impressive rock formations.
•  Explore sectors around Masouri: This area is a popular base for climbers, with numerous routes and easy access to accommodation and restaurants.
•  Find routes for your level: Kalymnos offers a wide range of climbing grades, although appropriate training and equipment are essential.
•  Enjoy the climbing community: Meet visitors from different countries who come together through their shared love of the sport.
•  Take a break by the sea: Between climbing sessions, enjoy a swim or relax at one of the island's beautiful beaches.

Of course, Kalymnos is not just for climbers. The island has a fascinating maritime heritage, traditional settlements and a coastline worth exploring. Pothia, the main town, is particularly interesting for its colourful waterfront and connections with the sponge-diving industry.

The climbing season is often particularly popular in spring and autumn, when temperatures can be more comfortable for outdoor activity. Conditions vary, so climbers should check local advice and route information before heading out.

Whether you're travelling with climbing gear or simply curious about why people come here from around the world, Kalymnos offers a memorable experience. It is an island where adventure comes naturally, and where the next great view might be waiting just above the next climb.

What exactly were people fleeing, and what made Texas such a haven?

Let's put the political talking points aside and talk about facts.

Yes, Texas generally has lower housing costs than California and New York. The numbers support that. But what about groceries, electricity, transportation, healthcare, wages and property taxes?

People in Texas were still struggling to afford rent, buy groceries, pay their bills and keep gas in their vehicles. Moving across state lines didn't magically eliminate the economic pressures facing working Americans.

And let's stop pretending inflation and rising living expenses were exclusively Democratic-state problems. They were national problems.

If you're going to argue that Texas offered a better quality of life, then show the complete picture: wages compared with living expenses, housing affordability, property taxes, insurance, healthcare and household purchasing power.

I'm not interested in Republican or Democratic campaign slogans. I'm interested in measurable results.

Show me the facts, not the political narrative.

🇮🇳 DRDO is preparing to validate the extended-range capability of India's Long Range Anti-Ship Hypersonic Missile (LR-AShM) before production clearance.

The missile has already demonstrated a range of around 1,500 km. DRDO is now targeting an extended range of up to 3,500 km.

• The boost-glide missile reaches hypersonic speeds, reportedly peaking at Mach 10.
• It can engage both stationary and moving maritime targets.
• Its manoeuvrable flight profile makes interception more challenging.
• DRDO is planning 2–3 trials to validate the extended range before production clearance, targeted for 2028–29.

At 3,500 km, this capability could significantly expand India's maritime denial reach across the Indian Ocean.

DRDO has also offered the system to the Army and Air Force for potential ground-attack variants.

If cleared, this could become a major addition to India's long-range conventional strike arsenal.

𝐆𝐚𝐳𝐚’𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬 

Gaza society reflects traditional Arab customs, including a strong tradition of keeping weapons.

Weapons were present in Gaza long before Hamas, during Fatah's time and even earlier. Gaza's Arab tribal society comprises several clans led by sheikhs who oversee daily affairs. Powerful clans governed Gaza long before Fatah's politicisation and Hamas's Islamisation of its society.

Gaza's armed groups are distinct from its clans. Hamas and other factions have organised military wings, while clans, often called "𝐇𝐚𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐬”, are extended family networks that can offer social support, mediation, and local representation. Individual clan members may carry weapons or join a faction, but this does not make the entire clan a militia.

Weapons in Gaza reflect overlapping histories of armed political factions, weak or contested policing, family and neighbourhood self-protection, and arms circulating through conflict and smuggling. These histories should not be reduced to a single "𝒄𝒍𝒂𝒏 𝒘𝒆𝒂𝒑𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒄𝒖𝒍𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆."

Gaza's weapons come through multiple channels, not a single "𝒄𝒍𝒂𝒏 𝒂𝒓𝒔𝒆𝒏𝒂𝒍." Armed political factions, conflict, smuggling, and periods of weak policing and public institutions have shaped this environment. Hamas and other factions have established and maintained their own military structures, while local armed groups may rely on family or neighbourhood ties.

𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑒 𝑤𝑒𝑙𝑙-𝑘𝑛𝑜𝑤𝑛 𝑒𝑥𝑎𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑒𝑠 𝑖𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒 𝑤ℎ𝑦 𝑎𝑛 𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑟𝑒 𝑓𝑎𝑚𝑖𝑙𝑦 𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑙𝑑 𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑏𝑒 𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 𝑎 𝑠𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑙𝑒 𝑎𝑟𝑚𝑒𝑑 𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛:

𝐃𝐨𝐠𝐡𝐦𝐮𝐬𝐡: Members of this Gaza City family have been associated with armed organisations, including the Army of Islam. Reporting also describes members with different political affiliations. The family's history does not mean every Doghmush is involved in armed activity.
𝐇𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐬: Some members have been linked to clashes with Hamas, while the wider family has at times rejected claims that a particular armed group represents it.
𝐀𝐥-𝐌𝐚𝐣𝐚𝐲𝐝𝐚: A family network in Khan Younis that has experienced armed confrontations with Hamas.
𝐀𝐛𝐮 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐛'𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐩: Yasser Abu Shabab led an armed group in southern Gaza that drew on local ties. Reporting connected it to aid looting and described Israeli support for anti-Hamas armed groups.

Not everyone who carries a weapon is a Hamas member or a terrorist. Some may be clan members protecting their family or tribe from criminal syndicates or rival factions. 

𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑦 𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑟𝑦 𝑔𝑢𝑛𝑠 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑒 𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑜 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑎𝑖𝑟 𝑜𝑛 𝑜𝑐𝑐𝑎𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑠𝑢𝑐ℎ 𝑎𝑠:

1. 𝑾𝒆𝒅𝒅𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒄𝒆𝒍𝒆𝒃𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔
2. 𝑭𝒖𝒏𝒆𝒓𝒂𝒍 𝒄𝒆𝒓𝒆𝒎𝒐𝒏𝒊𝒆𝒔
3. 𝑬𝒙𝒑𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒔𝒖𝒑𝒑𝒐𝒓𝒕 𝒇𝒐𝒓 𝒑𝒐𝒍𝒊𝒕𝒊𝒄𝒂𝒍 𝒐𝒓𝒈𝒂𝒏𝒊𝒔𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔
4. 𝑷𝒊𝒔𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒚𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒔𝒐𝒍𝒊𝒅𝒂𝒓𝒊𝒕𝒚 𝒘𝒊𝒕𝒉 𝒄𝒍𝒂𝒏𝒔 𝒐𝒓 𝒈𝒓𝒐𝒖𝒑𝒔
5. 𝑬𝒙𝒑𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒂𝒏𝒈𝒆𝒓 𝒐𝒓 𝒓𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒏𝒈𝒆 𝒂𝒈𝒂𝒊𝒏𝒔𝒕 𝒓𝒊𝒗𝒂𝒍𝒔

Armed self-protection in Gaza is better explained by conflict, political factionalism, and uneven state authority than by any inherent trait of Arab culture. Clan networks can influence local security, but they are diverse social institutions rather than uniform armed groups.

text:
4 November 2026.
Today in History.

1652
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The storm winds of the past few days had subsided by daybreak.
Several crops, including peas, barley, wheat and others, had been destroyed.
A number of structures inside the fort had also sustained severe wind damage.

1653
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The south-south-easter was still blowing at daybreak. At the same time, the clouds began to gather.
The Commander of the Cape, Jan van Riebeeck, writes that it was quite a sight to see the clouds rolling over Table Mountain.
The team that had been sent to the forest to saw planks and beams arrived at the fort later that morning with a fully loaded wagon.
Along the way, the team had encountered a Khoi man. Probably because of the events involving Harry, the team decided to bring the man back to the fort with them.
The Commander, however, immediately recognised him as a Saldanha man, having previously conducted a trade transaction with him.
The man was offered something to eat and drink, which he accepted.
Communication took place through gestures, as well as a few words that the Commander had learnt over time.
According to the man, "his people" were already on their way to the fort to engage in trading.
The man voluntarily spent the night inside the fort and walked back to his people the following day.

1654
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The south-south-easter began blowing late the previous afternoon. The same wind continued to rage throughout the night and into the following day.

1655
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak brought a cool, overcast day. The wind was moderate and blew from the west.
A ship, the Salmander, dropped anchor in Table Bay towards dusk.
The ship had been forced by the wind to anchor at Saldanha Bay and also near Dassen Island.
Many of her crew had been suffering from scurvy while they were waiting at the islands. An adequate supply of vegetables, birds and birds' eggs soon helped the crew recover.
Despite the above, the Commander sent fresh vegetables, meat and water on board.
The Salmander also brought news of a strange ship that had been sighted near Saldanha Bay.

1656
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The early morning brought a warm, sunny day at the Cape.
A number of men were sent to the forests to collect beams that had already been sawn and cut.
Firewood was also collected at Ronde Doorn Bosjen that day.
Most of it was intended for the brick kilns in which the bricks would be fired.
After consultation, it was decided to use only one kiln, as the demand for bricks was limited.

Sunday, 4 November 1657.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak at the Cape is described simply as pleasant.
No incidents are recorded.

1658
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak brought a dry day with a north-westerly wind. Large, rolling clouds moved constantly across the Cape.
The West Vriesland sent a small boat ashore. However, the wind pushed the vessel far off course, and the boat sank near the Salt River.
The Commander sent another boat to assist the men from the West Vriesland. Unfortunately, this boat capsized in the breakers, and four sailors drowned.

1659
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The entries for 3, 4 and 5 November 1659 were recorded together under the same date in the diary.
The days are described as pleasant, with a cool breeze blowing from the north (from the sea) every afternoon.

1795
The Republic of Swellendam accepts British rule.
Background.
A group of burghers entered Swellendam on 17 and 18 June 1759 under the leadership of Petrus Delport.
Landdrost Anthonie Faure, serving under the VOC, together with several other officials, was forced to resign and leave Swellendam.
In short, this was the origin of the Republic of Swellendam.
The Battle of Muizenberg took place on 7 August 1795, and shortly afterwards the Cape was permanently occupied by Britain.
On this day, the Republic of Swellendam accepted British authority and once again became part of the Cape Colony.

1834
Louis Tregardt's slaves confiscated on this day.
Background.
In 1828, Louis Tregardt sent his son Carolus (18) across the border into Gcalekaland to rent land there from Hintsa, paramount chief of the Gcaleka.
Approximately 8,000 sheep, 1,300 cattle and 33 horses were taken along.
Louis put his affairs in order and left the Colony in 1834.
Several other families, including that of Hans Dons de Lange, accompanied him.
A slave belonging to Louis, one Phillis, deserted during this period and made his way to Grahamstown, where he laid a complaint against Louis for mistreatment.
A certain Captain A.B. Armstrong, together with 25 Pandour soldiers (Khoikhoi soldiers), arrived at Louis's homestead on this day and confiscated his remaining slaves.
This event and its date represent a turning point in Louis Tregardt's life, as it was thereafter that he decided to leave the Colony permanently.
Tregardt and his family were at that stage settled along the Kei River in Gcalekaland. Although his lease agreement with the Gcaleka was still valid for some time, he, together with several other families, packed up and moved to the Bamboo Mountains.
The Gariep (Orange River) was permanently crossed early in the summer of 1836.

1835–1840.
The recollections of Voortrekker J.H. Hatting during the Great Trek.

1842
Major Smith had rejected Andries Pretorius's request to meet the previous day.
Later that same day, Pretorius left his camp with 50 armed Voortrekkers and moved towards the British camp.
According to Hatting, the force concealed itself behind a nearby hill, while one man proceeded towards the British camp.
This individual once again delivered a verbal request to Major Smith, asking him to meet Pretorius outside the laager.
Smith, however, sent word that he was not interested in talking.
At the same time, he made it clear that he had occupied Port Natal on the orders of the British Crown and that he was there, among other things, to protect the Zulu people.
Pretorius subsequently returned to the laager with the others.

1836
The diary of Louis Tregardt.
A short description.
Part Three.
Louis initially began writing his diary in pencil.
Later, however, he started using ink.
In 1899, Carolus related that his father wrote in the diary every evening after outspanning.
Carolus further explained that the sap of a waboom tree was used as ink, as were ink bushes on occasion.
According to him, there were three to four different types of ink bushes. The ink was boiled several times before being used.
A peacock feather was used as a pen, although a vulture's feather was sometimes used as well.

Saturday, 4 November 1837.
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Louis and the rest of the party gathered that morning to discuss a plan of action.
Jan mentioned that Botha had seen a low mountain pass over which they might possibly be able to trek.
Louis, on the other hand, was of the opinion that they should trek back a stage that day, or perhaps even further, so that they could get away from the tsetse flies.
Jan, however, was not keen on the "heavy" sand they had encountered on their way there.
Presumably, some of the others agreed with him, as no trekking took place that day.
Botha and Pieta shortly afterwards departed to investigate the mountain pass.
Willem and Cornelis looked after the sheep that day, while Isaak and Strijdom assisted with the cattle.
Louis must have taken a ride out to the cattle that day, as he recorded that the herd numbered 444 head.
The red cow also calved that day.

1837
The Battle of Kapain began on this day.
The Battle of Kapain was preceded by the Battle of Mosega on 17 January 1837.
Both Mosega and Kapain were the result of several preceding events.
Firstly, there had been the attack, together with the murders and destruction of the Erasmus camp during August 1836.
These events were followed a few days later by the Battle of the Vaal River and the Liebenberg murders near the present-day town of Parys.
Later that same year, in October 1836, the Battle of Vegkop also took place.
The Battle of the Vaal River and the Battle of Vegkop must be regarded as the first major clashes between the Matabele and the Voortrekkers.
Following these events, the Voortrekkers all withdrew to Blesberg – Thaba Nchu.
From there, the military campaigns against the Matabele (under Mzilikazi, their king) were launched, first at Mosega and then at Kapain.
The final and decisive Battle of Kapain began on this day, 4 November, and came to an end on 12 November 1837.

1837
There are no entries for this day in the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.

Sunday, 4 November 1838.
From the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.
Reverend Smit writes that someone in the laager fired the cannon during the early hours of the morning.
Everyone was awake afterwards. The culprit, however, remained unknown.
(Possibly some mischievous youngsters?)
The Reverend further writes that he secluded himself outside the laager early that morning to pray.
He subsequently preached from:
Joshua 5, verses 9–10,
as well as Jonah 2, verses 8–9.
Four couples were also married that day.
There were many people attending the service, and there was not enough room for everyone inside the tent.
Towards dusk, another service was held in the tent of the Voortrekker de Beer, where the sermon was based on Mark 6, verses 33–34.
After the service, joyful news reached the laager that five Cape-wagons carrying families were standing at the Tugela River and were on their way to join the laagers.
The family of J. Jakobs was apparently also on its way from the Colony.
(The Jacobs family mentioned by the Reverend was probably spelled Jacobs rather than Jakobs. In total, 43 different Jacobs families participated in the Trek.)

1863
The first railway line in South Africa ran from the Point to Durban.
On this day, the first railway line between two towns, namely Cape Town and Wellington, was opened.

1896
Jan Eloff was appointed Commissioner of Johannesburg.
At this time, Johannesburg was little more than a mining town.

Saturday, 4 November 1899.
Anglo-Boer War.
Day 25 of the war.
- At the very beginning of the war, the British War Office had planned for the entire British Army to advance through the Orange Free State along the central railway network and then systematically occupy the country.
Lieutenant-General Redvers Buller revised this plan on this day and divided the British Army into four sections:

1. Lieutenant-General Methuen would advance along the railway line to relieve Kimberley. He had 15,000 men and 30 guns at his disposal.
2. Lieutenant-General F. Clery would cover the right flank in Natal with 21,000 men and 30 guns.
3. Lieutenant-General Gatacre would cover the eastern section of the front with 4,300 men and 18 guns.
4. Lieutenant-General J.D.P. French would cover the western front towards Colesberg with 5,000 men and 18 guns.
All remaining troops fell under General F.W\.E.F. Forestier-Walker's command. His responsibility was to protect the telegraph lines in the Colony.
- Kimberley remained under siege.

Chief Commandant C.J. Wessels sent an ultimatum to Colonel Kekewich, demanding that he surrender or face the consequences.
Chief Commandant Wessels also proposed that the women and children leave the town.
- Free State commandos entered the Cape Colony, crossing the border at Norvalspont.

Sunday, 4 November 1900.
Anglo-Boer War.
Day 390 of the war.
- President M.T. Steyn and Chief Commandant De Wet left Klerksdorp and moved towards Bothaville and General Froneman.

Monday, 4 November 1901.
Anglo-Boer War.
Day 755 of the war.
- The government of the South African Republic was at Roodepoort, just west of Ermelo.
- General B. Hamilton's forces captured 93 burghers, 116 horses and 55 vehicles of various types at Oshoek, near Ermelo.
- General M. Maritz arrived in the vicinity of Piketberg.
- General J.C. Smuts was still in the Colony, at Matjiesfontein. Deneys Reitz and several others rejoined him.
- The Ladies' Committee visited the Mafeking concentration camp. According to them, conditions there had deteriorated dramatically since their previous visit.

They submitted a request for the camp superintendent, R.L. McCowat, to be replaced.
- General Bruce Hamilton's forces captured 93 fleeing civilians, 116 horses and 55 vehicles of various types at Oshoek, west of Ermelo.

1910
James Molteno officially opened the first Union Parliament of South Africa as Speaker on this day.
The first Union postage stamps also appeared on the same day.

1933
The first properly organised jukskei match took place on this day between the Klein Drakenstein and KWV teams.
The South African Jukskei Council was established as a result in October 1940.

1939
A group of Afrikaans-speaking men gathered on this day in the office of Dr H.F. Verwoerd.
At that stage, Verwoerd was still associated with Die Transvaler newspaper.
The purpose of the meeting was to discuss a draft constitution for a possible republic.
Among the well-known individuals present were Professor H.B. Thom, Dr T.E. Dönges, Dr N. Diederichs and Dr A. Hertzog.
For practical reasons, the task of drafting the document was entrusted to Dr Verwoerd.
Shortly afterwards, he submitted a 29-page draft constitution.

🚨Pro-war Z community treated the European protests as a secondary story. Reactions, however, varied. Some channels mocked European governments, while others offered detailed accounts of the protests’ causes or criticized the police for their harsh treatment of demonstrators. Despite these differences, both approaches fed into the broader narrative of chaos and European authorities’ loss of control:
⠀
▪ Two Majors — a Z channel linked to the security bloc
⠀
Responding to reports of an arson attack on Limoges town hall, the channel reposted a sarcastic remark:
⠀
“How France has flourished under Macron.”
⠀
A subsequent post acknowledged socioeconomic causes of the unrest but reproached Macron for supporting Ukraine’s armed forces “at the expense of the French.” The channel then described curfews and restrictions on demonstrations as a “rare display of authoritarianism.”
⠀
On October 25, it claimed that 70,000 police officers and gendarmes had been mobilized, alongside army units, special forces and armored vehicles. Its interpretation:
⠀
“A very convenient rehearsal for suppressing broader protests in the event, for example, of mobilization.”
⠀
▪ Rybar – a Z channel linked to Russia’s military ministry
⠀
Rybar cautioned against expectations of a continent-wide uprising:
⠀
“There is no sign of a pan-European revolution yet. […] The nearest-term scenario, therefore, is not a single wave but a series of national crises, each unfolding at its own pace.”
⠀
▪ Yuri Podolyaka – a leading Russian pro-war blogger
⠀
Podolyaka described the protests as “not merely a series of coincidences, but the execution of someone’s plan.” He speculated that:
⠀
“Its outcome is supposed to be a major war in Europe; ideally, as I understand it, for whoever commissioned it, Europe against Russia.”
⠀
His predicted sequence was the rise of “right-wing dictatorships,” the “elimination of the left” and then “a campaign of conquest to the east.” He concluded:
⠀
“And the timing fits very well with military preparations in European countries.”
⠀
▪ Zakhar Prilepin – a pro-war writer
⠀
Prilepin sided with demonstrators against European elites. He approvingly shared a statement by Haz Al-Din, chairman of the American Communist Party:
⠀
“The French elite want war with Russia. The French people should bring war against the rotten French elite instead.”
⠀
These reactions do not form a single coherent explanation. Yet they repeatedly portray European authorities as repressive or losing control. The most conspiratorial accounts go further: protests, police deployments and military preparations become parts of an alleged plan for war against Russia, reinforcing the narrative that Europe is preparing aggression against Moscow.

text:
Trump Lost Congress. America's AI Industry May Have to Rethink the Cost of Expansion.

The November 3 midterm elections delivered a serious political setback to Donald Trump. Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress, with Republicans losing important races in traditional strongholds including Texas, Ohio and South Carolina. Midterm losses are nothing unusual for the party holding the White House, but the scale of this defeat matters. In 2018, Trump lost the House while Republicans expanded their Senate majority. This time, his party lost control of Congress altogether.

Financial markets reacted quickly. Nasdaq 100 futures fell more than 2% at one point during the vote count, while the dollar weakened, Treasury yields declined and Asian technology stocks came under pressure. Investors were already questioning the enormous capital spending commitments being made across the AI industry. The election has added another consideration to those calculations: how much of America's planned AI infrastructure expansion will actually move forward under a divided government?

The more revealing developments, however, are taking place far from Washington.

For years, announcements of multibillion-dollar data center projects were welcomed as opportunities for local economic growth. They promised construction jobs, tax revenue and infrastructure investment. But as AI facilities grow larger and their electricity requirements increase, residents are paying closer attention to the costs that accompany those promises. New power plants, transmission lines, water infrastructure and land development all have to be financed somehow.

According to Ballotpedia, voters across 10 states faced 41 data center-related ballot measures on November 3. Of those, 28 would impose restrictions or express support for restricting development if approved. In Trenton, Ohio, nearly 80% of voters supported restrictions on new large data centers, affecting a proposed development route for an Amazon Web Services project. In nearby Ashville, more than 80% rejected a development framework involving data centers and an associated natural gas power plant.

These results are not simply evidence of opposition to AI. Many communities want investment, but they also want a clearer understanding of who benefits from it and who pays when things go wrong. A facility can generate substantial revenue for its owner while leaving local residents concerned about electricity bills, water consumption and the long-term use of public infrastructure.

The election gives those concerns greater political weight. Democrats themselves remain divided over how AI development should proceed. Progressives such as Bernie Sanders have called for a pause on certain large data center projects to reassess their energy and environmental impact. More moderate Democrats support continued investment while seeking stronger commitments on electricity costs, employment and community benefits. The disagreement is largely over the conditions under which expansion should take place, rather than whether the United States should continue competing for AI leadership.

There is also considerable overlap between the two parties. Before the election, the House voted 417 to 3 in favor of legislation requiring states to consider separate electricity rates for large power users. Washington may be divided over AI regulation, safety and technology policy toward China, but protecting households from the costs of large new electricity customers has attracted support across party lines.

Georgia offers a useful example of how these political changes can reach the balance sheets of technology companies.

Democrats gained a 3–2 majority on the Georgia Public Service Commission, which oversees utility rates, resource planning and major electricity supply arrangements. Before the election, Georgia Power had already secured regulatory approval for a phased electricity supply agreement of approximately 3.2 GW for OpenAI's Camellia project. The arrangement includes up to 1 GW of flexible demand, allowing electricity supply to be reduced during periods of grid stress.

The agreement also places infrastructure cost responsibilities on the project. Such arrangements were taking shape long before the election, but the incoming commission will have an opportunity to influence the terms of future investment. The central issue is whether the electricity demand projected by data center developers is sufficiently reliable to justify building expensive generation and transmission infrastructure years in advance.

Power companies cannot simply dismantle a new plant if a major customer withdraws or uses less electricity than expected. Someone must cover the remaining costs. Depending on the contracts and regulatory decisions involved, those costs may fall on developers, utilities, other large electricity customers or investors. That allocation of risk will increasingly matter when companies negotiate long-term power supply.

This is where the political story becomes a financial one.

A data center can have customer commitments, purchased GPUs and billions of dollars in financing, yet still fail to generate revenue on schedule if grid connections or construction approvals are delayed. Oracle's rising financing costs and the dependence of some compute infrastructure developers on long-term customer contracts and external borrowing already illustrate the financial pressure behind the expansion. These problems existed before November 3. Changes in permitting, electricity pricing and financial guarantees could make the difference between projects that reach operation and those that remain stuck on paper.

Large technology companies are better equipped to handle that uncertainty. Microsoft, Amazon and Google can negotiate long-term electricity agreements, provide substantial guarantees and shift investment between locations. Smaller compute providers often have less flexibility, particularly when their financing depends on a small number of customers and a specific delivery date.

That creates an awkward possibility for policymakers. Rules intended to protect households and hold technology companies accountable could also make it harder for smaller competitors to enter the infrastructure market. The companies best able to satisfy expensive regulatory and financial requirements may be the same companies those rules were intended to constrain.

The consequences could extend beyond the construction industry.

If building new compute capacity in the United States becomes more expensive or more difficult to finance, AI application providers will have another reason to examine how efficiently they use that capacity. Higher infrastructure costs do not automatically translate into higher API prices. Improvements in hardware, utilization and model efficiency can offset some of that pressure. But for businesses making millions of model calls every month, even modest differences in the cost of completing a task can have a meaningful impact on profitability.

A company running customer support, document processing or AI automation does not necessarily need the most capable frontier model for every request. Complex reasoning and high-value tasks may justify premium pricing, while routine classification, information extraction and many conversational workflows can often be handled by smaller or less expensive models.

This is where open-weight models and competing cloud inference services become commercially important.

Models such as DeepSeek and Qwen can be deployed by different providers across multiple regions. Businesses can compare them based on actual task performance, latency, reliability and total cost rather than relying on a single model vendor. An open-weight model is not inherently cheaper to operate, and deploying it outside the United States does not guarantee lower costs. The economic advantage comes from the combination of model efficiency, infrastructure economics and competition among providers.

For companies operating internationally, that flexibility creates more options. Certain workloads can be placed where compute is more economical, provided latency, data residency and other operating requirements are met. Others will remain close to customers or within specific jurisdictions. Over time, more businesses may adopt a mixture of models and infrastructure providers instead of committing all their AI workloads to one platform.

That could open opportunities for Chinese AI models in international markets. They do not have to outperform the most advanced American proprietary models on every benchmark to become commercially relevant. If DeepSeek, Qwen or other models can deliver acceptable results at a substantially lower cost for particular business tasks, companies have a financial reason to consider them.

There is another important distinction here. Wider adoption of Chinese open-weight models does not necessarily mean more revenue for Chinese API providers. American cloud platforms can host the same models and retain the customer relationships, billing infrastructure and service revenue. The commercial winners will be the providers that combine competitive model performance with reliable delivery, flexible integration and a convincing cost structure.

Seen in that context, the midterm elections are part of a broader change in the economics of AI.

America is unlikely to retreat from the global AI race. Trump still has substantial executive authority, and Democrats have little incentive to surrender the country's technological advantages. But the next phase of expansion will involve tougher negotiations over electricity, infrastructure financing, community benefits and long-term liabilities.

Capital spending can continue growing even as individual projects fail to secure financing or reach operation. Established operators with reliable power access may become more valuable, while heavily leveraged developers face greater pressure. At the same time, businesses purchasing AI services will keep looking for better performance at lower cost.

The result could be a striking division in the industry. AI infrastructure may become more capital-intensive and concentrated among a smaller number of large operators, while the market for AI models and inference services becomes more competitive and geographically diverse.

American AI infrastructure may become more expensive to build. That does not mean businesses around the world must pay more for every unit of intelligence they consume.

The 2026 midterm elections will not decide which AI model wins. But they may influence who can finance and operate the next generation of computing infrastructure, and how much of that cost eventually reaches the businesses using it.

As AI moves deeper into everyday commercial operations, the ability to deliver reliable intelligence at a sustainable cost may prove more valuable than simply owning the largest collection of GPUs.

text:
LESSONS FOR NIGERIA'S POLITICAL CLASS

There is a profound lesson for Nigerian politicians in the American midterm elections: political dominance is neither permanent nor an entitlement. It must be continually justified through competent governance, public confidence and demonstrable accountability.

The political experience of Texas, where no Democrat has won election to a full US Senate term since 1988, illustrates how deeply entrenched political loyalties can be. Yet no electoral stronghold is impregnable. Changing political circumstances, public dissatisfaction and effective opposition mobilisation can overturn what once appeared to be an unassailable political order.

The most important lesson is that incumbency does not confer immunity from electoral rejection. Political endorsements, enormous campaign expenditure, propaganda and well-oiled political machinery cannot indefinitely insulate an administration from the consequences of poor governance.

American voters are concerned about the realities of everyday life, the cost of living, employment, healthcare, housing and economic security. These are not matters that can be resolved through political rhetoric or grandiose promises.

Nigeria's political class must understand that citizens are not political subjects whose loyalty can be purchased, manipulated or inherited. They are sovereign voters entitled to demand measurable improvements in their living conditions.

Opposition parties, equally, must offer credible alternatives rather than merely exploit public dissatisfaction.

Above all, the legislature must exercise its constitutional oversight responsibilities rather than function as an appendage of the executive.

The ballot box is not a permanent certificate of political ownership,it is a periodic referendum on the performance of those entrusted with power.

Olufemi Aduwo
