text:
Is This a Turning Point?

Washington has shifted the political balance of power, but Wall Street faces a far bigger question: Who Will Pay for the Future?

Macroeconomic and market analysis | 4 November 2026
The loudest message of election night did not come from Washington. It came from towns, counties and small polling stations, where Americans voted in large numbers on something that, only two years ago, was considered a technical detail in business plans: data centers.

Of the 45 local ballot measures on whether to restrict or allow data centers, 30 had results as of 11:26 p.m. Eastern Time. Fourteen counts were complete, and the side seeking to restrict construction won all fourteen. The side seeking to allow it did not win anywhere. A few hours later, restriction was leading or had won in 29 of the 30 measures with results. Add the six measures decided earlier in the year, and the tally was almost perfect: the restrictors won every one. The results are unofficial, and roughly three quarters of precincts had been counted, but the direction is hard to ignore.

It will take Wall Street a few weeks to fully grasp this story. While investors were asking whether Congress would now turn Democratic, voters had already answered another, perhaps more important question: how much electrical grid capacity, water and land are they willing to sacrifice for computing capacity that others will use?

Democrats Won Congress. What That Means, and What It Does Not
According to projections by US media, Democrats won the House of Representatives in the midterm elections and, according to most reports, the Senate as well. The final picture will be known once counting is complete, and projections are not certified results. President Trump has reportedly already said he will accept the outcome.
The political significance is large, but it has to be read precisely. The new Congress begins work on 3 January 2027. Trump remains president, retains the veto and keeps broad executive powers over trade and foreign policy. Most major legislation in the Senate is still constrained by the 60-vote rule, and a veto can be overridden only by a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
Democrats therefore gain tools of oversight: committees, investigations, a stronger position in budget negotiations and in confirming senior appointments. What they do not gain is the ability to simply rewrite economic policy. So the real question for markets is: where will oversight actually bite? The most likely candidates are fiscal policy, which is left with no room for new large stimulus, scrutiny of the big technology companies and, which is where the story gets interesting, the regulation of data centers, energy use and water.
When checked, a prediction market was pricing the probability of an impeachment event before the end of Trump's term at around 82 percent. That figure sounds dramatic, but it has to be read with caution. Impeachment requires only a simple majority in the House, whereas removal requires a two-thirds majority of senators. Trading on that market was also relatively thin, at around 117,000 dollars. For portfolios, possible budget standoffs and regulatory disputes matter more than the mere existence of a proceeding.

Texas: When the Grid Matters More Than the Chip
Imagine a company that has ordered the chips, bought the land, convinced investors and already written future revenues into its projections. All it lacks is permission to connect to the electrical grid.

This is not a hypothetical. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican governor Greg Abbott in Texas, a victory the state has not seen in decades. Texas is also one of the key hubs of planned data center expansion, and by some estimates it is expected to host roughly a quarter of all new capacity coming online by 2030. On 21 September, Abbott halted the issuing of certain new permits and grid-connection procedures until reviews of the impact on the grid and on water resources are completed. His supporters hoped that, after a win, he would lift the measure. Now investors are asking whether a temporary administrative obstacle is becoming a permanent one.

Because of the Texas halt, a major question is also whether the timeline is at risk for roughly 50 gigawatts of projects, around a fifth of the recorded US project pipeline. An important caveat: these are not data centers that have been built, but projects at various stages of development, many of which may never be built in their original form. During the campaign, Hinojosa argued for additional restrictions and greater accountability for developers. This is not yet a confirmed regulatory outcome, but it is a risk that every scenario must include.

And this is where the investment story turns. Until now we asked how many graphics processors $NVDA can make and how quickly hyperscalers can buy them. From now on we must also ask who will build the power connections, who will pay for the grid expansion, who will supply the cooling water and who bears the cost if a project stalls over permits. As in the energy sector, which has known this for decades, the biggest obstacle is often the infrastructure that has to support the technology.

The Stock Market No Longer Rewards Every Piece of Good News
Tuesday's trading brought relief at first glance. The S&P 500 gained roughly 0.4 percent, the Nasdaq around 0.8 percent, and the Dow Jones lost 0.4 percent. Nvidia gained 2.3 percent and regained its title as the world's most valuable company, while Apple lost 1.9 percent after warning that higher memory costs would pressure its margins.

On closer inspection, the picture is less pretty. The rebound was carried by a narrow group of companies. By a rough estimate, the semiconductor index SOX lost around 19.5 percent from the start of October to the start of November, while the S&P 500 gave up about 2.6 percent. A gap of around 17 percentage points is not ordinary fluctuation but a marked relative weakness in the segment that had long been the engine of the rally. $INTC is down by more than half from its record after its biggest one-day drop since 1971. The four largest technology companies lost a combined total of around 894 billion dollars in market value within a few days of reporting results, and an ETF of so-called neoclouds is down for the year after an October slide, even though the S&P 500 is up.

Here lies the key distinction between three phenomena that the market likes to mix up. 
The first is a valuation correction: investors pay lower multiples for future growth. 
The second is a deterioration in business fundamentals: orders, margins and cash flows fall short of expectations. 
The third is a regime change: capital demands a higher risk premium even when business remains strong. October's moves are consistent mainly with the first and the third. There is no evidence for the conclusion that demand for AI infrastructure is drying up.

Three Suppliers, Three Different Bills
The after-hours results offered the strongest counterargument to the collapse thesis. At the same time, they showed how different in quality the same growth can be.

$AMD  generated 13.38 billion dollars in revenue in the third quarter, 45 percent more than a year earlier. The data center segment reached 8.5 billion dollars, almost twice as much as last year. Management expects total revenue growth of more than 80 percent in 2027. But the numbers hide a figure that deserves more attention: 1.07 billion dollars of non-cash expense related to purchase warrants that AMD offered to OpenAI and Meta as part of large chip supply agreements. This is not a cash outflow and not a sign of fictitious revenue, but it is an economic cost. The buyer gets the option of an equity stake in the seller, and the seller gains orders. Anyone following the cycle has to ask how much of the growth is being bought with equity incentives.

$ANET  generated 3.66 billion dollars in revenue, 58.5 percent more than last year, and for the next quarter it guides to 3.9 to 4.0 billion dollars and an adjusted operating margin between 48 and 49 percent. Strong growth combined with exceptional profitability is what investors are looking for.

$SMCI sold 19.9 billion dollars, against 5.0 billion a year earlier, but its gross margin fell sequentially from 17.5 to 12.7 percent, and operations consumed 434 million dollars in cash. Someone who looks only at revenue growth sees two similar successes. Someone who looks at margins and cash flow sees two different businesses.

$META and the Question of Who Finances the Build-Out
If the first link in the chain is the construction of data centers and the second is supplier revenue, the third link remains the most important test: will companies and consumers generate enough additional cash flow to justify the initial investment?

On 3 November, Meta announced a new bond issue of 15 billion dollars, including a tranche maturing in 2031 with a 5.85 percent coupon and a tranche maturing in 2033 with a 6.25 percent coupon. According to reports, at the end of September it had around 83.7 billion dollars of debt, and it estimates this year's capital expenditure at 135 to 145 billion dollars. Meta is not at risk; its credit quality and market access remain excellent. But the change is obvious: the cost of capital has become a central variable. Higher financing costs have a double effect, as they reduce the present value of future profits and raise the required return on new projects. That is why AI can keep growing at an exceptional pace while the shares of its suppliers nevertheless go through a long correction.

Bonds Are Sending a Message That Equities Should Not Ignore
After the election, US government bonds gained. The yield on ten-year Treasuries was around 4.91 percent in the morning, roughly six basis points lower than the day before, while the euro strengthened against the dollar by around 0.5 percent and traded at about 1.125.

The simplest explanation is an expectation of less fiscal expansion and more political gridlock. But bonds can also strengthen because investors are seeking safety or expect slower growth. The difference is essential. A fall in yields amid lower inflation and stable growth is good for equities. A fall driven by fear of weaker activity, together with widening credit spreads, is not.

Additional caution is warranted because of positioning. According to CFTC data, in the week to 27 October asset managers increased their net long positions in ten-year Treasury futures to a record level of roughly three million contracts. A crowded trade can drive a trend, but it also creates the risk of a sharp reversal if inflation picks up again. Today the quarterly refunding announcement from the US Treasury is due: net borrowing from the private sector is estimated at around 618 billion dollars for the last quarter of 2026 and roughly 800 billion for the first quarter of 2027. What will matter is not only the amount of debt but also its maturity.

And the labor market? September's job openings data showed 7.52 million vacancies, beating expectations. There were around 3.37 million quits and around 1.64 million layoffs, which is not the picture of a labor market in deep recession. If labor demand stays stable while energy remains expensive, the Fed will find it hard to cut interest rates quickly. That is precisely the environment in which high valuations are most vulnerable.

Gold and Copper: Two Stories About Patience
By rough estimates, $GOLD is down around ten percent this year and is on course for its worst year in more than a decade. But context changes the picture: in the three years before, it gained roughly 14.6 percent, 25.5 percent and 67.4 percent, which together comes to around 141 percent. According to the World Gold Council, central banks made net purchases of around 321 tonnes in the third quarter and 675 tonnes in the first nine months, which is six percent more than last year. Central banks do not think in terms of a few trading sessions. Gold strengthened after the election together with a weaker dollar and lower yields, but that is only a short-term layer on a long-term story.

$Copper is an even better test of discipline. The structural story is almost perfect: electrification, power grids, data centers and slow supply growth. UBS forecasts that the global copper deficit will grow from 219,000 tonnes this year to 379,000 tonnes in 2027, with a 2027 price target of 15,500 dollars per tonne. COMEX futures climbed in September to a record of roughly 6.93 dollars per pound and traded around 6.57 dollars in early November. Technical support from March is around 5.25 dollars, which is about a fifth below the price.

But history is unforgiving. In past cycles, copper fell after record highs by more than 70 percent in 2008, by around 58 percent between 2011 and 2016 and by almost 38 percent in 2022, and not because the world needed less copper, but because cycles, inventories, financing and positioning can dominate long-term demand for years. An investor can correctly identify a decade-long trend and still pick a very bad moment to buy.

The Sentiment Paradox
Short-term volatility jumped ahead of the election: the one-day VIX reached around 23.2 and exceeded the VIX at around 20.8, which shows that investors paid more for one day of protection than for a month. Beneath the surface, there is a more interesting contradiction. The survey of US individual investors by AAII shows that, on average, they hold more than 70 percent of their portfolios in equities, and their cash share is near a nine-year low, even though sentiment expressed in the surveys is persistently bearish. People speak pessimistically, yet their portfolios are optimistic. That is fuel for growth if conditions improve, and fuel for selling pressure if they deteriorate.

The summary of what the market is saying is almost literally understandable: prove the value of artificial intelligence soon, or cut capital spending sooner.

What to Watch in the Coming Weeks
For decision-making, a list of indicators is more useful than a forecast. First, whether the relative strength of semiconductors against the broader market stabilizes or keeps making new lows. Second, whether bond yields and credit spreads stay calm or spreads widen. Third, whether the large companies' capital expenditure keeps outpacing their cash flow. Fourth, whether the rebound spreads to most stocks or is carried by a handful of companies. Fifth, whether regulatory measures actually delay projects and contracts, or remain at the level of announcements. Today brings an additional test: the ISM services index, especially prices paid and employment, ADP employment, and results from $QCOM , $ARM and $APP after the close. Tomorrow the Bank of England decides, and US payrolls follow on Friday.

The Bill Will Be Paid
The election did not create the capital markets' difficulties. It did add a new layer of uncertainty at a moment when investors were already asking about the sustainability of the largest investment cycle in the history of the technology industry. A Democratic Congress can increase scrutiny of the concentration of economic power. The Trump administration will continue to shape trade and foreign policy. In between, companies will keep operating, investing and seeking capital.

Artificial intelligence remains technologically important and potentially transformative for the economy. But the market increasingly separates revenue from profit, profit from cash flow and cash flow from return on invested capital. The next chapter of the cycle will not be decided only in Washington or in the factories that make the most powerful chip. It will be decided by those who can turn growth into lasting free cash flow, and by those who must take on ever more of other people's risk to finance the next phase.

And perhaps we will remember November 2026 as the moment when Wall Street stopped asking only how big the future would be and began seriously calculating how much that future would cost. The voters in the counties have, in their own way, already started writing the bill.

Analytical view, 4 November 2026. Market levels refer to morning trading. This text is not individual investment advice.

text:
CBC’s US election coverage looked like CNN with a Canadian logo: it fails the JSP, strains the Broadcasting Act, and the Eurovision episode shows the government can steer the network when it wants

CBC’s election-night coverage of a Kansas Senate (or House) race treated the story exactly as an American cable network would: a real-time Associated Press projection, a detailed bio of the Democratic winner (Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor with no prior elected office), and a historical deep-dive into 1930–1932 Kansas politics, Charles Curtis leaving for the vice-presidency under Herbert Hoover, the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, its role in worsening the Great Depression, and an explicit parallel to the tariff powers Donald Trump is using today. The segment even dropped the classic Ferris Bueller’s Day Off economics-class line (“Anyone? Anyone?”)

None of that is required for Canadian audiences. A Canadian public broadcaster’s mandate under the Broadcasting Act is to offer information and analysis “concerning Canada and other countries from a Canadian point of view,” with programming that is “predominantly and distinctively Canadian.” The practical Canadian questions are concrete and bilateral: what does a Democratic gain in Kansas do to the politics of USMCA review, softwood lumber, dairy access, energy exports, or border measures? Instead, the coverage assumed an American cultural frame and an American political narrative

CBC’s Journalistic Standards and Practices require balance, impartiality, and a Canadian perspective. Framing Hoover-era protectionism as the direct historical precursor to Trump’s tariffs, while celebrating a Democratic flip with American pop-culture callbacks, is the opposite of that standard. It is indistinguishable from CNN or MSNBC election coverage

The Eurovision episode already showed the practical limits of the “arm’s-length” claim. Carney’s government wrote Eurovision participation into the budget next to a large CBC funding increase, sources confirmed the Prime Minister’s personal involvement, and he announced the decision as a foreign-policy signal. The Broadcasting Act forbids formal direction, yet the government shaped major programming choices when it served Carney's agenda. Coverage that systematically adopts American progressive framing on U.S. elections sits in the same pattern—especially with a PMO that includes an American Democratic operative in a senior U.S. relations and operations role

Taxpayers fund the CBC to serve Canadian interests under the Act and its own standards. When the product on election night is American history, American legislation, American movies, and American partisan framing, that purpose is not being met @brodiefenlon @PresidentCBCRC @CBCOmbud

text:
Ever look at Washington and think the 50/50 split is a rigged script to keep us from teaming up against them? Your head is in the right place…a completely unified country is how revolutions start.

But as conservatives, we know human nature and the free market explain this better than a conspiracy.

Think of the parties like two guys selling trucks in the same county. If one offers a better deal, he steals customers. The other guy doesn't go broke…he just adjusts his deal to get his half back. Both sides constantly adjust their bait to catch exactly half the pond.

King Solomon said there is nothing new under the sun, and he was right. Ever since the 1990s, this competition has been so tight that a unified government…holding the White House, House, and Senate…is incredibly rare, and it almost never lasts past the two-year midterms.

Our Founders (who were super freaking smart, btw) were terrified of absolute power, so they built a system full of friction. Whether our side wins or loses, remember: it is always temporary. The pendulum always swings back, the drivers swap out, and no single group ever gets permanent rule over us.

Try not to lose any more sleep on this. God is/has/and always will be, in control. 💯

POLAND, NORWAY AND FINLAND ARE PREPARING THEIR CITIZENS FOR A POSSIBLE WAR WITH RUSSIA

Three European countries are expanding military training programs as concerns grow over the Russian threat, Germany's Bild reports.

In Norway, 2026 has been designated the Year of Total Defence. Protecting the country is no longer considered exclusively the military's responsibility. Government institutions, businesses and ordinary citizens are expected to play their part.

Norway's Home Guard has more than 40,000 members, compared with approximately 23,000 personnel in the regular armed forces. Lawyers, electricians, bankers, farmers and other civilians periodically leave their jobs for military exercises. Around 5,000 armed reservists participated in major exercises in Oslo in September.

Former Norwegian Prime Minister Erna Solberg put it simply: "We stand in the Russians' way."

Finland trains approximately 45,000 reservists annually. They practice urban warfare, drone operations and battlefield medical assistance. Civilians can also attend voluntary courses in weapons handling and first aid.

In September, more than 2,000 people participated in civil defence exercises in Kuopio, preparing for cyberattacks, power outages and missile threats.

Poland has launched several civilian military training initiatives. Its "In Readiness" program offers weekend courses covering basic military skills and evacuation procedures. Around 18,000 people registered during the first weeks after its launch in 2025.

Another program, "Train with the Army," teaches volunteers weapons handling and other practical military skills. Demand has been so high in some cities that waiting lists have become necessary.

Polish schools also teach emergency survival, first aid and responses to armed conflict. Firearms training is available from age 14.

Europe is increasingly preparing not only its armies, but entire societies for the possibility of war.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed how countries along NATO's eastern and northern borders think about national security.

text:
🇷🇺 Russia Explores 100MW Floating Nuclear Power Plants for Four African Countries

Africa's growing economies need reliable electricity to support industrialisation, manufacturing, infrastructure development, and economic expansion. However, energy shortages and unreliable power supply continue to limit productivity across several parts of the continent.

As countries explore new ways to strengthen their energy infrastructure, Russia's state-owned nuclear energy corporation, Rosatom, is advancing discussions around an unconventional solution: floating nuclear power plants.

The company is reportedly exploring the deployment of 100-megawatt floating nuclear power plants (FNPPs) in four African countries: Egypt, Togo, Namibia, and Tanzania.

Unlike conventional nuclear power stations, which require extensive land-based infrastructure and lengthy construction processes, floating nuclear plants are designed as transportable power-generation units that can be positioned near coastal locations and connected to electricity grids.

The proposed technology could offer several opportunities for countries seeking alternative sources of reliable electricity.

One major advantage is deployment flexibility. Floating nuclear facilities could provide power to coastal communities and industrial locations without requiring the same level of onshore construction associated with traditional nuclear infrastructure.

Another important aspect is the proposed commercial arrangement. Under a potential Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) model, Rosatom could retain responsibility for operating, maintaining, and refuelling the facilities, while host countries purchase the electricity generated.

This approach could reduce the operational burden on countries that lack extensive domestic nuclear energy capabilities.

The potential applications extend beyond household electricity. Reliable power could support energy-intensive industries, mining operations, port infrastructure, and water desalination facilities.

However, deploying floating nuclear technology in African waters would require careful consideration of regulatory frameworks, nuclear safety, environmental protection, maritime security, financing, and long-term waste management.

The discussions also highlight a broader development within Africa's energy sector: the search for innovative infrastructure models capable of addressing the continent's growing electricity requirements.

As African economies pursue industrial growth, the ability to secure reliable and affordable energy will remain central to their competitiveness.

Floating nuclear power represents an emerging option in that conversation, although its actual impact will depend on how these proposals progress from discussions to implementation.

text:
Tristan Thompson on Building Wealth, Managing Risk, and Inspiring the Next Generation

In this episode of When Shift Happens, I sit down with NBA champion, entrepreneur, and investor @TThompson to discuss his journey from growing up in Toronto to competing at the highest level of professional basketball, and how those experiences shaped his approach to investing, wealth, and emerging technologies. We explore the lessons he learned from financial mistakes, why he believes patience and discipline matter more than chasing quick returns, and how he is positioning himself for a future shaped by digital assets, artificial intelligence, and robotics.

From Financial Struggles to an NBA Championship

Growing up in Toronto in a Jamaican family, Tristan watched his mother work three jobs while his family navigated financial hardship, government assistance, and his brother's epilepsy. These experiences fueled his ambition to create a better life for the people who had sacrificed so much for him.

His first sporting passion was soccer, influenced by Jamaica's historic qualification for the 1998 FIFA World Cup. But as he grew taller and basketball gained popularity in Toronto, particularly through Vince Carter and the Raptors, he found himself drawn to a different sport. That decision eventually took him to the University of Texas, the NBA, and an NBA championship. Basketball gave him the financial means to support his family, but it also developed the discipline, resilience, and competitive mindset that now guide his investments.

Why Tristan Invests in People Before Companies

After competing against some of basketball's greatest players, like LeBron James, Kobe Bryant, and Stephen Curry, Tristan believes that adaptability, not talent alone, determines who succeeds. He looks for similar qualities in entrepreneurs. "I invest in great founders that will do whatever they can to achieve greatness, but also still have some sense of reality on when to pivot."

That balance between determination and adaptability is particularly important because Tristan recognizes it as one of his own weaknesses. Raised with a tough-love mentality, his instinct when something goes wrong has always been to work harder, but becoming a parent helped him understand that persistence isn't always the answer. Different situations, like different children, require different approaches.

Today, he applies that lesson to venture investing. While prestigious university credentials can help founders attract capital, he is more interested in their work ethic, conviction, and willingness to dedicate themselves completely to building something meaningful.

Learning to Build Wealth Without Losing It

Tristan's entry into investing showed him that financial education matters, and that earning and managing money are entirely different skills. Professional athletes, particularly younger athletes who secure lucrative endorsement and name, image, and likeness deals, are vulnerable to people looking to profit from their wealth. His own approach was shaped by experienced mentors, and now he tries to offer that same guidance to younger athletes.

His advice is to start small, understand your appetite for risk, and never assume every investment will deliver extraordinary returns. In fact, his firsthand experience with a memecoin trade where he lost the potential for multiple seven figures taught him the importance of taking profits and how greed can undermine good decisions.

He believes this explains why wealthy people across different professions sometimes lose everything. Success can encourage overconfidence, excessive leverage, and the desire to prove that an investment thesis was right. The danger is especially real in crypto, where rapidly accumulated wealth can begin to feel disconnected from its real-world value. But for Tristan, growing up with limited resources taught him that money represents opportunities to support a family, purchase tangible assets, and build long-term security.

Taking Calculated Risks in Crypto and Venture Capital

Tristan's investment strategy combines long-term conviction with a willingness to take calculated risks. In crypto, Bitcoin represents approximately 10-15% of his personal wealth, and he considers it as both digital gold and a form of long-term savings or retirement account. He also holds Solana, which he credits for making financial products more accessible and easier for everyday users.

His venture investments follow a similarly diversified approach. Early-stage companies offer the possibility of substantial returns but carry significant risk, while later-stage opportunities are less risky. One successful investment was Poppi, which he invested in at the pre-seed stage and was later acquired by PepsiCo. He is also exploring opportunities in physical AI and robotics, including an investment in Prometheus, which could transform warehouse operations. For him, the broader lesson is that building wealth requires balancing conviction with an understanding that even promising investments can fail.

Investing in a Future Shaped by AI and Robotics

Tristan's interest in emerging technology extends beyond digital finance. He is particularly enthusiastic about robotics. He sees opportunities in practical applications that make businesses more efficient, from helping consumers find reliable service providers to automating warehouse operations. His investment thesis focuses on companies using technology to solve tangible problems rather than simply building another AI model.

However, he also recognizes that increased automation will transform employment. As machines take over more repetitive tasks, workers will need to demonstrate what makes their contributions difficult to replace. His answer is creativity.
"Life creates creativity. Stress creates creativity. Heartache creates creativity."
He believes human experiences, relationships, and problem-solving abilities will remain valuable even as technology advances.

The Next Championship Is Bigger Than Basketball

For someone who has already achieved success at the highest level of professional sports, Tristan's ambitions remain remarkably competitive. He wants to establish himself in venture capital and prove that business excellence doesn't require a conventional background or an elite university degree.
But his ultimate definition of success extends beyond personal wealth.
"I don't want to be at a table and be the only king at the table. I want to be at the table with a bunch of kings and queens."

Tristan wants to inspire the next generation to recognize that success and financial freedom aren't limited to careers in sports or entertainment. He hopes to show others, particularly those from backgrounds like his, that there are other paths to building wealth and creating better opportunities for their families. And he plans to keep building without losing sight of why he started.

text:
Poster Child for Green Energy Becomes Buyer of Emergency Power | Vijay Jayaraj, Washington Times

The road out of my hometown in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu runs between rows of wind turbines. For most of my life I treated them as scenery, admiring them as a technical marvel.

Danish engineers helped install the state’s first 110 turbines between 1985 and 1992, and the Muppandal cluster in Kanyakumari district grew into India’s largest onshore wind farm at 1.5 gigawatts. By 2012, wind was delivering up to 35% of the state’s electricity for days at a stretch, a share that industry observers said only Denmark had matched.

In 2017, a friend who ran a factory told me how erratic swings in electricity supply had caused damage and lost orders, wiping out months of profits. He linked the problem to the surging and fading of wind power on the grid. That was a warning. Nine years later, the entire state is experiencing the same grid failures at a far higher cost.

Poster child no more

Few Indian states received as much international praise for its renewable energy as Tamil Nadu. In 2018, the World Economic Forum recognized the state for generating more wind power than Sweden or Denmark, the Scandinavian countries that climate activists hold up as models.

Wind accounted for more than 28% of Tamil Nadu’s installed generating capacity, well ahead of Gujarat’s 19%. Today, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka lead India in wind installations, with Gujarat and Tamil Nadu alone holding nearly half the national total.

Now look at what that reputation buys in October 2026.

Tamil Nadu has signed the costliest power purchase deals in the country to keep the lights on during evening hours. The state confirmed it will buy 1,500 megawatts for six peak hours every day from October 15 to 31, mostly from natural gas plants at a cost of about $527,000 a day. Those emergency rates run six to seven times higher than an existing contract for thermal power and nearly double the rate being paid by a neighboring state.

Where the electricity went

Officials blame a heatwave for the need to buy additional power. Peak demand jumped nearly 30%, driven by El Niño conditions that kept air conditioners and fans running long after the usual summer peak. Central generating stations also cut back on generation to accommodate scheduled maintenance.

But the real culprit is a drop in wind production to about 14% of what contracts had promised. Nobody should be surprised. The wind season in Tamil Nadu ends every year around this time. Solar output drops to zero after sunset, which explains why the shortage is between 6 p.m. and midnight. Hydropower, a weather-bound source that depends on reservoir levels and monsoon inflows, offered no meaningful rescue.

Consider who filled the gap. Every bidder in the emergency tender was a gas-fired generator, some of them in Assam 1,400 miles away. Gas won because it starts and stops on command. The state that spent three decades celebrating wind turbines now pays a premium for the one quality they cannot offer – on-demand dispatchability.

Tamil Nadu is India’s second-largest state economy, with a quarter of its output coming from manufacturing, which requires an affordable, continuous supply of electricity.

This month, in Tiruppur, Tamil Nadu’s fourth-largest city, knitwear factories reported production losses as computerized machines failed under sudden outages and low voltage. They suffered the same damage my friend had described nine years ago. Spinning mills near Madurai were told to switch to diesel generators, whose electricity costs significantly more than the grid’s.

Tamil Nadu’s planners must stop relating to installed wind capacity as if it were a reliable source. A turbine that produces at 14% of its contracted level during peak demand cannot support a power grid for many millions of people. 

India’s second-largest economy needs an energy supply based on coal, natural gas, and nuclear.

text:
The Election Retrospective

With Democrats taking control of Congress, both parties face an uncomfortable question: When did winning political arguments become more important than solving America's problems?

Republicans promised fiscal responsibility. The deficit grew. They promised to expose government waste, but their own savings claims failed independent scrutiny. They promised economic relief, yet Americans confronted gasoline above $4 a gallon, diesel above $6, persistent inflation, and mortgage rates exceeding 7%.

They promised to avoid prolonged foreign wars. Instead, the United States entered another costly conflict, accompanied by assurances that a resolution was just weeks away.

Yesterday, voters handed Democrats control of the House and Senate. The political balance changed, but the country's problems did not.

Republican explanations will follow. The media was unfair. Democrats misled voters. Outside money influenced the election. Republican voters stayed home. Some arguments may have merit, but none substitutes for examining what Republicans accomplished with the authority voters gave them in 2024.

Americans expected stronger borders, lower prices, fiscal responsibility, economic opportunity, and greater government accountability. Those were legitimate expectations. The question is whether the results matched the promises.

The Economy Americans Actually Experienced

Washington spent much of 2026 debating whether the economy was strong. American families were confronting a different set of numbers.

By Election Day, regular gasoline averaged $4.15 per gallon nationally, compared with $3.04 a year earlier. Diesel averaged $6.29, up from $3.68. Those increases affected farmers, truckers, manufacturers, and ultimately consumers.

Annual inflation stood at 3.7% in September, while the average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.24% in late October. Families faced higher borrowing costs, businesses struggled with expensive financing, and retirees continued absorbing years of accumulated price increases.

Not every problem originated with this administration. Global energy markets, Federal Reserve policy, international conflicts, and earlier fiscal decisions all contributed.

But policy choices matter. The Iran conflict contributed to higher energy prices. Tariffs increased costs for certain businesses and consumers. Federal borrowing added pressure to financial markets, although its precise effect on interest rates is difficult to isolate.

Americans were entitled to ask whether government policies were providing economic relief or adding to their financial burdens.

Fiscal Responsibility Cannot Depend on Party Affiliation

Republicans have spent decades warning about excessive government spending. Yet fiscal year 2026 ended with a deficit approaching $2 trillion, approximately $218 billion higher than the previous year. By early October, gross federal debt had reached $40.25 trillion.

Both parties contributed to that debt, and Republicans inherited substantial financial obligations. But they also made decisions that affected its future.

The Republican-backed 2025 reconciliation law extended tax provisions, reduced spending in several federal programs, and increased funding for other priorities. Supporters argued that these changes would encourage investment and economic growth.

The Congressional Budget Office, however, estimated that the legislation would increase cumulative federal deficits by approximately $3.4 trillion over ten years, excluding additional debt-service costs.

That was a legislative choice, not simply an inherited problem.

Tax relief can be sound economic policy, but reducing revenue without sufficient offsets has fiscal consequences. Republicans should have acknowledged those consequences and explained how they intended to address them.

If trillion-dollar deficits were unacceptable under Democratic administrations, they should be unacceptable under Republican administrations.

DOGE: When the Numbers Didn't Add Up

Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency promised to expose waste and save taxpayers enormous sums. Its objective was worthwhile. Government should be efficient, transparent, and accountable.

But the Government Accountability Office's August 2026 review identified serious deficiencies in DOGE's reported savings.

As of July 7, DOGE claimed $110 billion in savings from contracts, grants, and leases. GAO could not verify the methodology behind 96% of reported grant savings. DOGE also claimed more than $1.7 billion in savings from a Defense Health Agency contract that was never terminated. GAO found no savings from that item.

Some DOGE actions produced potential savings, and those deserve recognition. But unsupported accounting should concern every fiscal conservative.

Government efficiency must be measured through verified savings, improved services, and sustainable spending reductions—not impressive headlines.

Tariffs: The Difference Between Promises and Results

President Trump repeatedly presented tariffs as a way to protect American industries, generate revenue, and make foreign countries pay.

Tariffs can provide negotiating leverage and protect strategic industries. But American importers pay them, and substantial costs can reach businesses and consumers.

Research by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that tariffs increased consumer prices, including through higher costs for manufacturers relying on imported components.

On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, creating substantial refund obligations.

Republicans should have demanded clearer answers about which industries benefited, who paid more, and whether American manufacturing became more competitive. Trade policy should be measured by actual investment, productivity, wages, and economic security.

The War and the Limits of Presidential Promises

Trump campaigned on ending conflicts and avoiding prolonged foreign wars. On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched military strikes against Iran.

Iran presents legitimate national security concerns. But Americans also deserve clearly defined military objectives, credible cost estimates, and an exit strategy.

On March 31, Trump suggested the United States could conclude its military campaign within two or three weeks. The conflict continued beyond that timetable.

Presidents cannot control every development in a military conflict. But when they offer specific timelines, they create expectations and assume responsibility for explaining why those expectations were not met.

Congress has an equally important obligation to demand clear objectives and oversee military expenditures.

On March 5, 215 House Republicans voted against a resolution directing the removal of American forces from unauthorized hostilities with Iran. Supporters argued that the president needed flexibility, while critics emphasized Congress's constitutional responsibilities.

But Republican opposition subsequently grew. On June 3, the House voted 215–208 in favor of a war-powers resolution seeking to end unauthorized American military involvement. Four Republicans joined Democrats, demonstrating that concern about the conflict had crossed party lines.

That distinction matters. Not every Republican lawmaker simply followed the White House, and congressional independence should be acknowledged regardless of party.

Supporting America's military does not require unquestioning support for every military decision.

The Warning Signs Were Visible

A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted October 29–November 2 found Trump's approval rating at 32%. Among likely voters, 52% supported or leaned toward Democratic congressional candidates, compared with 44% for Republicans.

Those numbers cannot establish why every voter made a particular choice. Candidate quality, turnout, local concerns, and historical midterm patterns also matter. But they demonstrated dissatisfaction Republican leaders could not reasonably ignore.

Republicans can point to tax relief, deregulation, investment incentives, and border enforcement as accomplishments. Those policies deserve fair consideration.

But Americans experience the economy through household expenses, not presidential announcements. A rising stock market does not automatically resolve financial pressure on a family struggling with groceries, insurance, or a mortgage.

Voters are entitled to compare what leaders promised with what they experienced.

Democrats: Victory Is Not Permission to Waste Two Years

Democrats now face their own test.

They can devote the next two years to politically motivated investigations, treating impeachment as a substitute for an economic agenda. Or they can demonstrate that they understand the responsibilities of governing.

Congress must investigate credible allegations of wrongdoing. Impeachment remains a legitimate constitutional remedy when the evidence warrants it. Oversight and productive legislation are not competing responsibilities; Congress can and should do both.

There are practical opportunities for bipartisan progress.

First, Congress could establish a credible long-term fiscal framework addressing spending, debt reduction, and the sustainability of Social Security and Medicare.

Second, lawmakers could address affordability through housing construction, permitting reform, energy infrastructure, and healthcare competition.

Third, both parties could strengthen accountability by requiring independently verified federal savings reports and more transparent reporting of major government programs.

These proposals will require difficult negotiations. With a Republican president remaining in office, meaningful legislation will require compromise.

Impeachment proceedings do not themselves lower grocery prices. Televised confrontations do not balance the budget. Political victories do not repair infrastructure or strengthen retirement security.

Democrats should not allow opposition to Donald Trump to become their entire governing identity. They now share responsibility for confronting the problems they criticized Republicans for failing to solve.

The Lesson Washington Keeps Refusing to Learn

Republican losses do not prove that conservative principles are wrong. Nor does Democratic control of Congress establish that Democrats have better answers to every national problem.

But the election provides an opportunity to examine what was promised, what was delivered, and what should have been done differently.

The national debt still exceeds $40 trillion. Energy prices remain elevated. Housing is expensive, families face financial pressure, and America needs a credible foreign policy.

Republicans should examine their governing record without treating every criticism of Trump as an attack on conservatism. Democrats should recognize that investigating an administration cannot substitute for addressing the country's needs.

Both parties should challenge their own leaders, acknowledge inconvenient facts, and accept responsibility for the decisions they make.

The American people do not elect members of Congress simply to campaign, investigate their opponents, or defend their political parties.

We elect them to govern.   @GOP @TheDemocrats  @Bannons_WarRoom @FoxNews @TheCardinal @roanoketimes @WSJ @NBCNews @ABC @CBSNews @SpeakerJohnson @POTUS

text:
We closed on a small farmhouse east of Kewaunee in August, two acres, a barn I use as a shop, and an old apple tree behind the machine shed with limbs hanging over the roof. I'd already decided to have it taken down before winter.

The mail comes to a box at the end of the driveway. Last month I was walking back to the house sorting it, and I almost put an envelope in the pile with the grocery flyers. It was a window envelope with a blue stripe, the kind the electric co-op uses, and I had a bill due. But through the window I could see the card inside, and it wasn't a statement. It was a white three-by-five index card, handwritten in pencil. Instead of my name, it said:

*44.47193, -87.53041*
*Feb. 9*
*Please read before you cut anything.*

The envelope was addressed to me by name, in the same pencil. In the top left corner, where the co-op's logo and return address were supposed to be, someone had crossed it all out with a ballpoint and written *B. Marjorie, Bay Shore Manor, Rm 114.* The postmark was Green Bay, October.

I'd bought the house in August. I read the date twice. February was six months before I'd made an offer, and the house hadn't even been listed until April.

I'll admit my first thought wasn't a good one. I figured someone had been watching the property, or me, and I went through every possible way a stranger could have my name. It turned out there was an ordinary one. Property sales are public record in Wisconsin. Anyone can look up a buyer after closing, and a transfer return lists both names.

I put the coordinates into my phone and walked out. The pin dropped behind the machine shed, a few feet from the trunk of the apple tree. The grass there was a little greener, but that was all...

Our participants had changed their usual Monday plans to join us. In recognition of that departure from their everyday routines, kiRin offered a prayer to steady their footing and wish them safety in their steps.

Please listen to the bells and her voice, captured here in black and white.

text:
At a Pride Parade in Pittsburgh, one father’s simple act of kindness left a lasting impact. Howie Dittman showed up wearing a shirt that read “Free Dad Hugs” and offered embraces to anyone who needed one. What began as a small gesture quickly became one of the most moving moments of the day.

Throughout the event, Dittman gave more than 700 hugs to LGBTQ+ individuals. Many of them shared stories of rejection from their own families. For some, the hug brought tears — a powerful reminder of the acceptance and love they had been missing for years.

Photos and videos of Dittman’s hugs spread rapidly across social media, including Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram. His actions inspired thousands and helped popularize the hashtags #FreeDadHugs and #LGBTQSupport. People from around the world shared messages about the importance of family support, love, and acceptance.

Dittman explained that he wanted to show how much a parent’s support can mean to a young person. He believed that a simple hug could help someone feel valued, seen, and less alone. His message resonated deeply and sparked meaningful conversations about family relationships and mental health.

The story was later picked up by several media outlets, drawing widespread attention and praise for Dittman’s compassion. His quiet act of kindness became a powerful symbol of acceptance and highlighted the importance of standing by loved ones — no matter their identity.

text:
Here is the relevant word-for-word material from George Cary Eggleston’s Red Eagle and the Wars with the Creek Indians of Alabama (1878), specifically the surrender scene in Chapter XXXII (“Red Eagle’s Surrender”).

Eggleston notes that the details come mainly from accounts such as Pickett’s (drawing on Weatherford’s own later retellings) and are accepted in their main features by writers including Eaton, Meek, and Parton. There is no separate first-person written “account” by Jackson of the meeting beyond the dialogue attributed to him in the scene. Afterward, the book states that Jackson treated Weatherford as a friend and later took him as a guest to the Hermitage for protection.

Jackson’s words in the scene
General Jackson came running out of the marquee with Colonel Hawkins, and in a furious manner exclaimed:

“How dare you, sir, to ride up to my tent after having murdered the women and children at Fort Mims?”

Weatherford’s reply (from Eggleston’s account, drawn mainly from Pickett) was:

“General Jackson, I am not afraid of you. I fear no man, for I am a Creek warrior. I have nothing to request in behalf of myself; you can kill me if you desire. But I come to beg you to send for the women and children of the war party, who are now starving in the woods. Their fields and cribs have been destroyed by your people, who have driven them to the woods without an ear of corn. I hope that you will send out parties who will safely conduct them here, in order that they may be fed. I exerted myself in vain to prevent the massacre of the women and children at Fort Mims. I am now done fighting. The Red Sticks are nearly all killed. If I could fight you any longer I would most heartily do so. Send for the women and children. They never did you any harm. But kill me, if the white people want it done.”

After Weatherford’s reply and the bystanders’ shouts of “Kill him!”,

General Jackson commanded silence, and in an emphatic manner said:
“Any man who would kill as brave a man as this would rob the dead!”

He then invited Weatherford to alight, drank a glass of brandy with him, and entered into a cheerful conversation under his hospitable marquee. Weatherford gave him the deer, and they were then good friends.

Jackson told Weatherford what terms he had offered to the Creeks, and added:

“As for yourself, if you do not like the terms, no advantage shall be taken of your present surrender. You are at liberty to depart and resume hostilities when you please. But, if you are taken then, your life shall pay the forfeit of your crimes.”

text:
Lessons from the Bookshelf
Yesterday's Knowledge, Tomorrow's Wisdom

Day 4 of 44: French

Wednesday, 4 November 2026
French: Learning Another Language, Understanding Another World
I have always believed that education is not something we complete, but something we continue throughout our lives.

Recently, I have been adding to my collection of vintage Teach Yourself books, those wonderfully practical little volumes that encouraged generations of people to broaden their knowledge, develop new skills and explore subjects they might otherwise never have encountered.

Looking at 44 of these books, covering everything from Geometry, Forestry and Electricity to Biology, Carpentry, Photography and Management, I was struck by a simple thought.

How much of what these books taught remains relevant today, and what wider lessons might we learn from them?

That question inspired this daily series, Lessons from the Bookshelf.

Each day, I take one book, explore its subject, consider the knowledge and principles it represents, and reflect upon what those lessons mean for our modern lives.

Some take us into engineering, science and mathematics. Others explore language, craftsmanship, business, nature, sport and human understanding.

But this series is about more than the subjects themselves.

It is about curiosity, reasoning, patience, creativity, responsibility and the importance of lifelong learning.

Today, we turn to French, a language whose influence extends far beyond France itself, and whose study teaches us something particularly valuable about communication, culture, confidence and understanding people whose experiences differ from our own.

Because learning another language is not simply about finding different words for familiar things.

It is about discovering that the world can be understood, described and experienced in more than one way.
What does learning French really mean?
French belongs to the Romance family of languages, having developed principally from the Latin spoken in Roman Gaul.

Over centuries, it absorbed influences from other languages, including those of the Franks, and developed into the language we recognise today.

French is spoken across several continents, including Europe, Africa, North America and parts of the Caribbean and Pacific.

It is an official language of numerous countries and international organisations.

Its influence upon English is particularly significant.

Following the Norman Conquest of 1066, Norman French became associated with government, law, administration and the ruling classes in England.

Over time, thousands of French-derived words entered English.

Consider words such as government, justice, parliament, authority, liberty and responsibility.

Their histories remind us that the English language developed through centuries of cultural contact and exchange.

Indeed, many of the words we use when discussing British institutions have roots extending well beyond Britain.

That is not a weakness in our national identity.

It is part of the fascinating history through which that identity developed.
Lesson One: Communication is about understanding, not merely speaking
One of the first challenges encountered when learning French is recognising that direct translation does not always work.

A sentence that sounds perfectly natural in English may require a different structure in French.

Expressions may carry meanings that cannot be conveyed adequately through literal translation.

Even apparently simple words can depend heavily upon context.

This teaches us an important lesson.

Communication is not simply the transmission of information.

It is the successful creation of understanding.

We can speak clearly, confidently and at considerable length without necessarily ensuring that another person understands what we mean.

This is particularly relevant in business and public services.

An engineer may explain a technical problem using terminology familiar to colleagues but incomprehensible to a customer.

A government department may produce guidance that is legally precise but unnecessarily difficult for ordinary citizens to follow.

A manager may issue instructions without considering whether employees have the information needed to carry them out.

In each case, the problem may not be the accuracy of the words.

It may be the failure to communicate their meaning effectively.

Good communication is not measured by how much we say, but by how well we are understood.

Learning another language encourages us to recognise that distinction.
Lesson Two: Confidence develops through making mistakes
Anyone who has attempted to learn a foreign language will recognise the experience.

You know what you want to say.

You have practised the vocabulary.

You understand the grammar.

Then somebody asks you a question, and suddenly every word you have learned appears to disappear.

It can be rather humbling.

But it is also valuable.

Language learning requires us to accept that mistakes are part of progress.

We mispronounce words.

We select the wrong tense.

We misunderstand a question.

Occasionally, we produce a sentence that means something entirely different from what we intended.

Yet every attempt provides an opportunity to improve.

This is a lesson that extends into professional development.

An apprentice learning a trade will not perform every task perfectly at the first attempt.

A newly appointed manager will encounter situations that experience alone can teach them to handle.

Someone establishing a business will inevitably discover that certain assumptions were incorrect.

The important distinction is between making a mistake and refusing to learn from it.

Of course, mistakes involving safety, professional responsibility or significant financial consequences require appropriate safeguards.

But within a supportive learning environment, reasonable errors should become opportunities for development rather than occasions for humiliation.

Confidence does not come from never making mistakes. It comes from learning that mistakes need not prevent us from improving.
Lesson Three: Understanding another culture does not require abandoning our own
Language and culture are closely connected.

The words people use, the expressions they favour and the conventions governing conversation often reflect aspects of their history and society.

French provides many examples.

The distinction between tu and vous, for instance, introduces learners to different conventions of familiarity, formality and respect.

The appropriate choice depends upon context, relationships and social expectations.

Understanding these conventions requires more than memorising vocabulary.

It requires cultural awareness.

Yet appreciating another culture does not mean surrendering our own identity.

Quite the opposite.

Learning about other societies can help us understand our own customs more clearly.

We begin to recognise that practices we regard as entirely natural may be unfamiliar elsewhere.

We also discover that many human concerns are remarkably consistent.

People want security.

They value friendship and family.

They seek opportunities for their children.

They appreciate fairness, dignity and respect.

Their traditions may differ, but their fundamental aspirations often overlap.

This is particularly important in a world where differences of nationality, culture and religion can sometimes be exaggerated.

Understanding another person's culture does not require agreement with every aspect of it. It requires the willingness to approach differences with curiosity rather than automatic suspicion.
Lesson Four: Listening is an essential skill
When learning French, speaking often receives considerable attention.

But listening is equally important.

A learner must become familiar with unfamiliar sounds, accents, rhythms and patterns of speech.

They must resist the temptation to translate every individual word before considering the meaning of the sentence.

They must pay attention.

This provides a useful reminder about communication more generally.

Listening is not simply waiting for an opportunity to speak.

It requires concentration, patience and a willingness to consider what another person is actually saying.

In public debate, we sometimes appear more interested in preparing our response than understanding the argument being presented.

In business, important information can be overlooked when senior managers assume that they already understand the problem.

In personal relationships, misunderstandings frequently arise because people respond to what they believe was intended rather than what was actually expressed.

Learning a language encourages us to become more attentive listeners.

And attentive listening is one of the foundations of mutual respect.
Lesson Five: Education opens doors that may otherwise remain closed
For generations, books such as Teach Yourself French offered people an opportunity to acquire knowledge outside formal education.

Someone who had left school early could begin studying a foreign language.

A person preparing to travel could develop practical communication skills.

An employee could improve their prospects of working with international customers.

A retired individual could pursue an interest that had remained unexplored for decades.

The importance of that accessibility should not be underestimated.

Education is often discussed in terms of qualifications, examinations and career progression.

Those things matter.

But learning also provides independence, confidence and personal satisfaction.

Not every subject needs to lead to a professional qualification to justify the time spent studying it.

Sometimes learning is valuable simply because it broadens our understanding.

A person who learns enough French to speak with a neighbour, navigate a railway station or enjoy a conversation during a holiday has achieved something worthwhile.

And that achievement belongs to them.
Why French remains relevant today
Modern technology has transformed language learning.

Translation applications can provide almost instantaneous assistance.

Artificial intelligence can explain grammar, generate practice conversations and help learners improve their pronunciation.

Digital platforms make it possible to communicate with people across the world.

These developments are genuinely useful.

But they do not make language learning redundant.

A translation application may communicate the literal meaning of a sentence without fully conveying its tone, humour or cultural significance.

Automated systems can also make mistakes, particularly when dealing with ambiguity, specialist terminology or complex contexts.

In professional environments, those errors may matter.

A misunderstood contractual provision, technical instruction or safety warning can have serious consequences.

Human language skills therefore remain valuable, even when supported by technology.

There is also something technology cannot entirely reproduce.

The personal connection created when someone makes the effort to communicate in another person's language.

A simple greeting, a polite question or an expression of thanks can demonstrate consideration.

It tells the other person that we recognise their language and have made an effort to meet them part of the way.

That matters in international business.

It matters in diplomacy.

And it matters in ordinary human relationships.
The economic value of understanding one another
Britain's economic future depends partly upon its ability to trade, collaborate and build relationships internationally.

French remains relevant to commerce, diplomacy, science, education and international development.

France is an important economic partner for the United Kingdom, while French-speaking markets extend across several continents.

For British businesses seeking international opportunities, language skills can complement technical expertise and commercial understanding.

An engineering company may possess an excellent product.

A consultancy may offer valuable specialist knowledge.

A manufacturer may be capable of delivering exceptional quality.

But commercial success also depends upon understanding customers, negotiating effectively and establishing trust.

Language skills can contribute to all three.

This does not mean that every British employee must become fluent in French.

Nor does it diminish the international importance of English.

It simply recognises that businesses benefit when people possess the ability and willingness to communicate across linguistic and cultural boundaries.

The same principle applies to public services working with diverse communities.

Clear communication can improve accessibility, reduce misunderstandings and help people make informed decisions.
The wider lesson: Curiosity is stronger than prejudice
Perhaps the most important lesson from learning another language is the recognition that our own experience represents only one perspective.

We discover different ways of expressing familiar ideas.

We encounter customs whose origins we may not initially understand.

We learn that humour, politeness and social expectations do not always translate directly.

And, gradually, what once seemed unfamiliar becomes understandable.

That process does not eliminate disagreement.

People can understand one another perfectly well and still hold fundamentally different opinions.

But understanding provides a better foundation for disagreement than ignorance.

It allows us to challenge ideas without automatically dismissing the people expressing them.

It encourages us to distinguish between cultural differences and genuine matters of principle.

And it reminds us that respect is not dependent upon complete agreement.

In a society where public discussion can sometimes become unnecessarily confrontational, that is a lesson worth remembering.
A final reflection
Looking at this vintage Teach Yourself French book, I find myself thinking about the generations of people who opened similar volumes with little more than curiosity and determination.

Some may have wanted to improve their employment prospects.

Others may have been preparing for their first journey abroad.

Some may simply have enjoyed the challenge of learning something new.

Whatever their motivation, they were doing something valuable.

They were expanding the boundaries of their own understanding.

And that is one of the great pleasures of education.

Learning does not always change the world around us.

Sometimes it changes the way we see it.

French teaches vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation.

But the wider lessons concern patience, confidence, communication, cultural awareness and the willingness to recognise perspectives beyond our own.

Those lessons remain every bit as relevant today as they were when these books first appeared on our shelves.
Today's closing thought
Learning another language does not diminish the value of our own.

It gives us another way to understand the world, another opportunity to connect with people and another reason to recognise how much we share.

Perhaps the greatest achievement of learning another language is not discovering how differently people speak, but discovering how much we have in common.

Tomorrow, Day 5: English Grammar

We return to our own language to explore why grammar matters, how clear communication influences understanding, and whether the rules we learned at school remain as important in an age of instant messaging, artificial intelligence and increasingly informal communication.

text:
Ukrainian children who fled Russia’s full-scale invasion arrived in Britain and found that, if they wanted to take a GCSE in a language from home, schools could steer them toward Russian. There was no Ukrainian GCSE. Some pupils were pushed to sit an exam in the language of the nation that had forced them from their homes.

WHAT THE MINISTER ADMITTED

Schools minister Georgia Gould has apologised to those children. “So many students were pushed into having to do Russian,” she said, adding that she was sorry they had been put in that position. Pupils described the suggestion as insulting. Ukrainian and Russian are different languages, and these were children displaced by Russia's invasion, so the reaction is justified.

The failure was not that schools lacked a convenient timetable slot. England’s exam system offered a Russian qualification but no Ukrainian equivalent, then left refugee children to deal with the consequences. An exam board’s reluctance to develop a qualification for a relatively small group of students was allowed to outweigh what those students were actually being asked to do.

WHAT CHANGES NOW

The Department for Education is providing £340,000 for exam board AQA to develop a Ukrainian GCSE, with the qualification due to be ready in England in 2028. That will let future pupils study and be examined in Ukrainian instead of being directed to Russian as a substitute.

This decision follows years of lobbying by Ukraine’s government and Ukrainian community groups in Britain. They were speaking up for more than 30,000 Ukrainian children who fled to the UK after 2022. Kyiv’s education ministry warned the department in 2024 that, without a Ukrainian GCSE, school staff were pressuring children to take Russian.

The apology matters because a minister has acknowledged what happened to those pupils. The funding can change the exam options. But a 2028 launch also means the children pushed toward Russian have already passed years inside a system that made their own language unavailable.

text:
The camel’s nose is inside the tent, and I am appalled by the election results.

Democracy depends on public trust: confidence that the rules apply equally, that elections are conducted fairly, and that wrongdoing carries consequences. That trust has eroded, and mine has eroded with it. I no longer have confidence that our elections are consistently fair and impartial.

In my view, the Democratic Party offered little beyond opposition to Donald Trump. That hardly constitutes a governing vision. Any credible allegations of fraud or noncitizen voting—including New York, California, Michigan, and Minnesota—deserve thorough, transparent investigation. Did wrongdoing occur? If so, was it significant enough to affect the results? Those questions demand evidence and public accountability.

We stand at an inflection point. The choices we make now will determine whether we preserve freedom, security, and prosperity or descend into dependency, decline, and misery.

I fear that, like Rome, our republic is choosing “bread and circuses” over the vigilance, sacrifice, and the resolve required to defend it. A republic cannot endure if its citizens take its freedoms for granted and abandon the responsibility of preserving them.

$LITE just agreed to be acquired by $MRVL, reported a strong quarter, won a second large NPO/CPO program backed by more than $5 billion in purchase commitments, and started to see OCS revenue scale.

Its next-quarter outlook moved higher again. Investors are debating dilution from the deal, but those long-term commitments are hard to ignore.

$COHR has long-term capacity commitments stretching into 2028 and is focused on CPO, silicon photonics, and 1.6T.

Its next earnings report will come down to margins and the pace of large-customer deliveries. Along with Lumentum, it remains one of the key names in the move toward NPO and CPO.

$AAOI is expanding its Texas manufacturing footprint to ramp 800G and 1.6T module capacity.

It has large 1.6T orders from cloud customers and offers a U.S.-based supply option close to hyperscalers. It is also a smaller company, so the upside and the volatility can both be much larger.

Expectations across optical networking are already high. An announced opportunity is no longer enough. Investors want volume shipments and recognized revenue.

The sector is moving from concept stories into execution.

A faster ramp can still surprise the market. A delay can turn good news into a sell-the-news event very quickly.

text:
Kalispera from a sunny Thessaloniki. Today, I’d like to turn my attention to what November might bring.

Early US midterm projections point to @TheDemocrats  taking both chambers of #Congress. If that holds, legislative gridlock and closer scrutiny of large tech companies are possibilities I’ll be watching.

For now, I’m more interested in what companies are reporting. According to @FactSet, 82% of S&P 500 companies that had reported by 30 October beat earnings estimates. Blended third quarter earnings growth reached 30.2% YoY. What caught my attention was how small the average beat was by historical standards. Analysts had already anticipated much of that growth.

October showed how leadership can change even as corporate earnings hold up. I expect that selectivity to continue in November.

In #tech, I’ll be looking at how much cash companies retain after funding the infrastructure their growth requires. In European #defence, I’ll be watching how quickly manufacturers can turn procurement commitments into deliveries and what margins they can earn on those contracts. In both cases, the price I pay matters as much as the demand I can see.

I’m also keeping an eye on #healthcare, #industrials and #energy. A business with modest growth can still offer an attractive return if it uses its capital well and I can buy it at a sensible price.

I don’t have a strong view on where the index will finish November. What could change my mind about an individual company is more concrete. If it needs more capital than I expected to earn the same profit, I have to reconsider what I’m willing to pay for it.

text:
FLUTTER $FLUT — Q3 EARNINGS: PROFITS FALL 25%, GUIDANCE CUT AND BUYBACKS PAUSED
Flutter delivered a disappointing quarter, with slowing growth, weaker profitability and declining customer activity.
THE NUMBERS
🔹 Revenue: $3.87B vs $4.01B est. 🔴; +2% YoY
🔹 Adj. EPS: −$0.18 vs +$0.28 est. 🔴
🔹 Adj. EBITDA: $360M vs $411M est. 🔴; −25% YoY
🔹 Monthly players: 13.67M, −3% YoY
🔹 Free cash flow: $35M, +40% YoY
FY26 GUIDANCE — CUT
🔹 Revenue: $17.34B–$17.89B vs $17.8B est.
🔹 Adj. EBITDA: $2.35B–$2.65B vs $2.59B est.
SEGMENT PERFORMANCE
🔹 U.S.: $1.46B, +6% YoY
🔹 International: $2.42B, flat YoY
🔹 UK & Ireland: $889M, +4%
🔹 Southern Europe & Africa: $836M, +13%
WHAT'S CHANGING
🔹 $873M non-cash impairment in Brazil
🔹 $500M cost savings targeted by 2029
🔹 Share repurchases paused indefinitely
🔹 FanDuel Predicts trading volume: $119M, +102% QoQ
MY TAKE
What concerns me is that revenue grew just 2% while adjusted EBITDA declined 25%. That's not the operating leverage I'd expect from a business with Flutter's scale.
Prediction markets offer another growth opportunity, but strong trading-volume growth doesn't automatically translate into meaningful profits.
The Brazil impairment, reduced guidance and paused buybacks also suggest management has significant work ahead.
Flutter still has valuable market positions, particularly through FanDuel. But the next test is restoring customer growth, improving margins and proving that prediction markets can generate sustainable returns.
