text:
North Korea hacks Binance via LinkedIn

Let’s dive into today’s tech news with a twist of irony: the largest crypto hack in history wasn’t pulled off by some cutting-edge AI wizardry but by good old-fashioned social engineering tactics.
How Did It Happen?

So here’s the big question: how did North Korean hackers manage to steal $6.3 billion from Binance? The answer is surprisingly simple—they tricked a software engineer into downloading malware through LinkedIn and then used that access to exploit internal AI tools.

1. LinkedIn Scam: A Binance engineer was contacted by someone posing as a Project Director on LinkedIn. This fake recruiter arranged interviews with HR and even an alleged CEO of a fictitious company.
2. Malicious Software: Another engineer fell for a deceptive ad campaign, downloading a tampered version of Homebrew, a popular package manager.
The Inside Job

Once the hackers had control over an engineer’s laptop, they leveraged Binance’s internal AI tools to gain access to other employees’ accounts. Specifically:
• Compromised Laptop: Hackers used the compromised laptop to exploit Binance’s own AI tools.
• Access Granted: They discovered that one of the engineers had a container deployment permission token on their computer.
No Magic Bullet

Despite initial speculation about advanced AI hacks, it turns out this was all about social engineering. The hackers didn’t rely on any groundbreaking technology—they simply tricked employees into downloading malware and sharing sensitive information. Binance’s own internal tools were then used against them.
What Happened to the Engineer?

Binance has a policy prohibiting non-public-facing roles from maintaining LinkedIn profiles, but they declined to comment on whether this engineer violated that rule or if disciplinary action will be taken. The company also noted that it had previously detected and prevented 75 North Korea-related hacking attempts in 2026.
Aftermath

The hack resulted in the theft of around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency, though Binance managed to recover about $2.5 billion through cooperation with Tether and Circle. Withdrawals were temporarily halted for 48 hours but have since been restored. The company has stated that all customer funds are safe and they’ve replenished 98% of the stolen coins from reserve funds.
So What Changes for You?

This incident highlights the importance of vigilance when it comes to social engineering attacks. Whether you’re on LinkedIn or browsing the web, always be cautious about clicking links or downloading software from unverified sources. And if your company has strict policies around online activity, make sure you adhere to them.
The Awkward Bit: Why?

The real question here is why this happened at all. Binance had detected similar attempts before and yet fell victim to a relatively straightforward phishing scheme. This raises concerns about the effectiveness of current cybersecurity measures in place for both companies and individuals.
What’s Next?

As we move forward, it’s crucial to stay informed and proactive about security threats. Keep an eye out for suspicious activity on social media platforms like LinkedIn, and be wary of any unsolicited job offers or software downloads. Companies need to step up their training programs to educate employees about the risks of social engineering attacks.
What Is Stored?

Binance stores a wealth of sensitive data including customer information, transaction records, and internal communications. The hackers accessed this data through compromised employee accounts, exploiting both LinkedIn profiles and tampered software packages like Homebrew.
What Is Excluded?

The hack did not involve any direct theft from customer wallets or user accounts. Instead, the attackers gained access to Binance’s internal systems and exploited them to drain funds from company-controlled wallets.
User Controls

Users can protect themselves by:
• Keeping their LinkedIn profiles up-to-date but private.
• Avoiding clicking on suspicious links or downloading software from untrusted sources.
• Reporting any unusual activity to IT security immediately.
Availability

Binance has since restored normal operations and continues to monitor for further threats. The company’s response, including the recovery of stolen funds, demonstrates a robust emergency protocol in place.
What This Does Not Prove

This incident does not prove that AI is ineffective or unnecessary. Rather, it highlights the importance of combining advanced technology with strong human oversight and cybersecurity practices.
Practical Takeaway

The Binance hack serves as a stark reminder that even sophisticated companies can fall prey to basic social engineering tactics. It underscores the need for continuous education and vigilance in protecting sensitive information and systems from external threats.

text:
The caption calls it a baby.

Muskox bulls can weigh close to 400 kilograms. That is nearly 900 pounds of wool, bone and stubbornness, wearing a coat so thick it looks like weather.

So when someone looks at an animal like that and reaches for the word "little," one of two things is happening. Either it is the best joke on the Arctic internet, or something far more interesting is going on underneath it.

I think it is both.

Thirty seconds. Open tundra. One person, one animal, and a question the clip never says out loud: how does a creature built to outlast wolves, blizzards and the end of an entire age of giants end up standing where it does, next to who it does?

I am not going to tell you what happens. I am going to tell you why it matters, because the clip is short and the reason is very, very long.

Start with what a muskox actually is, because almost everyone gets it wrong.

It is not an ox. Its closest relatives are not cattle at all. Biologically it sits nearer to sheep and goats than to anything you would hitch to a plow. The scientific name, Ovibos, literally means "sheep-ox," which tells you that even the people whose job is naming animals threw up their hands and split the difference.

The Inuit name is better. Umingmak. The bearded one.

That one word does more work than the entire English name. It does not describe a function or a food source or a mistake. It describes a face you would recognize across a valley, and a presence you would treat with a certain amount of respect before you ever got close.

Now put that animal on a timeline.

Muskoxen shared the frozen north with woolly mammoths. When the climate shifted and the mammoth world collapsed, the muskox did not go with it. The last mammoths, living on Wrangel Island, died out roughly four thousand years ago, by which point the pyramids of Giza had already been standing for centuries.

Think about what that means. The animal in this clip belongs to a lineage that watched the giants disappear and simply kept walking. It was not the biggest. It was not the fastest. It was the one that did not need anything the Ice Age was about to take away.

What it needed was a coat, and the coat is the secret.

Under the long outer guard hair, which can hang almost to the ground like a heavy skirt, a muskox grows an underlayer called qiviut. It is routinely described as roughly eight times warmer than sheep wool, finer than cashmere, and it does not shrink when washed. The animal sheds it every spring in great soft drifts that people in the far north have gathered off the ground for generations.

Pause on that image, because it is the first clue to the whole story: an animal that is, in a very literal sense, insulated against the world. Layered, sealed, built so that cold, wind and distance cannot get in.

And yet.

The reason muskoxen survive is not only the coat. It is a strategy, and it is the most quietly moving defensive behavior in the animal kingdom.

When wolves close in, the adults do not scatter. They do not run in every direction hoping the predator picks someone else. They turn and gather into a tight ring, or a line, with the calves pushed into the middle and the horns pointed outward. Everyone who can fight forms the wall. Everyone who cannot is behind it.

The whole species is organized around a single rule: nobody gets left outside.

I keep coming back to that rule, because it reframes the word in the caption. "Baby" in a muskox herd is not a cute label. It is the thing the entire formation exists to protect. It is the center of the circle. Every pound of those enormous bodies and every inch of those horns has one job, and the job is the one in the middle.

So when a human uses that word for an animal this size, they are borrowing the highest-stakes word in muskox culture.

Whether they are allowed to, whether it is earned, whether it is a joke or a confession, is the part I want you to see for yourself.

Now the uncomfortable part.

Everything I just told you about muskoxen is a reason to keep your distance.

Wildlife agencies in muskox country give the same blunt advice year after year: do not approach, do not crowd, do not assume calm means safe. A muskox that feels cornered or surprised can charge, and the animal can sprint at roughly 60 kilometers an hour, about 37 miles per hour, carrying all that weight on four short legs.

During the rut, bulls settle their disagreements by backing away from each other, turning, and running straight in for a head-on collision. The sound of it carries across the tundra. The horns fuse into a single bony shield across the forehead, called a boss, and that shield exists for exactly one reason: to take impacts that would end most other animals.

This is the animal.

Hold that in your head. Not as a warning, but as a measuring stick. Everything you see in the next thirty seconds has to be measured against it.

Because here is what I cannot stop thinking about.

In nature, closeness is almost never free. When a wild animal lets you near, it is not doing you a favor out of kindness. It is spending something. Every animal runs a constant, invisible calculation about threats, and distance is the currency it uses to keep that calculation safe. The greater the animal, the more it can afford to spend, and the more the spending means.

Biologists have a name for the idea behind this. A signal only carries meaning if it could have been withheld. A guard dog that never barks tells you nothing when it stays quiet. A wild animal that never lets anyone close tells you nothing when it keeps its distance. But when an animal that could end the interaction at any moment, easily, does not, that is information.

It is the difference between a gift and a default.

So the question that makes this clip so hard to turn away from is not "is the animal cute." It is a much stranger one: what exactly is the animal choosing, and what is it choosing it over?

I want to be careful here. I do not know the history behind this encounter, and I am not going to pretend I do. I do not know whether this animal has spent years around people, whether it has been raised near a research station, whether the human has a long relationship with this herd or this single animal, or whether none of the above is true and the whole thing happened by accident of temperament.

There is a spectrum in how animals and humans end up near each other.

At one end are wild animals that flee at the first hint of a person.

In the middle are habituated animals, ones that learned that a particular kind of person at a particular kind of place is not a threat, and adjusted their calculation accordingly. This is not taming. Habituation is a quiet negotiation the animal conducts with its own fear, and it can end badly for both sides if people misread it.

And at the far end are individual animals that, for reasons researchers can describe but never fully explain, develop something that looks very much like preference.

Where does this clip sit on that line? The clip does not hand you the answer. I have a guess. I am keeping it to myself, because I would rather you form your own.

There is another reason this lands the way it does, and it has to do with how humans are wired.

In 1943 the Austrian ethologist Konrad Lorenz described what he called the baby schema: a set of features, large foreheads, broad faces, round proportions, that trigger an automatic caregiving response in the human brain. We do not choose it. It fires. It is why we melt at puppies and kittens and cartoon characters whose proportions were engineered to exploit exactly that reflex.

A muskox is not on anyone's list of conventionally cute animals. The face is broad and low and framed by a mane that looks like it belongs to a different, larger creature. Nobody designed it to be adorable.

And yet people who spend time near muskoxen describe the same thing again and again: a sudden softness toward an animal that, by every rule of design, should not trigger it.

That mismatch is where the interesting emotion lives. It is not the easy affection we give to something small and helpless. It is the more complicated feeling we get when something powerful lets us see that it is not only power.

Researchers who study dogs have found that mutual gaze between a dog and its owner raises oxytocin in both of them, the same bonding hormone that links mothers and infants. Two species, a feedback loop of attention, a chemical handshake. That finding comes from dogs, whose ancestors spent many thousands of years choosing to live beside us.

Nobody has done that study with a muskox. Nobody needs to. Anyone who has ever felt a large animal decide to stand next to them knows the feeling is not a metaphor. Something in the body registers it as an event.

That is the whole reason a thirty-second clip about an animal and a person can outrun almost everything else on your timeline. It is not content about an animal. It is content about being selected.

Hold that thought, because it has a shadow side, and we need to talk about it.

The shadow side is simple, and every person who has ever worked with wildlife knows it by heart.

The moment a wild animal's closeness becomes the thing we reward, we start training ourselves, and everybody else, to chase it.

One viral clip of a large animal calmly sharing space with a human is a lovely thing. A thousand copies of it, made by people who watched the original and decided to try it for themselves, is how animals get hurt. It is how an animal that learned to relax around one careful person ends up approached by a crowd of strangers who read none of the signals. It is how a patient negotiation turns into an incident report.

So there will be two camps in the replies. You can already hear them.

One camp will say this is the most beautiful thing they have seen all year.

The other will say it is irresponsible, that you do not walk up to a wild animal that could kill you, that the only thing the clip teaches is bad judgment.

Both camps will be right about something. That is the part that makes it worth arguing about.

The first camp is right that the human heart is allowed to be moved by an animal behaving in a way that surprises us. Dismissing that as sentimentality is its own kind of dishonesty. It is one of the oldest forms of curiosity we have.

The second camp is right that the animal pays the price when the rest of us misread the lesson. Compassion that ignores consequences is not compassion. It is a mood.

Where is the line? I do not think there is a clean one, and I do not trust anyone who claims there is. The line moves with the animal, the place, the history, the person, the distance, the day. It is a judgment call made in real time by someone who knows the specific creature in front of them, and you cannot read that judgment off a thirty-second video.

What you can do is notice that the question exists. That is already more than most viral videos ask of you.

Let me add one more word to the table, because I have been circling it the whole time.

The title of the clip is an introduction.

"Introducing" is a strange verb for a post like this. You introduce someone to someone. It implies a third party, a host who stands between two parties and says, in effect, you two should know each other. It implies the introduction is a gift, offered to you, the viewer, as the one being introduced.

So who is introducing whom here? Is the human introducing the animal to the audience? Is the animal introducing itself? Is it possible that the title is secretly a role reversal, and that the person is the one being presented, to a creature whose opinion matters more?

I do not have an answer. I have a suspicion that the phrasing was chosen on purpose and that the person who wrote it knew exactly how much it was carrying.

There is a bigger background to all of this, and it is worth knowing before you press play.

Muskoxen have a complicated history with people, and it is not all warmth.

In parts of their range they were hunted to the edge. In Alaska, wild muskoxen were wiped out by the late nineteenth century. The animals living there today descend from a few dozen individuals shipped over from Greenland in the 1930s, a rescue project assembled out of fear that a whole species was slipping away from a continent. Several other populations around the Arctic, including herds in Norway and parts of Russia, trace back to deliberate reintroductions.

That means that in some places, every muskox you see exists because enough people decided it should.

For the Inuit, Inuvialuit and other northern peoples, the relationship has been far older and far more practical. The animal provided meat, hides, horn and the legendary wool. It also demanded a kind of knowledge, how to read it, how to approach, how to stay out of a charge, that was handed down like any other survival skill.

I mention this because the internet tends to flatten relationships with animals into two categories: pet and photo subject. The real history of this species is a long, practical, respectful, sometimes brutal co-existence, one that never needed to be cute.

What changed is the setting. Now the animal appears on a phone screen to people who will never stand on a tundra, and the question we are all quietly asking is whether we can be trusted with that kind of access.

Then there is the weather.

If I stopped here, I would be giving you a tidy portrait of a tough animal that has always won. That would be a lie, and I said I would not do that.

The Arctic is warming faster than almost anywhere else on Earth, and muskoxen have one particular weakness that the warming exposes. In winter they survive by pawing through snow to reach the plants beneath. When freezing rain falls on snow, or when a thaw is followed by a hard refreeze, the snow turns into a sheet of ice. The food is still there. It is just sealed off.

Animals that outlasted mammoths can starve standing on top of their own meals.

In bad years, whole herds have been hit. Population swings in parts of the Canadian Arctic and Greenland have been severe enough that researchers now track them closely. The coat, the circle, the horns, the fused skull, none of it helps against a sheet of glass laid over the ground.

So the animal in this clip is not just a survivor. It is a survivor in a very particular moment, one where the thing that threatens it is no longer something you can face down with a wall of horns.

That changes the emotional math.

It means the closeness you are about to see, whatever it is, is not happening in an unchanging wilderness. It is happening in a world that is moving under the animal's feet, and in which every human who stands near one is also, whether they planned to or not, standing next to a question about the future.

There is something unbearably gentle about that.

There is a clock running underneath all of this, and it is easy to miss.

Summer on the tundra is brief. The growing season lasts a matter of weeks. In that window the plants flush green almost overnight, and a muskox spends nearly every waking hour doing one thing: eating. It is building the fat and the condition that will carry it through a winter long enough to break most animals.

Think about the economics of that. For these animals, energy is the only real wealth. Every step that does not feed them, every flight from a threat that turns out to be nothing, every moment spent on alert, is paid for out of a budget that cannot be refilled until next year.

So when an animal in that exact season gives its attention to something that is not food and not danger, that attention has a price tag, even if no one can see it. Curiosity is a luxury on the tundra. It is spent by animals that are secure enough, or settled enough, or trusting enough to afford it.

That is one more reason the question of what this encounter really is deserves a slower look than a scroll allows.

Because whatever it is, it happened inside a very small window of a very short season, on a hillside most of us will never stand on, between two beings who each had better things to do.

Let me step back and ask why a clip like this travels at all.

We live inside screens full of people performing for other people. Almost every second of video you see has a human at the center of it, angled toward the camera, aware of being watched. It is an enormous, exhausting hall of mirrors.

Then something arrives from the other side of that glass: an animal that has no idea there is an audience. It is not performing. It cannot be coached, cannot be edited into a better version of itself, cannot decide to seem more likable. Whatever it does is the only version.

That is the real draw. Not cuteness. Authenticity so complete that it feels almost unfair.

When an animal like that is shown responding to a person, we are not watching a trick. We are watching a decision made by a mind that does not know how to fake anything. That is why the smallest gesture, a shift in weight, a turn of the head, can carry more emotional charge than an entire scripted scene.

I want you to notice how rare that is.

Most of what we call connection between people involves a layer of translation, politeness, strategy. Between a person and an animal, the layers are stripped away. There is no small talk. There is only an answer to the question: is this safe, and do I want to be here?

Think about what it would mean to be the person on the receiving end of a yes.

There is a second layer, and it concerns scale.

The tundra is the most honest landscape on the planet. There are no trees to hide behind, no walls, no crowds. Everything that happens there happens in the open, where it can be seen from kilometers away. A shape on a hillside is either something that matters or something that will pass. A figure can be a speck for a very long time before it becomes anything else.

In country like that, even the smallest meeting between two living things is a major event on the horizon.

Maybe that is why people who work in the Arctic talk so often about the strange intimacy of it. You can spend days without seeing another person. Then a single animal appears, and the distance between you and it becomes the most important number in your life.

The cruelest thing about that number is that you cannot control it alone. You can only offer your side of it, calmly and honestly, and wait to see what the other side does.

Which brings me back to the person in this clip, and I want to say something about them without saying anything about what they do.

I do not know who they are. I do not know their job, their history, their relationship with the animal. What I know is that whatever you are about to watch required a particular kind of person, one willing to be still, willing to be small next to something huge, willing to let the animal set the terms of the encounter.

That is a skill. In wildlife work it is arguably the most important one, and it is almost invisible, because when it is done right, nothing dramatic happens. The best handling of a large animal looks like absolutely nothing.

Think about how counterintuitive that is for a platform that rewards spectacle. The most skillful moments in this field produce no spectacle at all.

And yet here we are, with a clip people cannot stop sharing, which suggests that even in a feed built for noise, a certain kind of quiet still wins.

I should be honest about what this post is and is not.

It is not a summary. I have deliberately not told you what is on the screen, because the point is that you should see it with your own eyes and have your own reaction, not mine.

It is not a claim that this is the most remarkable thing ever filmed. It is not a claim that the animal is safe, that you should try anything like it, or that the animal feels any particular way about anyone. Those are all things I do not know, and I would rather admit that than pretend.

It is a claim about attention. That an animal descended from creatures that outlived the mammoths, wearing a coat the north designed over thousands of generations, built around a rule that nobody gets left outside, deserves to be looked at properly. Not skimmed. Not scrolled past at the speed of a thumb.

If you do watch it, watch it twice.

The first time, watch for the story. Let yourself react. Notice what your chest does.

The second time, watch for the distance. Not the distance between the person and the animal on the screen, but the distance you carried into the clip, the one between what you expected a creature like that to do and what it did.

The size of that gap is the whole video.

A thought on what we owe the animals that let us watch.

Every clip like this is a small withdrawal from a trust account. The animal cannot consent to being filmed, cannot read the comments, cannot tell the difference between a careful observer and a crowd. All it can do is go on being what it is, and hope that the people who see it respond with care rather than appetite.

That is a lot to ask of an audience. It is also, I think, the best argument for looking at this kind of footage slowly: with respect for the one who did not choose to be seen, and for the person who knew how to stand close without taking anything. Care is the only fair price for a view this rare, and it costs us nothing but patience, restraint, and a little humility.

One more thing before you go, because it changes how the word "little" lands.

Humor is how people talk about things they respect too much to say plainly.

Think about the nicknames we give to the biggest animals. The enormous dog is a "baby." The bull-sized horse is a "sweetheart." The grizzly is "just a big teddy bear" right up until it is not. We soften the language precisely when the animal is large enough that softness is a decision. A joke gives us a way to say something tender without having to defend it.

Seen that way, "my little baby muskox" is not a mistake in scale. It is a tiny act of translation. It is someone doing what people have always done in front of something much bigger than themselves: making a small, warm sentence to stand next to it.

And there is a quieter possibility, which is that the person means every word.

Animal behavior researchers have spent the last few decades documenting something that people who live near animals have always insisted on: individuals differ. Not just by species, but one by one. There are bolder animals and shyer ones, curious ones and cautious ones, animals that approach and animals that never will. Personality, in the plain sense of the word, is not unique to humans.

If that is true of a fish or a bird, it is certainly true of a mammal that lives for well over a decade in the wild, remembers its herd, and reads its surroundings with a pair of eyes that have been paying attention since birth.

Which makes the central question less abstract. Not "how does a muskox behave around people," but "what kind of individual is this particular one?"

Nobody can answer that from a distance. That may be the most honest thing about the whole clip.

Now think about what a muskox calf is.

In spring, calves arrive into a world that is still cold and still full of wolves. They are small enough to be carried off by almost anything, and within hours they are on their feet, following a mother whose body is a windbreak and whose herd closes ranks around them. For a short time, every adult in sight is working for the smallest member of the group.

A grown muskox is what that calf becomes if the circle holds.

Which means that somewhere inside the dark, shaggy, horned animal you are about to see is a creature that once stood on legs it barely knew how to use, in the center of a ring of its own kind, while everyone else faced the cold.

That is the thing I cannot unsee when I look at an animal like this. Under every giant is a baby that someone protected. It is true of muskoxen. It is true of us. The caption is accidentally the most accurate sentence in the post.

So here is what I am left with.

A species that survived the end of the Ice Age by making a wall of itself around the vulnerable.

A coat built to keep the whole world out.

A set of rules, written into every muscle, that say do not let anything get close.

And then thirty seconds in which, apparently, something does.

I will not tell you who gets close, or how, or what it looks like when a few thousand years of instinct are asked a question and answer it a different way than expected. That is yours.

I will only say that I have watched it more times than I would like to admit, and that I notice something different every time. Not about the animal. About me. About how badly I wanted the distance to close, and how little I understood about what it costs.

Thirty seconds. That is all it ever asks.

The caption says baby. The Ice Age says otherwise.

Go and see which one is telling the truth.

$MCRB Q3 2026 earnings: Seres Therapeutics halves its operating costs, but cash runs low

Seres Therapeutics, a developer of oral bacterial drugs, halved its underlying spending while waiting for a partner to fund its clinical trials. Excluding a non-cash charge for exiting a building lease, operating expenses fell 52% from a year ago to $11 million by our math. Interim chief executive Richard Kender outlined plans to test lead drug SER-155 for preventing gut inflammation in cancer immunotherapy patients, but every trial remains on hold until new funding arrives.

• Operating expenses, excluding lease charges: $𝟏𝟏.𝟎𝐌 (-52% from a year ago by our math)
• Cash plus October Nestlé payment: $𝟑𝟎.𝟎𝐌 (by our math ($17.5M at Q3 end))
• Operating lease liabilities: $𝟑𝟓.𝟖𝐌 (-57% from the end of 2025)
• Cash outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (funds operations through Q1 2027)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the clock ticked down to two quarters of remaining cash without a partnership deal, and detailed trial slides showed weaker durability in the new colitis program. While 12 of 15 colitis patients improved without steroids at Day 15, seven of those 12 needed gut-targeted immunosuppressives by Day 43, and the new prevention plan will not even reach regulators until the first quarter of 2027.

The question now is whether Seres can sign a licensing partner before its cash runs out at the end of March 2027. Either the new Nature Medicine publication and colitis plan attract a pharmaceutical partner to fund the trials, or the company must seek emergency financing on harsh terms. A partnership announcement before the end of the first quarter of 2027 will decide it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐧
Seres Therapeutics develops oral bacterial drugs to prevent infections and gut inflammation in cancer patients. While seeking a partner to fund its clinical trials, the biotechnology group has cut its operating costs and exited excess lab and office space in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

In July, the company agreed to end its lease at 200 Sidney Street, which "materially eliminates the Company’s obligations under the lease as of December 31, 2026". That agreement triggered a $5.7 million non-cash accounting charge this quarter, following a $5.8 million charge for shrinking another lease in the second quarter.

• Operating expenses excluding lease charges: $11.0 million, down 51.6% from a year ago by our math
• Research and development: $5.6 million, down 55.7% from a year ago
• General and administrative costs: $5.4 million, down 42.5% from a year ago

These reductions matter because Seres has collected its final milestone payment from selling VOWST, its first approved gut drug, to Nestlé Health Science. Lower overhead and smaller rent bills starting in 2027 will stretch its remaining cash while management negotiates with potential partners.

What to watch: first-quarter 2027 operating expenses, once the 200 Sidney Street lease ends on December 31. Another drop in quarterly spending would give management more time to sign a partnership deal.

🟢 𝐍𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐦-𝐂𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚
SER-155 is the company's main experimental drug, a capsule of cultivated bacteria designed to protect the gut lining and stop dangerous bacteria from entering the bloodstream. Its most advanced use is in adults receiving stem-cell transplants from donors (allo-HCT) to treat blood cancer.

On November 3, the medical journal Nature Medicine published the full results from the drug's Phase 1b trial in 34 transplant patients. Patients taking SER-155 had a 77% lower relative risk of bacterial bloodstream infections than those on placebo, and they spent an average of 11.9 fewer days on systemic antibiotics.

Peer-reviewed publication validates the science for potential pharmaceutical partners, because infections are a leading cause of death in the first 100 days after a transplant. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has already agreed to the Phase 2 trial design, which includes an early data check after half the patients finish.

What to watch: any partnership or licensing announcement for SER-155 before the end of the first quarter of 2027. Securing external funding would allow the company to start the Phase 2 transplant study immediately.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐳𝐞𝐧 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐋𝐞𝐟𝐭
Despite holding FDA agreement on its Phase 2 stem-cell transplant study since early 2026, Seres still cannot afford to start the trial on its own. Interim chief executive Richard Kender said: "We continue to seek capital through partnerships and other sources to advance our programs in irEC and in allo-HCT, which is Phase 2 ready, pending funding."

The drugmaker ended September with $17.5 million in cash and collected its final $12.5 million VOWST buyout payment from Nestlé in October. That $30.0 million total by our math covers operations only through the first quarter of 2027, leaving five months from the November release date to find new money.

Every clinical program in the pipeline now carries a "dependent on funding" condition, including the newly announced colitis prevention study and the SER-428 liquid formulation. Because the company has no remaining payments due from Nestlé, it has no internal cash source left to extend its timeline.

What to watch: financing or partnership disclosures before March 31, 2027. Entering 2027 without a partner would force the company to raise money on unfavorable terms or halt clinical operations.

🔴 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐨𝐢𝐝𝐬 𝐛𝐲 𝐃𝐚𝐲 𝟒𝟑
Seres is expanding SER-155 into immune checkpoint inhibitor-related enterocolitis (irEC), severe gut inflammation and diarrhea caused by cancer immunotherapies such as Keytruda. In July, the company reported that 12 of 15 patients (80%) in an investigator-run treatment study at Memorial Sloan Kettering achieved a clinical response at Day 15 without immunosuppressive drugs.

Detailed slide data this quarter show a less durable picture by Day 43. Only 5 of the 15 patients (33.3% by our math) stayed completely off immunosuppressive drugs through Day 43, while 7 of the 12 initial responders (58.3% by our math) "received non-systemically acting, gastrointestinal-targeted immunosuppressives for mild residual or moderate recurrent symptoms".

This cuts against the headline claim of an immunosuppressive-free treatment, because over half the responders still needed gut-targeted steroids within six weeks. That recurring inflammation helps explain why management now wants to give SER-155 earlier to prevent colitis rather than treat active cases.

What to watch: the FDA's feedback on the proposed colitis prevention study after the first-quarter 2027 submission. If regulators require a large trial to prove prevention, the cost will exceed what Seres can fund alone.

🔴 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐮𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐩𝐬
Following the 15-patient treatment trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering, Seres decided to develop SER-155 to prevent colitis in cancer patients starting immunotherapy, rather than treating it after symptoms begin. Kender said: "We also think this development approach offers a time and capital efficient path to clinical data."

However, the company will not submit the study design to the FDA until the first quarter of 2027—the same quarter its cash runs out. Furthermore, the release notes that optimizing the preventive dose "could include a healthy volunteer study component or a dosing lead-in element" before testing the broader cancer population.

Testing prevention takes more patients than testing treatment, because moderate-to-severe colitis only strikes about 25% of immunotherapy patients, so 75% would not get severe symptoms anyway. Adding a dose-finding lead-in further delays clinical results.

What to watch: the final trial design and patient enrollment target after FDA discussions in early 2027. A mandatory lead-in study would push meaningful efficacy data well into 2028.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟓.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Total current and long-term lease obligations fell 36.9% from last quarter and 56.9% from $83.0 million at the end of 2025, by our math. Exiting the 200 Sidney Street building and shrinking the 101 Cambridgepark Drive lease removed $47.2 million in future rent liabilities, reducing fixed cash drain starting in 2027.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟗.𝟗𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Weighted average diluted shares rose 13.8% from 8.77 million a year ago and 2.4% from the second quarter. The increase stems from at-the-market stock sales completed in late 2025 and ongoing employee stock compensation, diluting existing shareholders while the biotech group searches for non-dilutive partnership capital.

𝐆𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟗𝟑 𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐚𝐧𝐝  ⇘ decelerating
Grant revenue rose 68.9% from $351 thousand a year ago, when the award began, but dipped 19.4% from $736 thousand in the second quarter. The money comes from CARB-X, a non-profit accelerator funding SER-428, a liquid bacterial drug for intensive-care patients on feeding tubes.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐑𝐮𝐧𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐐𝟏 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from Through Q1 2027
Unchanged. Seres still expects its $17.5 million in September cash plus the $12.5 million received from Nestlé in October to fund operations through March 2027. Deep cuts to research, overhead, and facility leases kept the timeline intact without adding extra quarters. The forecast excludes any money from future partnerships or stock sales.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐧𝐨 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐄𝐑-𝟏𝟓𝟓 𝐲𝐞𝐭?
SER-155 holds FDA Breakthrough Therapy status, an agreed Phase 2 stem-cell transplant protocol since January 2026, and a Nature Medicine publication, yet remains unpartnered with two quarters of cash left.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟎 𝐒𝐢𝐝𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?
Terminating the lease removed $20.9 million in balance-sheet lease liabilities this quarter, but management has not disclosed the exact dollar reduction in annual cash rent starting in 2027.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞 𝐦𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐞?
Because moderate-to-severe colitis affects only about 25% of immunotherapy patients, proving prevention requires a much larger sample size than the 15-patient treatment trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐨𝐢𝐝𝐬?
Slide 16 reveals that 7 of the 12 Day-15 responders received gut-targeted immunosuppressives by Day 43 for residual or recurrent symptoms, raising questions about how long a 12-day SER-155 course lasts.

text:
A 21-year-old nursing student packed her car, lied to professors about a family bereavement, and drove deep into the freezing White Mountains of New Hampshire, only to spin out into a snowbank, turn away a passing school bus driver offering help, and vanish off a remote highway in under ten minutes.

The reason might surprise you.

On the afternoon of February 9, 2004, Maura Murray, an academically accomplished junior nursing student and track athlete at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, emptied her bank account of $280, bought alcohol at a local liquor store, and sent an email to her professors claiming she would be away for a week due to a death in the family, a claim her relatives later confirmed was completely fabricated.

Driving her black 1996 Saturn sedan north toward the White Mountains, Maura had no declared itinerary, hotel reservation, or confirmed passenger.

Around 7:27 PM, as darkness fell over Route 112 in Woodsville (Haverhill), New Hampshire, her car failed to negotiate a sharp, unlit curve near the Wild Ammonoosuc River, spinning out and striking a snowbank on the shoulder:

Local resident and school bus driver Butch Atwood lived down the road and pulled up in his bus to check on the crash.

He found a young woman inside, shivering and shaking, with deployed airbags. She pleaded with him not to call the police or AAA, claiming she had already called roadside assistance herself.

Knowing there was zero cellular coverage in that mountain notch, Atwood drove straight to his house nearby to phone 911.

When Haverhill Police Officer Cecil Smith arrived on scene at 7:46 PM, just nineteen minutes after the 911 dispatch, the Saturn was locked, its windshield was cracked on the driver’s side, and a rag had been deliberately stuffed into the tailpipe.

Maura was gone.

No footprints led away through the heavy waist-deep snowbanks lining the road, indicating she had either walked along the frozen asphalt or stepped into an unidentified vehicle.

The subsequent search became one of the most scrutinized missing-persons investigations in modern history, sparking the rise of true-crime crowdsourcing and internet sleuth communities:

The Stuffed Exhaust: Investigators discovered a clean white rag wedged into the car's tailpipe. Her father, Fred Murray, explained that he had instructed her to plug the pipe if she parked idling to suppress thick exhaust smoke coming from the failing cylinder, though speculation persisted that someone else may have tampered with it.

The Scent Track: Bloodhounds picked up Maura’s scent from her running gloves, tracking it roughly 100 yards east down Route 112 before the trail abruptly vanished in the middle of the roadway, a classic indicator that she likely got into a passing car, whether voluntarily seeking shelter from the sub-zero chill or falling prey to an opportunistic predator.

The A-Frame House & False Leads: Over the years, searchers combed hundreds of square miles of dense forest, drained ponds, and used ground-penetrating radar on properties across Grafton County, including an excavated basement in an A-frame home where rumor claimed she was buried. Every dig and canine alert returned negative for human remains.

Theories continue to divide federal investigators, state police, and amateur detectives:

Did she flee into the woods fearing a DUI arrest after two car accidents in forty-eight hours, succumbing to paradoxical undressing and terminal hypothermia in an uncharted crevice?

Did a passing local or opportunistic serial offender offer her a ride out of the freezing weather, only to murder her miles away?

Or did she orchestrate a calculated escape to vanish off the grid and forge an entirely new identity across the Canadian border?

Over two decades later, Maura Murray’s case remains open, an enduring emblem of the internet era’s obsession with unresolved disappearances.

text:
“One man’s impact”

When my wife was 16 she found a small lump in her neck. Two days later she was in the care of St Jude’s Children’s Research Hospital in Memphis TN. She was treated for Hodgkins Lymphoma for 9 months and has been cancer free since. She was 16 at the time. Her family never received a bill- for anything. For 15 years she has been cancer free she has gone back for annual checkups and as a St Jude For Life patient where they evaluate long term impacts of treatment to improve data and study the impact those treatments have on patients. The hospital puts her up in their on-campus housing and offers to reimburse travel. Again, no cost to patients or their family. 

Between appointments I had time yesterday to stop into a memorial building for founder Danny Thomas. He was an actor from the 1930’s and on. He appeared in a major sitcom and would later go on to produce the Andy Griffith and Dick Van Dyke shows. He had $10 left to his name in 1937 and prayed to St Jude that if he could make $70 he would someday dedicate his life to the work of the Saint. He dropped $7 of his last $10 in the offering tray. The next day he got a toothpaste advertising gig for $75. 20 years later he continued to dwell on his promise and the American Lebanese Syrian Associated Charities (ALSAC) was founded by Danny Thomas in 1957. He called himself a “noble beggar”. He eventually had enough money to build a hospital for treating children with childhood cancer where they don’t have to pay a dime in 1962. Tens of thousands of children have been treated since and childhood cancer survival has gone from 20% in 1960’s to over 80% today. 

As we stood in the building there was a display where you could write a note on what inspired you at St. Jude. I wrote “One man’s impact”. One man leaned his time and resources and potential into something that changed the world. 

In 1962 when the hospital opened and was dedicated Danny said “If I die tomorrow I will know why I lived”. I hope you all know and have the ability to execute your purpose here with the time you’ve been given.

text:
If you really, really think a country wouldn’t accept a massive amount of free territory taken from one of its biggest enemies just because of racism, then there’s honestly no point in arguing with you. 

I’ll give you one last real-life historical example.

France literally allied with the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century to fight the Habsburgs. A Catholic kingdom cooperated militarily with a Muslim empire despite centuries of religious hostility between Christian Europe and the Ottomans. France even allowed the Ottoman navy to use one of its ports.

Now, do you think the average religious French person suddenly started loving Muslims? No, they fucking didn’t. France simply recognized that the Ottoman Empire was a useful ally against a common enemy.

That’s literally the same logic I’m applying to Marley and the Middle East Alliance. The Middle East Alliance was already at war with Marley. Marley was their enemy, just as the Habsburgs were enemies of both France and the Ottomans. If Paradis offered to use the Founding Titan to destroy Marley’s military and then give the Middle East Alliance a huge portion of Marleyan territory, why would they automatically reject that offer?

They wouldn’t need to suddenly love Eldians, just as France didn’t need to suddenly love Muslims to cooperate with the Ottomans. They would simply need to recognize that working with Paradis against Marley could serve their interests.

And here’s another example: Britain and France fought each other for centuries before eventually allying against Russia in the Crimean War.

Do you seriously think the British and French suddenly forgot centuries of hostility and started loving each other? Of course not. They had a common enemy, and cooperation was more beneficial than continuing their rivalry.

Now apply that exact same principle to Hizuru, Paradis, and the Middle East Alliance. Marley was already hostile to the Middle East Alliance, and Hizuru already had ties to Paradis. All three had potential reasons to cooperate against Marley. Paradis could provide the military power through the Founding Titan, while Hizuru and the Middle East Alliance could provide diplomatic recognition, economic cooperation, and international support.

And unlike those historical examples, Paradis wouldn’t even be asking the Middle East Alliance to fight a massive war against Marley. The Founding Titan could do the military work, and the Middle East Alliance would receive territory from its defeated enemy in return for an agreement.

I’m not saying racism against Eldians would magically disappear. I’m saying that racism doesn’t automatically override every political, military, and economic interest a country has.

The Middle East Alliance wouldn’t have to like Eldians. It would only have to prefer gaining territory and weakening Marley over continuing to fight a devastating war against it.

You can argue that such an agreement would be difficult to negotiate, that other countries might intervene, or that the alliance might eventually collapse. Those are reasonable objections. But acting like the Middle East Alliance would automatically refuse an enormously beneficial deal simply because its people hate Eldians ignores how countries have behaved throughout history.

Countries don’t need to be friends to have common interests. That’s the entire point.

text:
1) The Hitchhiker’s Guide To What Last Night Means On Capitol Hill
 
Political observers will rank the midterm elections of 2026 alongside the epic sea changes of 1994, 2010 and 2018. It’s generally thought that the 1994 midterm which propelled Newt Gingrich to the Speakership was the most seismic. That’s largely because Republicans hadn’t controlled the House in 40 years. But 2026 will likely rival 1994 simply because of how Democrats overperformed in House races in Trump-favored districts, overcame redistricting in Texas and Florida which Republicans designed as a firewall to safeguard their majority and the fact that Democrats won in states like South Carolina and Kansas which are typically lay-ups for Republicans.
 
It’s always about the math. But this is also about the MAP Don’t forget that heading into this cycle, 23 of the 35 seats favored Republicans. On paper, this looked like an easy year for the GOP.
 
The question is just how large the margins might be for Democrats – and what that means when it comes to working – or not working – with President Trump. The President has signaled he’ll veto extreme measures which comes from Congress under Democratic control. But also offered to work together on certain issues.
 
Democrats could argue the vote was a mandate to rebuke the President. Some won’t be willing to work with him at all. President Trump is out the door in a little less than two years. He suffered historic losses in states and districts which he carried by double digits two years ago. Democrats are already threatening administration officials that they had better “lawyer up,” promising a host of inquests into alleged corruption, influence peddling and questions about the administration by several cabinet officials.
 
Yes, there will be lots of attention trained on Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and DSA-affiliated members coming to Washington like Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-NY), Claire Valdez (D-NY), Melat Kiros (D-CO), Donavan McKinney (D-MI) and Chris Rabb (D-PA). They will push Medicare for all. An effort to defund ICE. They will oppose money and aid to Israel.
 
But how much of that truly gets across the finish line?
 
While Democrats made extraordinary gains in both the House and Senate, they did so with moderates. Newly-minted House Democrats who flipped solid GOP turf are the true majority makers. Not progressives. So while hard-left Democrats might pitch bills to pack the Supreme Court or convert Washington, DC and Puerto Rico into states, the pathways for those measures is challenging. Democrats – regardless of where they reside on the political spectrum – won on a message of affordability. Democrats must show they can move the meter on gas prices and the cost of groceries. Maybe make things better for farmers.
 
Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-OH) upset Rep. Mike Carey (R-OH) in central Ohio. Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke (D-WI) defeated Derrick Van Orden (R-WI). Rep.-elect Christine Bohannan (D-IA) defeated Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA). Rep.-elect Fred Wellman (D-MO) unexpectedly toppled Rep. Ann Wagner (R-MO). Democrats are just renting these districts for now. They will be in play again in 2028. However, for the first time in years, Democrats have seriously encroached into Republican turf in the Midwest and the south. That phenomenon is emphasized even more so by the victories of Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-KS), Josh Turek (D-IA) and Annie Andrews (D-SC). These moderates didn’t get there by tying themselves to the left. They can’t support some of the more extreme themes propounded by progressives and the DSA. So it’s doubtful those left-wing ideas go anywhere.
 
However, that sets the table for a schism between moderates and progressives and could spark an internecine firestorm inside the Democratic party.
 
That said, there is also another mathematic calculus at work.

MIDTERM ELECTION OUTCOMES: IMPACTS ON POWER & UTILITIES (BofA SUMMARY)

🔹 Federal policy: Democratic gains increase policy uncertainty for utilities but have limited immediate impact on regulated utility economics.

🔹 Permitting reform: A narrower path to bipartisan permitting reform could delay transmission, generation, pipeline and other infrastructure projects needed to meet rising electricity demand, with failure to pass legislation during the lame-duck session acting as a sector headwind.

🔹 State-level impact: State elections are more consequential because governors, legislatures and utility commissions directly influence large-load policy, authorized returns, capital recovery and regulatory oversight.

🔹 Georgia & Texas: The greatest incremental policy risks are in Georgia and Texas, where Democratic victories could bring tighter data center rules and greater uncertainty for utilities.

🔹 Other state risks: Ohio and Wisconsin face increased data center policy uncertainty, Kansas presents headline risk, while Iowa and Michigan appear more manageable due to an emphasis on formal customer protections and regulatory frameworks.

🔹 Regulatory continuity: Florida, Louisiana, North Dakota and Oklahoma offer more continuity-oriented regulatory environments, with NEE being a potential beneficiary of continued stability in Florida.

🔹 Stock implications (Southern Company): SO faces greater risk from Georgia policy changes.

🔹 Stock implications (American Electric Power & FirstEnergy): AEP and FE face reduced confidence in incremental Ohio data center growth.

🔹 Stock implications (Sempra, CenterPoint Energy, AEP, Entergy & Vistra): SRE, CNP, AEP, ETR and VST face greater Texas policy uncertainty.

text:
Texan arrested for selling Forced Reset Triggers in Florida

Skyeler “Bleau” Jackson, 24, says he is the first person ever charged with an eight-year-old Florida statute that may prohibit the possession of Forced Reset Triggers, or FRTs, which are completely legal in most other free states.

He may be right.

FRTs have long been a frequent target of the anti-gun media, which falsely claimed they turned rifles into machineguns. Thankfully, federal law now makes them legal, but a Florida state law still bans FRTs in the Sunshine State.

Florida’s poorly written statute certainly hasn’t been used much since 2018 when then-Governor Rick Scott—now a U.S. Senator—signed the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Act, which created the law.

FRTs aren’t even mentioned in the statute, which bans “bump-fire stocks” as well as anything else that can “alter the rate of fire of a firearm to mimic automatic weapon fire or which is used to increase the rate of fire to a faster rate than is possible for a person to fire such semiautomatic firearm unassisted by a kit, a tool, an accessory, or a device.”

Whether FRTs are even illegal in Florida is a judgement call, which in Jackson’s case was made by investigators working for the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office.

No one from the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office even told Jackson what he allegedly did wrong, as he sat in their county jail for nine days last February.

No one from the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office was even willing to discuss his case: Calls and emails for this story were not returned.

Jaskson, a native Texan who lives in San Antonio, learned in court that he faces up to 10 years in prison and $10,000 in fines if he is convicted of two counts of violating the “bump-fire stock” statute for selling FRTs to “undercover” sheriff’s deputies at a West Palm Beach gun show.

“I was arrested February 11th. The warrant was signed. There were three charges: Two counts of possession of a bump stock and one count of possession of a firearm in commission of a felony, which was dropped,” Jackson said. “I didn’t have any bump stocks. I am the first person ever charged with that statute since the law has been in place. Essentially, they made a huge mistake.”

The arrest

Jackson sold a few FRTs at a West Palm Beach gun show in early February. He was stopped in his dad’s car near the event.

“The deputy told me I had a taillight out. He said, ‘Can I show you?’ I got out and he arrested me and like 14 cars pulled up—all blacked-out SUVs. There were five cops on me. They took off my jewelry and asked me if I had any explosives, like I was some kind of terrorist. There was one guy in charge. He was wearing a fisherman’s shirt. He asked if there were any guns in the car—after I had just left a gun show. That was the beginning of the end of it,” Jackson said.

There wasn’t much of an interrogation during the car stop. The detective in charge offered only confusing questions.

“He said the only way I was gonna get out of it was if I could name gang members. Gang members? I’m from Texas. I told him I didn’t know anything about that,” Jackson said. “He told me I was going to jail, and my bond would be around $2,000, which was total BS.”

Palm Beach County deputies took Jackson to their jail, where he was stripped, searched, fingerprinted and photographed. He ended up in a holding cell with another inmate. The next day he was taken to his bond hearing. He waited his turn and watched inmate after inmate appear before the judge. Almost all had been arrested for battering their spouse. Their bonds were $200 or nothing at all.

“Then it was my turn. The prosecutor said, ‘Look at all these bump stocks we’ve recovered’—I never had a single bump stock. My bond was going to be $175,000, but my attorney negotiated it down to $70,000,” Jackson said.

Jackson was able to secure his release after spending nine days in the county jail.

“They never told me what I was supposed to have done wrong,” he said. “I don’t think the judge even knew what the statute was or what it meant.”

According to Sheriff’s Office reports, deputies were working “undercover” at the gun show when they were told that a vendor—Jackson—was selling FRTs.

Jackson reportedly had a video at his booth that showed how the triggers operated. Reports claim he told the “undercover” investigators that the FRTs were easy to install on their firearms. He also showed them documents on his phone that proved they were legal.

Florida lawmakers introduced a bill during the last legislative session that would have repealed section 790.222—the “bump-fire stock” statute. Unfortunately, the bill died in the House Criminal Justice Subcommittee

For now, the charges against Jackson stand.

Takeaways

Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw has spent 53 years in law enforcement. At 78 years old, he is one of the oldest active law enforcement officials in the country.

While most Florida sheriffs are Republicans, Bradshaw is a registered Democrat, which may explain why he would prioritize gun-show enforcement.

Jackson has been studying the charges he faces since his arrest.

He has been told the “undercover” deputies took a video of the actual sale, but he hasn’t seen it yet.

Said Jackson: “My big takeaway is that I don’t have a takeaway yet. When this is all over, I’ll have it. I’m not bitter, I just want to know more or less why I was targeted for FRTs, especially in Florida.”

text:
Two men dressed as cops spent 81 minutes in a Boston museum and left with $500 million in art.

The FBI calls it the largest property theft in U.S. history.

It happened early on March 18, 1990, at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. The men posed as Boston police officers, got inside and restrained the guards in the basement.

They took 13 works, including a Vermeer and a Rembrandt.

The museum's chief of security says $500 million is likely an underestimate.

The museum offers $10 million for all 13 works in good condition. The FBI does not pay the reward.

The FBI believes the works are hidden, likely in several places. Some, it says, moved to Maine, Connecticut and possibly mid Atlantic states about 20 years ago. It adds that it could be wrong.

No one has been charged. The FBI says it cannot discuss specific people it has investigated.

What is unclear: where the works are, whether they survive, and who the thieves were.

Empty frames still hang where the paintings were.

81 minutes inside. 13 works gone. $500 million in art, and none of it found.
